Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत By mid-2026, most non-trivial agent work is done by several agents cooperating — a research agent hands off to a writer, a billing agent talks to a support agent from a different vendor, an orchestrator delegates to a specialist inside another org's cloud. A2A (Agent-to-Agent) is the open protocol that lets those agents find each other, describe what they can do, and hand tasks back and forth — even when they were built on different frameworks by different teams. Where MCP connects an agent to its tools and data, A2A connects an agent to another agent. They compose; they don't compete. What you'll learn State exactly what A2A is for — and where the MCP boundary sits Read an Agent Card and know what a receiving agent will do with it Walk a task through all eight lifecycle states, including the two that are interrupted rather than terminal Choose between SSE streaming and webhook push for long-running tasks Recognize the non-obvious features: signed cards, multi-tenant endpoints, and structured data parts आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-07-20। A2A is stabilizing but the spec still evolves: the v1.0.1 release, new bindings, and SDK feature gaps land regularly. Treat exact method names, error codes, and SDK support claims below as perishable and check the linked spec and the a2aproject/A2A repo before shipping a production integration. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

Every agent framework — LangGraph, CrewAI, the Claude Agent SDK, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft's Agent Framework, custom in-house loops — solved tool use by leaning on the model's native tool-calling and, increasingly, on MCP as the universal tool-and-data connector. That gave us agent ↔ tool. What none of them solved on their own was agent ↔ agent across a boundary. Two problems kept coming up: Discovery. How does agent A know that agent B exists, what it can do, how to authenticate against it, and whether it supports streaming? A hand-rolled README is not a protocol. Task hand-off. Once A wants B to do something, how do they exchange the work (not the model's chat) — including files, structured data, progress updates, and the fact that B might need to pause and ask A for input? Framework-specific answers (LangGraph subgraphs, CrewAI crews, subagents inside one runtime) work great inside one process. They stop at the org boundary. A2A is the piece that lets an agent in your product delegate to an agent in someone else's product without either side leaking its internals — Google's Todd Segal calls it "the secure foundation for personal, team, and domain-specific agents to work together seamlessly across any platform." Governance sits with the Linux Foundation, and by April 2026 the project reported 150+ supporting organizations including AWS, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, and IBM.

Both are open protocols. Both use JSON over HTTP. They solve different problems and are designed to compose: MCP = agent-to-tool. An MCP server exposes tools (search, read_file, run_query) and resources (docs, prompts) to a model-driven client. The client is an agent; the server is a passive capability provider. See MCP & connecting to tools for how Claude uses it. A2A = agent-to-agent. An A2A endpoint exposes an agent — an entity with its own reasoning loop that will decide how to solve a delegated task. Both sides are agents; either can call the other. The concrete difference shows up in the wire format. An MCP tools/call returns a result and closes. An A2A SendMessage opens a task — a stateful thing with its own lifecycle that can stream updates, ask for clarification, or run for hours in the background. If your endpoint's answer is always "here's the result of one function," it's a tool — publish it via MCP. If it's "let me think about that and get back to you, and I might need to ask a follow-up question," it's an agent — publish it via A2A. Most serious systems will run both: an agent whose inside uses MCP to reach tools, and whose outside speaks A2A so peers can hand it work.
documents.s: MCP vs. A2A — the mental model

documents.t: An Agent Card is a JSON document served at a well-known URL that tells any potential caller everything they need to talk to your agent. Think OpenAPI + robots.txt, for agents. Every A2A interaction starts by fetching one. The card includes: Identity — id, name, description, provider (org details). Endpoints — the service URLs and which protocol bindings (JSON-RPC, gRPC, REST) are available. Capabilities — feature flags: streaming, pushNotifications, extendedAgentCard. Skills — declared agent functions with input/output schemas (this is what B says it can do). Security schemes — one or more of APIKey, HTTPAuth (Basic/Bearer), OAuth2 (Authorization Code, Client Credentials, Device Code), OpenIdConnect, MutualTLS. The caller reads this to know what credentials to bring before the first call. Signature — an optional cryptographic signature over the card. That last field is the one worth pausing on. A Signed Agent Card lets a receiving agent verify that the card was actually issued by the domain owner — the DNS/PKI equivalent of "yes, this really is agents.acme.com, not something an attacker planted." Combined with mTLS auth, it closes the door on rogue Agent Cards being served from spoofed hosts, which is how you'd otherwise get a prompt injection at the discovery layer: an attacker's Agent Card lying about what tools it exposes and what data it wants.
documents.s: The Agent Card — the piece of the spec that matters most

documents.t: Once you SendMessage to an A2A agent, the work becomes a Task — a first-class object with an ID you can poll, subscribe to, cancel, or list. The task moves through eight states, and it's worth noticing that only five are terminal: SUBMITTED — the server acknowledged the task. WORKING — active processing. INPUT_REQUIRED — interrupted: the agent needs more information from the caller. Not an error; expected in real workflows. AUTH_REQUIRED — interrupted: the agent needs the caller to authenticate (or re-authenticate) before it can continue. COMPLETED — success. Terminal. FAILED — error. Terminal. CANCELED — caller-initiated cancellation. Terminal. REJECTED — the agent declined the task (policy, capability, quota). Terminal. The interrupted states are the point. Legacy RPC assumes one call → one result. Real agent work looks like "start the analysis, come back an hour later, notice I need to ask a clarifying question, wait for the answer, resume, finish." A2A models that natively. Your calling code has to be a small state machine, not a synchronous await.

Long-running tasks need a way to deliver updates. A2A gives you two async models — pick per task, not per agent: Streaming (SendStreamingMessage / SubscribeToTask). Server-Sent Events over the open HTTP connection. Client stays connected, receives TaskStatusUpdateEvent and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent in order. Great for interactive UIs and short-to-medium tasks. Falls over if the client can't hold a connection (mobile, serverless, browser tabs going to sleep). Push notifications (webhook config). The client registers a webhook via CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig. The server POSTs updates to that URL as they happen. The client can be totally offline in between. This is the mode for tasks that outlive an HTTP connection — think "run this overnight" or "call me back when the batch job finishes." Both require the agent to advertise support in its Agent Card (capabilities.streaming: true and/or capabilities.pushNotifications: true). A conforming caller checks first and downgrades cleanly.

An A2A Message is composed of one or more Parts. Each Part can be one of: text — string content (the chat-y part). raw — binary file, base64-encoded in JSON. url — a reference to an external file (avoids inlining huge blobs). data — a structured JSON object or array, with an optional metadata map. The data part is what makes A2A useful for machine-to-machine work. Two agents can exchange typed payloads — an order, a purchase spec, a JSON diff — without pretending to have a natural-language conversation about it. This is also what makes protocols like Agent Payments (AP2) layer cleanly on top of A2A: the payment intent rides in a data part with a known schema.

This one is easy to miss. A single A2A endpoint can host many agents, served through the GetExtendedAgentCard method after authentication. A SaaS vendor can offer one URL and return different, tenant-specific Agent Cards depending on which API key or OAuth scope the caller presents. From the caller's side it looks like one endpoint per agent; from the vendor's side it's one deployment. If you're building agent-serving infrastructure, this is the pattern that lets you scale without one hostname per tenant.
documents.s: Multi-tenant endpoints — one URL, many agents

documents.t: The full protocol has a lot of surface, but the happy-path flow is short: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Discover⌄ Fetch the Agent Card from a well-known URL. Verify its signature if one is present. Read `capabilities`, `skills`, and `securitySchemes` to decide whether this agent can do what you need and what auth you'll bring. ←PreviousNext→ 2Authenticate⌄ Obtain the credential the card asked for — an API key, an OAuth2 token, an mTLS cert. If you're going to talk to many agents, cache tokens; A2A doesn't dictate a session model. ←PreviousNext→ 3Send the message⌄ Call `a2a.SendMessage` (or `a2a.SendStreamingMessage` for SSE) with a Message composed of Parts. You get back a `taskId`. ←PreviousNext→ 4Track⌄ Choose: hold the SSE stream open, or poll `a2a.GetTask` by ID, or register a webhook via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig`. Handle `INPUT_REQUIRED` and `AUTH_REQUIRED` by responding with follow-up messages, not by treating them as failures. ←PreviousNext→ 5Consume the result⌄ On `COMPLETED`, read the `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent` payloads for outputs. On `FAILED` / `REJECTED`, inspect the error code — the spec defines typed errors like `ContentTypeNotSupportedError`, `UnsupportedOperationError`, `VersionNotSupportedError`, and `ExtensionSupportRequiredError`. ←PreviousNext→

Discovery is just an HTTP GET. This is the shape of a request a client would make to inspect a candidate agent before ever sending it work: Fetch and inspect an Agent Card CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ GET https://agents.example.com/.well-known/agent.json Accept: application/json # Response (abbreviated): # { # "id": "acme/support-router", # "name": "Acme Support Router", # "provider": {"organization": "Acme, Inc."}, # "endpoints": [ # {"url": "https://agents.example.com/a2a", "protocol": "jsonrpc"} # ], # "capabilities": { # "streaming": true, # "pushNotifications": true, # "extendedAgentCard": true # }, # "skills": [ # {"id": "route_ticket", "inputSchema": {...}, "outputSchema": {...}} # ], # "securitySchemes": { # "primary": {"type": "oauth2", "flows": {...}} # }, # "signature": {"alg": "EdDSA", "value": "..."} # } Note what's not in the card: nothing about the model behind the agent, its prompt, its tools, or its private state. That opacity is deliberate — A2A treats a peer agent as a black box you delegate work to, not a system you introspect.

Treating INPUT_REQUIRED as an error. It isn't; it's the protocol asking your code to respond. If your caller code only branches on "did it succeed or fail," you'll break every interactive workflow. Ignoring the Agent Card's capabilities. Sending a streaming request to an agent that didn't advertise streaming: true gets you an UnsupportedOperationError. Read the card, downgrade cleanly. Assuming the streaming connection is durable. Mobile clients, serverless runtimes, browser tabs — they all drop the SSE connection. For anything longer than "a chat turn," prefer push notifications. Skipping signature verification because it's optional. If you're consuming Agent Cards from outside your org, verify the signature — otherwise you've created a discovery-layer prompt injection vector. Confusing A2A with MCP. Publishing an A2A endpoint for a stateless single-shot function is overkill; that's a tool, and MCP is the right protocol. Publishing an MCP tool for something that takes minutes and needs to ask clarifying questions is under-engineering; that's an agent, and A2A is the right protocol. Check yourself 0/4

Put together with the rest of the agent picture: Inside an agent, MCP is how you reach tools and data — including remote MCP servers you didn't write. Between agents in one framework, you use whatever the framework gives you — subagents in Claude Code, LangGraph subgraphs, CrewAI crews, etc. This is fastest but locks you to one runtime. Between agents across frameworks, teams, or vendors, A2A is what you reach for. Read Open-Source AI Agent Frameworks for the runtime side; A2A is the wire between those runtimes. The rule of thumb: if the boundary is a process boundary, framework-native handoffs are fine. If it's an org, cloud, or trust boundary, use A2A.
documents.s: Where A2A sits in your stack

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत What you'll learn Understand what 'memory' means in this class of tool: not a saved transcript, but observations extracted by a second model that watches your tool calls Learn the six-hook lifecycle and the exit-code contract that decides whether a broken memory layer degrades quietly or blocks your coding session See the detail almost nobody checks: the observer is a separate model on a provider you choose, and claude-mem's own cost dataset maps its hosted observer to a DeepSeek model — your session content does not necessarily go to Claude Follow the three-layer recall that makes the token arithmetic work — a ~50-100-token index hit before a ~500-1,000-token detail fetch — and why that ordering is the whole design Know where the data lands: SQLite with FTS5, a Chroma vector store that indexes every extracted fact separately, and a worker on port 37700 + (uid % 100) Work out who pays for the compression, and why a $30/month hosted tier exists at all Avoid five documented failure modes, starting with the one where the observer's reasoning tokens ate the session's output budget Apply an eight-point evaluation checklist to any agent memory layer before you let it read every file your agent touches Every coding-agent user hits the same wall. You spend an hour establishing context — which module owns what, why the previous approach failed, the one gotcha in the build — and then the session ends and all of it is gone. Tomorrow you explain it again. claude-mem is the most popular answer to that problem by a very wide margin: 103,252 stars on GitHub as of 26 October 2026, Apache-2.0, and shipping fast enough that it went from v13.38 to v15.2.1 in the twelve days before this page was written. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity, Claude Desktop and several others. This page is not an install guide — the README does that well. It is the thing the README does not do: explain what the tool actually is architecturally, what it costs, what reads your code, and what breaks. Most of what follows comes from the repository's own docs/ folder, which is detailed, honest, and almost certainly unread by the large majority of those 103,000 stargazers. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-10-26। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। स्रोत: Primary: the thedotmack/claude-mem repository — README.md, docs/architecture-overview.md (hook table and timeouts, data flow, worker port formula, SQLite schema, Chroma document naming, dedup hash, generator restart backoff, the exit-0/exit-2 degradation contract, the two session-id types), docs/security.md (cmem_ key prefix, SHA-256 storage, the local-dev bypass requiring two env vars, BullMQ/Redis notes), docs/ip-boundary.md (the open-core split), docs/expense-pricing/README.md (the cmem-observer to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash mapping on/after 2026-08-08, and the ~98%-input working shape), and the GitHub release notes for v15.0.0, v15.0.2, v15.1.0, v15.2.0 and v15.2.1. Star count (103,252), licence (Apache-2.0), creation date (2025-08-31) and last push (2026-10-26) verified via the GitHub API on 2026-10-26. Pricing ($30/month after a 30-day trial) and the 'moves memory generation off your primary agent's subscription' framing are from cmem.ai. This project ships multiple releases per week and renames features between majors — treat every specific port, flag, command, default and price here as a snapshot, and check the current release notes before relying on one. The architecture-overview hook table lists Setup plus five lifecycle events; the README describes six hooks including UserPromptSubmit and Stop separately. Where the two disagree, this page follows architecture-overview.md and says so.
documents.s: The Third-Party Memory Layer: How claude-mem Actually Works

documents.t: The first mental model to discard is "it saves my chats". It does not. The unit of storage is an observation: a structured note with a type, a title and a narrative, extracted by a model from what your agent did. The flow, from the repo's own data-flow diagram: You submit a prompt. The session-init handler registers the session and asks the worker for semantically relevant context. Your agent uses a tool. The PostToolUse hook posts that tool usage to the worker, which enqueues it. The worker's SDKAgent — a model session, running in a background daemon — reads the queue and produces observations and summaries. Those land in SQLite, get synced into a Chroma vector store, and get broadcast to a local UI over server-sent events. So the thing watching your work is a second model, and the thing it reads is every tool call: file reads, file writes, command output, search results. That is the price of admission for this entire category of tool, and it is worth saying plainly before any of the rest. What you'll learn A memory layer is not a storage feature. It is a second model with a standing subscription to everything your first model touches. Evaluate it the way you would evaluate adding any model to your pipeline — what it reads, where it sends it, who pays for its tokens, and what happens when it fails.
documents.s: What it stores is not your transcript

documents.t: claude-mem installs as a set of lifecycle hooks, each invoked as a single shell-free command of the form claude-mem hook claude-code <event>. Per docs/architecture-overview.md: Event Handler What it does Timeout Setup version-check.js Sub-100 ms version-marker check; prints a hint to run npx claude-mem repair on mismatch 60s SessionStart worker start + context Starts the worker service and injects prior context 60s UserPromptSubmit session-init Registers the session, starts the SDK agent, semantic injection 60s PostToolUse observation Captures tool usage and enqueues it in the worker 120s Summary summarize Requests a session summary from the SDK agent 120s SessionEnd session-complete Ends the session and drains pending messages 30s Now the part that will matter to you at 2 a.m. The hook orchestrator implements an explicit degradation contract: Transport errors — ECONNREFUSED, timeouts, 5xx from the worker — exit 0. Non-blocking. The worker being down never blocks your coding session. Client bugs — 4xx, TypeError, ReferenceError — exit 2. Blocking, on the stated reasoning that these indicate a bug needing a fix. That is a defensible design, and it has a consequence worth internalising: "the memory daemon is dead" is harmless, but "the memory daemon is answering 400" is not. A malformed request, a schema drift after a partial upgrade, or an expired key that surfaces as a 4xx is in the category the tool deliberately chose to make loud. This is also why the Setup hook nags about npx claude-mem repair after an external plugin upgrade — a version-skewed install is exactly how you reach the blocking branch. Watch out If a coding session starts failing immediately after you updated a plugin, check your memory layer before you debug your agent. The published contract here is that transport failures degrade silently and client-side failures block — so the symptom of a half-upgraded install is a session that will not start, not a session without memory.
documents.s: The six hooks, and the one contract that matters operationally

documents.t: Any memory system can store things. The hard part is retrieval that does not cost more context than it saves — dump twenty remembered notes into every session start and you have made the problem worse. claude-mem's answer, shipped as the default in v15.0.0 on 20 October 2026 under the name Smart memory search, is a three-step search the agent reasons through rather than a single retrieval: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Search the compact index⌄ A full-text query (SQLite FTS5, optionally hybridised with Chroma vectors) returns a compact list of hits with observation IDs. The README puts these at roughly 50-100 tokens per result — enough to judge relevance, not enough to be useful on its own. ←PreviousNext→ 2Inspect the timeline around what looks relevant⌄ Given a promising observation ID, fetch the chronological context around it. This is the step that distinguishes 'a note that matches your keywords' from 'the note that matches, plus what happened immediately before and after it'. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fetch full details for the selected IDs only⌄ Only now does the full observation text enter context, at roughly 500-1,000 tokens each. The README's claim for this ordering is about ~10x token savings versus fetching details up front. ←PreviousNext→ The three steps are exposed to the agent as MCP tools — search(query, type, date, project, limit), timeline(observation_id, query) and get_observations(ids[]) — which is why the agent can reason between them instead of the retrieval being a fixed pipeline. The transferable lesson here has nothing to do with claude-mem. Filter on cheap representations, then pay for detail on the survivors. It is the same pattern as reading a search-results page before opening a tab, the same pattern as a database index before a row fetch, and it is the correct shape for any retrieval you bolt onto an agent. If you are designing your own, see context engineering for the general framing and how agent memory actually works for the taxonomy this tool sits inside.
documents.s: The three-layer recall is the actual idea

documents.t: Everything local lands under ~/.claude-mem/. Two stores, with distinct jobs: SQLite (claude-mem.db), with FTS5 for full-text search: Table Purpose sdk_sessions Session lifecycle, and the mapping between the two session IDs observations The extracted notes: type, title, narrative, content hash session_summaries Per-session request / learned / completed user_prompts Your prompt history pending_messages The per-session work queue observation_feedback Usage signals per observation ChromaDB (chroma.sqlite3) for vector embeddings, accessed through chroma-mcp over stdio. The detail worth noticing: each observation produces several documents, not one — obs_{id}_narrative for the main text plus obs_{id}_fact_0, obs_{id}_fact_1 and so on for each extracted fact. Facts are embedded individually, which is why a query about one specific detail can retrieve an observation whose overall summary is about something else. The worker is an Express daemon on a per-user port: 37700 + (uid % 100). If you have seen localhost:37777 in the project's own release notes and docs, that is one uid's port, not a constant — which is a small thing that will cost you ten minutes exactly once. What you'll learn The worker binds a local HTTP API and serves a UI from it. docs/security.md is explicit that the server beta defaults to API-key auth, that keys use a cmem_ prefix and are shown once with only a SHA-256 hash stored, and that the loopback development bypass requires two environment variables set together (CLAUDE_MEM_AUTH_MODE=local-dev and CLAUDE_MEM_ALLOW_LOCAL_DEV_BYPASS=1) and must not be used behind a reverse proxy or on a publicly reachable bind address. Treat that as a hard rule: this daemon holds a searchable index of everything your agents read.

Here is the fact that most surprised me, and the reason this page exists. The observer is a separate model call, and you choose its provider at install time: npx claude-mem install --provider [host|openrouter|gemini|anthropic]. Four options, four different answers to "where does my session content go". The repository's own cost-accounting dataset, in docs/expense-pricing/README.md, documents how to price observer traffic — and in doing so documents what the hosted observer is. Its join recipe says to resolve the model id cmem-observer to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash on or after 2026-08-08, and to deepseek/deepseek-chat before that. There is an apparent contradiction here worth resolving, because you will hit it if you read the repo yourself: docs/architecture-overview.md labels the observer component SDKAgent (Claude Agent SDK), which sounds like it must be Claude. Both things are true at once. The Agent SDK is the harness — the loop that manages the session and parses responses — and it can be pointed at a non-Anthropic endpoint, which is exactly what the v15.0.2 release notes imply when they describe observer requests going to "OpenRouter, the cmem.ai gateway, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints". The SDK is the client; the provider flag decides who answers. Read the DeepSeek mapping carefully too, because it is easy to over- or under-state. It does not mean the project is hiding anything — the provider is a documented install flag and the dataset is published in the open repo. It does mean that a tool named claude-mem, on its hosted path, has been pricing its observer as a DeepSeek model, and that if your assumption was "this runs on Claude because of the name", the assumption was wrong. If your code cannot go to a third-party inference provider, --provider anthropic or a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoint is the choice you have to make deliberately. The same dataset also tells you the shape of that traffic: the project's own notes treat observer usage as roughly 98% input tokens, which is exactly what you would expect from a process whose job is reading tool output and emitting short notes. Prompt-heavy, output-light. And that is the whole economics of the hosted tier. The paid product, CMEM Pro, is described on cmem.ai as hosted observation and cloud sync at $30/month after a 30-day free trial, with the pitch that hosted observation moves memory generation off your primary agent's subscription. In other words: by default, something has to pay for a second model to read everything your first model does. Either that is your own provider account and plan limits, or it is $30/month to someone else. The site is also careful to say the effect on token use depends on your workload and provider, and that Pro does not change the price or limits of another subscription. What you'll learn Any memory layer has a hidden second bill: the cost of the model that writes the memories. Before you install one, answer three questions. Which model does the extraction? Whose account pays for it? And is the content it reads allowed to go there? For claude-mem the answers are configurable, documented, and not what the name implies by default. The licensing split is also published, in docs/ip-boundary.md, and it is a clean open-core boundary worth knowing if you are planning to build on it: Apache-2.0 covers the memory engine, server, CLI, SDKs, REST schemas, MCP tools, the Claude Code and generic agent adapters and the storage adapters. Reserved commercial areas include hosted Magic Recall, team/org memory sync, the admin dashboard, SSO/SAML/SCIM, enterprise RBAC and audit UI, the DLP/policy engine, managed evals and private connectors. So the engine is genuinely yours to embed; the team and enterprise surface is not.
documents.s: Who pays for the compression — and which model reads your code

documents.t: These are all from the project's own release notes and architecture docs, which is the best possible source for a gotcha list. 1. The observer's reasoning tokens ate the session's output budget. Fixed in v15.0.2 (23 October 2026): observer requests to OpenRouter, the cmem.ai gateway and OpenAI-compatible endpoints now disable reasoning by default, because reasoning tokens were filling the output budget and leaving a session with nothing left to emit. This is the single most instructive bug in the list — it is a pure consequence of putting a reasoning model in a budget-constrained extraction role, and it will recur in anything you build that does the same. 2. Two session IDs that are not interchangeable. contentSessionId comes from the host and is invariant for the session; memorySessionId comes from the SDK agent and changes on every worker restart. The architecture doc calls the conversion between them critical for foreign-key constraints. If you query the SQLite store directly, this is the first thing that will confuse you. 3. Deduplication has a 30-second window. The content hash is SHA256(memory_session_id + title + narrative) truncated to 16 hex characters, and a repeat within 30 seconds returns the existing ID instead of inserting. Useful, and also a reason identical-looking observations can legitimately coexist if they arrived 31 seconds apart. 4. Generator crashes retry three times, then stop. Backoff is 1s, 2s, 4s; after more than three consecutive restarts the worker stops retrying and lets the iterator end. The counter resets when the generator completes work naturally. Pending messages survive restarts and are cleared by the parser path on the next valid response — so a persistently crashing observer means a silently growing queue, not lost input. 5. The install footprint is larger than npm install. npx claude-mem install sets up Bun and uv globally, runs bun install in the plugin cache, and writes a version marker. The README is explicit that npm install -g installs the SDK only and that you must use npx claude-mem install. Two package-manager runtimes installed globally by a memory tool is a reasonable engineering choice and also a supply-chain surface you should know you accepted — vetting agent skills is the general discipline. Watch out Release velocity cuts both ways. Between 13 and 25 October 2026 this project shipped v13.38 through v15.2.1 — two major version bumps in twelve days, with features renamed across them (the viewer, the recall mode, the work views). A tool this active fixes bugs fast and also breaks your notes fast. Pin a version if you are documenting it for a team, and read the release notes before upgrading rather than after.

docs/security.md and the README together give a usable picture: The local engine stores memory on your machine, under ~/.claude-mem/. Cloud sync is opt-in; if you enable it, synced data is also stored by CMEM. The site's own guidance is to read the privacy policy before connecting. CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false skips the sign-in flow. Content wrapped in <private> tags is excluded from storage entirely — not written to the observation store, and not written to profile or project memory. That last one is the control most worth remembering, because it is the only in-band one. Everything else is a configuration decision you make once at install; <private> is the thing you can reach for mid-session when a secret, a customer name or a production hostname is about to pass through a tool call. It is also, by construction, a control you have to remember to use. For the broader question of what an agent ships off your machine in the normal course of doing its job, see what your agent uploads. Inspect what a memory layer has actually recorded about you CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Where the local stores live, and how big they have got du -sh ~/.claude-mem/ 2>/dev/null ls -la ~/.claude-mem/ # Which worker port is yours (the formula, not the number in the docs) python3 -c "import os; print(37700 + (os.getuid() % 100))" # Read the observation store directly — it is plain SQLite sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db ".tables" sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db \ "SELECT type, title, substr(narrative,1,90) FROM observations ORDER BY rowid DESC LIMIT 15;" # Which model actually wrote your memories (the field the cost docs join on) sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db \ "SELECT generated_by_model, COUNT(*) FROM observations GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;" # And your own prompt history, which is stored separately sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db \ "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM user_prompts;" What you'll learn Column names come from the schema table in docs/architecture-overview.md and the join recipe in docs/expense-pricing/README.md, which names generated_by_model and created_at on observation rows. A project shipping two majors in twelve days may rename them — if a query errors, run .schema observations and adjust. The point of the exercise is not the exact SQL; it is that you can and should read what a memory layer wrote about you, because it is a local SQLite file and nothing stops you.
documents.s: What leaves your machine, and the one control to know

documents.t: This category is going to keep growing, and the questions generalise. Run these before you install the next one. Guided walkthrough1 of 8 1What is the unit of storage?⌄ A raw transcript, a model-extracted note, or a compiled knowledge artefact? Extraction means a second model's judgement sits between what happened and what you remember — which is usually what you want, and is also a place for errors to become permanent. ←PreviousNext→ 2Which model does the extraction, and whose bill is it?⌄ Ask explicitly. claude-mem makes it a flag with four values and documents its hosted observer as a DeepSeek model in its own cost dataset. If a tool will not tell you, that is your answer. ←PreviousNext→ 3Is retrieval filtered before it is fetched?⌄ A memory layer that injects everything it has at session start is a context tax, not a context saving. Look for a cheap index step before a detail step, and check what the index entry costs in tokens. ←PreviousNext→ 4What happens when it fails?⌄ Find the degradation contract. claude-mem publishes one: transport errors exit 0 and never block, client errors exit 2 and do. A tool without a stated contract will eventually block your session for a reason you cannot see. ←PreviousNext→ 5Can you read and delete the store yourself?⌄ A local SQLite file you can query and rm is a very different privacy posture from an opaque cloud index. Check both the local format and whether sync is opt-in or opt-out. ←PreviousNext→ 6Is there an in-band exclusion control?⌄ You will need to stop one specific thing from being recorded, mid-session, without reconfiguring anything. <private> tags are claude-mem's answer; a tool with no equivalent means your only control is 'do not use it for this work'. ←PreviousNext→ 7What does installing it actually install?⌄ Global runtimes, a background daemon, an MCP server, hooks on every tool call. All reasonable individually; worth counting before you accept them. ←PreviousNext→ 8How fast does it move, and do you need it to?⌄ Fast releases mean fast fixes and fast breakage. If you are rolling this out to a team, pin a version and own the upgrade, rather than letting every developer sit on a different major. ←PreviousNext→ Key takeaways claude-mem is not a transcript store. It is a second model in a background daemon that reads every tool call and writes structured observations — which is the real cost and the real capability of this entire tool class. The observer is a separate model on a provider you select at install time (host, OpenRouter, Gemini, or Anthropic). The project's own cost dataset maps its hosted cmem-observer id to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash from 2026-08-08, so the name does not tell you where your code goes. Someone has to pay for the extraction. By default that is your own provider account; CMEM Pro's $30/month pitch is explicitly that hosted observation moves memory generation off your primary agent's subscription. Recall is three steps, not one: a ~50-100-token index hit, then timeline context, then a ~500-1,000-token detail fetch for selected IDs only. 'Filter cheap, fetch expensive' is the transferable pattern and the reason the token math works at all. The degradation contract is published and asymmetric: transport failures exit 0 and never block your session, client-side failures exit 2 and do. A half-upgraded install is therefore a session that will not start. Observer traffic is roughly 98% input tokens by the project's own accounting — a reading process, not a writing one. Price it that way. Each observation becomes multiple Chroma documents, one per extracted fact plus the narrative, which is why a query about a small detail can surface a note that is nominally about something else. The v15.0.2 fix is the most instructive bug in the project: a reasoning model in an extraction role spent the output budget on reasoning and left sessions with nothing to emit. Disable reasoning on any model you use as a summariser. Two package-manager runtimes (Bun and uv) get installed globally, a daemon binds 37700 + (uid % 100), and an MCP server joins your agent. All defensible, all worth counting as surface area before you accept them. The one in-band control is the <private> tag, which excludes content from storage entirely. Everything else is decided at install time. Check yourself 0/6

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत For two years agents have been very good at deciding to buy something and very bad at actually paying for it. The workaround was always the same — pre-provision an API key, hand the agent a shared credit card, and hope it doesn't rack up a bill you can't unwind. In 2026 that gap closed. A small stack has emerged around one big idea — use HTTP 402 the way it was always meant to be used — and a real, generally-available AWS service now wraps it in the guardrails an actual business needs. This page is a practical field guide to that stack: how x402 works on the wire, why the upto scheme is the interesting one, what AgentCore Payments actually gives you at GA, and where the sharp edges are. What you'll learn Read a raw x402 challenge and understand the three headers, the two facilitator calls, and the three payment schemes Tell exact from upto and know which one your endpoint should advertise Set a payment session's spend cap and expiry so an agent cannot drain your wallet on a bad prompt Choose between Coinbase Privy (crypto rails) and Stripe Privy (card rails) inside AgentCore Payments Recognize the three real threats: prompt-injection-to-buy, facilitator misbehavior, and 'upto' over-settlement आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-08-27। Numbers here decay fast — settlement volume, supported chains, exact SDK package names, and Bazar catalog contents move week to week. AgentCore Payments GA'd on 2026-08-18. Confirm the payment-session field names and Coinbase / Stripe integration surface against the AWS blog and the x402-foundation repo before you ship, and treat any header capitalization or scheme name as authoritative from the spec, not this page. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: Agent Payments: x402, MPP and AgentCore GA

documents.t: The moment an agent has real spending authority, four things break at once: The API key model was a workaround. Every "agent-friendly" API today asks you to mint a key, top up a balance, and hand the string to the agent. That's the human doing the accounting; the agent is just a client. Anything the agent buys spends the human's pre-committed pool. Cards were designed for one buyer per session. Cards assume there is a person clicking "Pay". Agents want to fan out — buy 200 tiny things across 30 sites in an hour — and each purchase should be atomic, cheap, and reversible. There is no discovery. Human buyers can read a pricing page. An agent needs a machine-readable "here's what this costs and how to pay for it" inline in the response. Guardrails have to be enforced somewhere other than the agent. If the only limit is a prompt saying "spend under $10", the agent will disobey it at some point. The limit has to live in infrastructure the model can't argue with. x402 attacks the discovery problem. AgentCore Payments attacks the guardrail problem. They are complements, not competitors.
documents.s: Why "the agent just pays" is harder than it sounds

documents.t: x402 is an open protocol maintained by the x402-foundation/x402 organisation on GitHub (Apache-2.0, ~6.5k stars at time of writing). Its whole trick is to give HTTP status code 402 Payment Required the semantics people always assumed it had. The full flow is exactly six moves. There is no session, no login, no key. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 11. Client asks⌄ Agent makes a normal HTTP request to a paid endpoint. No auth header, no wallet. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Server challenges with 402⌄ Server responds `HTTP/1.1 402 Payment Required` and sets a `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header carrying a base64-encoded `PaymentRequirements` object: the price, the accepted token(s), the network, the merchant address, the scheme, and an expiry. That's the machine-readable price tag. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Client signs a payment payload⌄ Agent's x402 client SDK reads the challenge, picks one of the requirements it can pay, and constructs a signed `PaymentPayload` (an EIP-712-style signature, or the equivalent on Solana/Aptos/Stellar). Nothing is on-chain yet — this is an *authorization*, not a transfer. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Client retries with the signature⌄ Same request, this time with a `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header containing the signed payload. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Server verifies (via facilitator)⌄ Server hands the payload to a *facilitator* — a small optional service that runs `POST /verify` to confirm the signature and the client's on-chain balance, then, once the server has produced the response, `POST /settle` to actually submit the transfer. The server can also run its own facilitator. ←PreviousNext→ 66. Server returns 200 + settlement proof⌄ Response body carries the paid content; a `PAYMENT-RESPONSE` header carries a base64-encoded settlement receipt so the agent can audit that what it authorised was what actually cleared. ←PreviousNext→ Two design points are worth pausing on. First, the server — not the client — decides when to settle. If the request fails after step 4, the server never calls /settle, so the agent is not charged; the signature was an authorisation with a short expiry and it simply times out. That is the property that makes x402 usable at all for agents: a failed download is a free download. Second, the facilitator never has custody of client funds; the protocol's stated invariant is "all payment schemes must not allow facilitators to move funds outside client intentions." A rogue facilitator can refuse to settle; it cannot over-settle.
documents.s: x402 on the wire — the whole protocol in one flow

documents.t: x402 defines schemes as how the amount is agreed, not what currency is used. The current stable set: exact — the server advertises a fixed price and the client signs for exactly that amount. Best for content with a known cost per read: "$0.02 for this article". Simple, boring, correct. upto — the server advertises a ceiling. The client signs authorising up to that ceiling; the server chooses the actual charge at settlement time, up to the cap. This is the one that unlocks the interesting economics. batch-settlement (EVM) — for high-frequency use. The client posts an escrow deposit once, then racks up many off-chain vouchers that get redeemed in a single batched on-chain settlement. Same trust model, dramatically lower per-request gas. upto is the scheme that makes pay-per-inference and dynamic pricing possible. If you sell inference by the token, you don't know at request time how many tokens the completion will use; you only know at response time. With exact you either overcharge (round up to the ceiling and refund — needs a second on-chain move) or undercharge (the client pays for 4k tokens and you generate 10k). With upto the client signs "charge me for at most 10k tokens' worth", you produce the response, then you settle for the actual usage. The AWS AgentCore Payments GA release specifically highlights this as the pattern their launch enables: "the upto scheme within x402 enables an agent to set a spending ceiling rather than committing to a fixed price." Watch the failure mode: if the server settles the ceiling instead of the actual usage, the client has no on-chain recourse for the difference — the signature covered it. The /settle call's amount parameter is trusted. In practice this is why you want a facilitator you either run yourself or trust; more on that below.
documents.s: The three schemes — and why upto is the interesting one

documents.t: The current x402 monorepo publishes SDK packages for EVM, SVM (Solana), AVM, Aptos, Stellar, TVM, Hedera and Keeta, but the traffic today is heavily concentrated on Base (Coinbase's EVM L2) and Solana, both settling in USDC. In TypeScript the packages you'll actually import are @x402/core, one of the chain modules (@x402/evm, @x402/svm, …), and a client wrapper — @x402/fetch for a drop-in fetch() replacement that transparently handles the 402→sign→retry loop, or @x402/express / x402-hono on the server side. Python has a single x402 pip package; Go has github.com/x402-foundation/x402/go/v2. Cloudflare ships an even shorter path: the agents/x402 submodule inside its Agents package gives you an MCP client with x402 built in, and x402-hono is the paywall middleware for a Worker. So a Cloudflare Worker that turns a route into a paid endpoint is roughly: Turning a Hono route into an x402 paywall CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import { Hono } from "hono"; import { paymentMiddleware } from "x402-hono"; const app = new Hono(); app.use("/premium/*", paymentMiddleware({ network: "base", facilitator: "https://facilitator.x402.org", routes: { "/premium/summary": { price: { asset: "USDC", amount: "0.05" }, scheme: "exact", recipient: "0xYourMerchantAddress", }, "/premium/inference": { price: { asset: "USDC", maxAmount: "0.50" }, scheme: "upto", recipient: "0xYourMerchantAddress", }, }, })); app.get("/premium/summary", c => c.text("The paid content.")); app.get("/premium/inference", c => c.text("The paid inference result.")); export default app; A caller using @x402/fetch doesn't need to know any of this — the wrapper sees the 402, signs, retries, and returns the eventual 200 response the same way a normal fetch would.
documents.s: The chains and SDKs you'll actually meet

documents.t: x402 alone is a protocol. It gets you how an agent pays. It does not get you whether it should. That is the problem Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments — GA on August 18, 2026 after a preview in May — actually solves. The primitive to understand is the payment session. Every payment an agent makes has to run inside one, and a session has exactly two caps: A maximum spend amount in a specified currency. An expiry time. Both are checked deterministically at the infrastructure layer — outside the model, outside the agent framework, outside anything the model can talk itself out of. A request that would push cumulative spend over the cap is rejected before the payment payload is even signed. A request after the expiry is rejected the same way. That is the guardrail. The model does not need to be well-aligned for it to hold; it needs to be well-constrained, and constraint lives in the session. Around that primitive AgentCore GA'd: Coinbase & Stripe Privy wallet integration. The credentials live in AgentCore Identity Secrets Manager; the agent never sees them; a short-lived derived token is what actually authorises wallet operations. End users can top up with a card (Stripe) or with USDC (Coinbase). Quick Create for Coinbase. You provision Coinbase credentials from inside the AgentCore console or CLI without leaving the platform. The Machine Payment Protocol (MPP) — the payment abstraction on top of x402 that lets an agent pay for MPP-compatible services and x402 endpoints with the same session and the same session cap. MPP is where card-rail and stablecoin-rail payments meet. A curated x402-enabled MCP server directory — "Coinbase Bazar" — exposed to the agent through AgentCore Gateway. Discoverability of paid endpoints is ranked on "social proof, metadata richness, description quality, and availability," which is a polite way of saying they're trying not to become a listing of shitcoin drainers. Framework plugins. A Strands Agents plugin and a LangGraph middleware ship at GA, so the payment session context is threaded through your agent loop without you writing an HTTP client for x402 by hand. The Strands wiring is intentionally small — you build a AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig with the payment-manager ARN, the user ID, the payment-instrument ID and the session ID, and add the plugin to the agent. The session enforcement happens under the plugin. AgentCore Payments — Strands plugin, minimal shape CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from agentcore_payments import AgentCorePaymentsPlugin, AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig import os plugin = AgentCorePaymentsPlugin( config=AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig( payment_manager_arn=os.environ["PAYMENT_MANAGER_ARN"], user_id="test-user-123", payment_instrument_id=os.environ["PAYMENT_INSTRUMENT_ID"], payment_session_id=os.environ["PAYMENT_SESSION_ID"], ) ) # Attach plugin to your Strands agent; the payment session caps # (max spend + expiry) are set when you mint the payment session, # NOT in the plugin config. Every payment attempt emits a CloudWatch log entry and an AgentCore Observability span; the built-in dashboards show success rates, average transaction value, and end-to-end health per agent. This is the observability piece that makes "the agent bought something weird" actually debuggable a week after the fact.
documents.s: AgentCore Payments GA — what AWS actually shipped on 2026-08-18

documents.t: A common misread is that x402 and AgentCore Payments are "crypto for agents". They are not. x402 happens to have shipped first on stablecoins because on-chain settlement is the only rail with true machine-native, permissionless per-request settlement. But AgentCore's MPP abstraction and the Stripe Privy integration mean an agent's session can be funded from a card. What Stripe Privy provides in this context is a card-backed wallet with delegation — the human user hands the agent a scoped, revocable authority to spend against a card, and the AgentCore session enforces the spend cap on top. For businesses that don't want stablecoin custody at all, this is the path. Choosing: Coinbase / Privy (USDC on Base or Solana). Best when you need true per-request, sub-cent settlement; when you want no chargeback; when the counterparty is another agent. Stripe Privy (card). Best when the merchant is a normal business without on-chain rails, when the average ticket is large enough that stablecoin fees don't dominate, when you want the buyer to have card-network dispute rights.
documents.s: Not just crypto — where Stripe fits

documents.t: Autonomous agent payments open a small, specific attack surface. The three you should design against: Prompt-injection-to-buy. A malicious page in an agent's context can instruct it to buy things. The defence is not "make the model refuse" — it's the session cap. Set the smallest spend ceiling that will complete the legitimate task, and set the shortest expiry. If a prompt injection makes the agent try to spend $10,000 and the session cap is $5, the injection fails. This is exactly the same lesson as Cryptographic context injection: Grok — trust boundaries live outside the model. Facilitator misbehavior. The /verify call is honest by construction (a bad /verify can only reject), but a compromised or byzantine facilitator can refuse to /settle after the server has delivered content, silently overcharge in upto mode, or delay settlement past the payload's expiry so the client's signature stops being valid. Defence: prefer facilitators you run yourself for merchant-side use; on the client side use @x402/fetch's built-in receipt check to fail loud if PAYMENT-RESPONSE disagrees with what you signed. upto over-settlement. In upto, the settled amount is server-supplied. A dishonest server can settle at the ceiling regardless of actual usage. The mitigation lives outside the protocol: emit a signed usage receipt in your response body (tokens generated, seconds streamed, bytes served) and refuse to trust a settled amount that isn't consistent with it. Some client wrappers will refuse to accept a settlement if you provide a callback that returns the expected max. These are also the shape of what Cloudflare's WriteGuard is trying to address at the MCP layer — treating "cost money" as a write with attribution and audit — but AgentCore's session cap is the load-bearing control today. Combining a WriteGuard-style write-tier policy at the MCP layer and a payment-session cap at the wallet layer is the belt-and-braces posture that most production deployments will settle into.
documents.s: The three threats worth taking seriously

documents.t: x402 gives an agent a way to transact. MCP gives it a way to reach the endpoints where transactions happen. A2A gives it a way to delegate work to another agent that may itself be paid. In practice you'll see all three composed: an A2A hand-off invokes a peer agent that uses MCP to reach an x402-priced tool, and the caller pays through its AgentCore session. When people talk about "the money layer for agents" this is what they mean — not a single product, but a stack where discovery, capability, and settlement each have a protocol and none of them requires humans in the loop. Check yourself 0/6
documents.s: Where this fits in the wider agent picture

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम A submission titled "Opus 5.5 is good at explainer videos" sat near the top of Hacker News with 319 points and 175 comments — and reading the thread, the most interesting thing is how many people got the mechanism wrong. They assumed a video model. It isn't one. What is happening is stranger and far more useful: a coding model writes a deterministic animation program, and a separate renderer turns that program into frames. The model never sees a pixel of the output. Which means the whole thing behaves like software — diffable, re-renderable, parameterisable, and debuggable — instead of like a slot machine you re-prompt until it looks right. This page is the practical guide that thread was missing: how the pipeline works, which of the three render engines to pick (and which one the models are measurably bad at), the two failure modes that silently break agent-written animation code, the pacing arithmetic that separates a watchable explainer from an unreadable one, and where the money actually goes. What you'll learn Explain why a coding model beats a video model at explainers — and what it gives up Name the reason Math.random() is banned in a frame-rendered animation, and what replaces it Pick between Remotion, Motion Canvas and Manim on licence and on how well models write them Spot the two traps in agent-written animation code: the Manim fork split and the stale Remotion API Compute a minimum dwell time per slide instead of guessing, so viewers can actually read Predict which line item dominates the bill (it is usually not the LLM) आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-25। Volatile here: the Hacker News score, the community-reported per-video costs, the claim that one model is better than another at a specific library, the Remotion version and its package layout (checked at remotion@4.0.529), and the star counts. Re-check any of those before you build a budget or a template on them. Durable: the mechanism (a program rendered frame by frame), the determinism constraint, the licence split between the three engines, and the pacing arithmetic — none of that changes with a model release. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: AI Explainer Videos: The Code-Driven Pipeline

documents.t: Two completely different things get called "AI video". Diffusion video models (the family covered in generative media) take a prompt and emit pixels directly. Excellent for b-roll, a drone shot, a texture, a mood. Bad at anything that must be exactly right: legible text, a correct architecture diagram, your actual product UI, a number that has to say 40%. Code-driven animation goes the other way. A coding model writes source code for an animation — React components, a TypeScript scene graph, or Python — and a renderer executes it. Text is text, so it is sharp and spelled correctly. A diagram is a layout, so it is accurate. Your logo is your logo file. That split explains the HN thread's most common workflow report: the model "creates an HTML page and uses raw JS timed animations", then the frames get captured and assembled with ffmpeg. It also explains what the approach gives up — it cannot invent photographic imagery, so most real pipelines call an image model or a video model for b-roll and composite it in. The consequence worth internalising: your explainer becomes a repository. Change the price on slide 4, re-render, done. Localise the voiceover, re-render twelve languages from the same scenes. That is not a property any prompt-to-video model gives you.
documents.s: The mechanism: the model writes a program, not a video

documents.t: Here is the detail that quietly decides whether your pipeline produces clean video or a flickering mess, and almost nobody writing about this mentions it. A renderer like Remotion does not screen-record your animation. It opens the composition in headless Chrome, sets the clock to frame 0, screenshots, sets the clock to frame 1, screenshots, and so on — and it does this across multiple threads, opening the page multiple times. Frames are produced out of order, in parallel, in separate browser contexts. Everything follows from that: Animation must be a pure function of the frame number. In Remotion that is literally the API: useCurrentFrame() gives you the frame, interpolate() maps it to a value. No timers, no requestAnimationFrame, no CSS transitions driven by wall-clock time. A CSS transition renders whatever it happened to be mid-flight when the screenshot fired. Math.random() is broken by construction. It returns a different value in each thread and each page load, so a "random" particle jitters to a new position every frame. Remotion ships random(seed) — a seeded mulberry32 PRNG — precisely for this: random(1) always returns 0.07301638228818774. Same for spring(), which is a cached pure calculation keyed on (frame, fps, config). Dropped frames stop being possible. A screen recording of a heavy animation drops frames when the CPU can't keep up. Frame-by-frame rendering just takes longer. This is why a 5-minute render on a laptop can produce a video that plays perfectly smoothly. Watch out If you only remember one rule for prompting an agent to write animation code: forbid wall-clock time. No setTimeout, no CSS transition, no Date.now(), no Math.random(). Every visual value must be derived from the current frame number. Models will reach for CSS transitions because that is what the web corpus is full of.
documents.s: Why determinism is the whole trick

documents.t: All three are real, actively maintained, and produce broadcast-quality output. They differ on language, on licence, and — importantly — on how reliably a model writes them. Remotion Motion Canvas Manim Language React / TypeScript TypeScript (generators) Python Repo remotion-dev/remotion motion-canvas/motion-canvas (~19.2k stars) ManimCommunity/manim (~41k) · 3b1b/manim (~94k) Licence Source-available + Company Licence MIT MIT Sweet spot Product/launch video, UI, text-heavy explainer Timeline-precise motion graphics Mathematical and algorithmic visualisation Model-written quality Strong — and it ships official agent skills Decent Weakest of the three (see below) Two things on that table deserve more than a row.

Remotion is not MIT. It is source-available with a two-tier commercial licence, and the threshold is small enough to catch most teams: free for individuals, non-profits, evaluation, and for-profit companies with up to 3 employees; a paid Company Licence for for-profit organisations with more than three. The second split matters more if you are building a product rather than a video: Remotion for Creators — seat-based, intended for low-volume rendering within and for your own company, explicitly not for serving personalised videos to your end users. Remotion for Automators — render-based, which is the tier you land in the moment an agent renders videos for customers. From version 5.0 it carries mandatory telemetry reporting with a license key. So "my agent generates a video per signup" is not a Creators use case. Price it as Automators before you ship it. If that is a dealbreaker, Motion Canvas is MIT and covers a lot of the same ground.
documents.s: Remotion's licence is the gotcha, not the code

documents.t: This one burns people who have never heard of it, and it also explains an observation from the HN thread — that strong coding models write worse Manim than you would expect, with community reports that Gemini currently handles it better than Opus 5.5. There are two Manims: 3b1b/manim — Grant Sanderson's original, the one from the famous videos, ~94k stars, installed as manimgl. ManimCommunity/manim — the community fork, ~41k stars, the one that is actually documented and maintained for general use, installed as manim. They are API-incompatible and both are imported as from manim import *. Every tutorial, StackOverflow answer and blog post in the training corpus is one or the other, unlabelled. So the model writes plausible code that mixes both dialects, and Python raises on a method that exists in the other fork. It is not a reasoning failure; it is a poisoned-namespace failure. The fix is boring and it works: pin the fork in your prompt and in your environment, and give the agent the version's real API surface instead of letting it recall one. Pin the Manim dialect before the agent writes a line CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Use ManimCommunity Manim (the "manim" package on PyPI), NOT 3b1b/manimgl. Before writing any scene, run: python -c "import manim; print(manim.__version__)" and confirm the version. If a class or method you want is not in that version's API, do not use it — check with: python -c "import manim; print([n for n in dir(manim) if 'Text' in n])" Never mix manimgl APIs (e.g. ShowCreation) with community APIs (Create).
documents.s: The Manim trap: two forks, one import name

documents.t: The same poisoned-corpus problem hits Remotion for a different reason: the library moved faster than the training data. In current Remotion, media components live in @remotion/media, and the trimming props are trimBefore / trimAfter. Preview and render can even use different components deliberately — Html5Audio from remotion while previewing, Audio from @remotion/media when rendering, switched on useRemotionEnvironment(). A model trained mostly on older material writes import {Audio} from 'remotion' with startFrom, which is the old shape. That code may still run. It may also silently do nothing useful, which is worse. This is exactly why Remotion publishes official Agent Skills — a set of twelve skills that hand an agent the current best practices instead of hoping it remembers them. They are designed for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and friends, and they follow the same open format covered in SKILL.md as an open standard. Install Remotion's official agent skills CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npx skills add remotion-dev/skills The skills are granular, which is the point — you invoke the one that matches the phase of work: /remotion-create to scaffold, /remotion-markup for animation and typography, /remotion-studio to preview, /remotion-render to render, /remotion-captions for subtitles, plus remotion-best-practices as the umbrella when you are not sure. Vendor-maintained skills are the cheapest available fix for a model's stale knowledge of a fast-moving library: one install, and the agent stops guessing.

The single biggest quality lever is not a better prompt for the whole video. It is splitting the job so the model does judgement work and the renderer does determinism work — with a human-readable artefact in between. Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Generate a storyboard as data, not as code⌄ Ask for a JSON scene list first: per scene, a title, the on-screen text, the visual intent, and a duration in seconds. This is the cheap, reviewable step. You can read twelve scenes in thirty seconds and fix the narrative before a single component exists — and fixing the story is the edit that most improves the video. Code generated from a reviewed storyboard is also far more consistent than code generated from a paragraph of vibes. ←PreviousNext→ 2Fix the pacing in the storyboard, before any rendering⌄ Do the reading-speed arithmetic below on each scene's text and clamp the durations. Doing this at the data layer costs nothing; doing it after the components exist means re-timing every animation that depends on the scene length. ←PreviousNext→ 3Write the voiceover script per scene, then synthesise it⌄ Script per scene, not per video, so audio boundaries line up with visual boundaries. Synthesise each scene to its own audio file with a TTS API. Then measure the real duration of each clip — the synthesised audio is the ground truth for scene length, not your estimate. ←PreviousNext→ 4Re-derive scene durations from the real audio⌄ This is the step everyone skips and it is why so many AI explainers have visuals racing ahead of the narration. Read each audio file's actual duration, convert to frames, and feed those durations back into the composition as props. Never hardcode a frame count you guessed. ←PreviousNext→ 5Build the components from the storyboard, frame-derived only⌄ Now let the agent write the animation code, scene by scene, against the frozen storyboard. Enforce the determinism rule: every value from useCurrentFrame() and interpolate(), randomness from a seeded helper, no CSS transitions. Preview in the studio — a real preview catches layout errors that no amount of code reading does. ←PreviousNext→ 6Add captions from the audio you already have⌄ Do not ask the model to guess word timings. Transcribe your own voiceover locally and use the token-level timestamps. Remotion ships install-whisper-cpp for exactly this: installWhisperCpp(), downloadWhisperModel(), then transcribe() with token-level timestamps on, and toCaptions() to post-process. Captions are also the cheapest accessibility win available and they are what makes the video watchable muted. ←PreviousNext→ 7Render, then measure the render⌄ Render from the CLI so it is reproducible in CI. Then tune concurrency with a real measurement instead of a guess — Remotion has a benchmark command that runs the same render repeatedly across several concurrency values and compares them. ←PreviousNext→ Render from the CLI, then find your real concurrency CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # deterministic render, reproducible in CI npx remotion render src/index.ts MyExplainer out/video.mp4 # stop guessing --concurrency: measure it npx remotion benchmark src/index.ts MyExplainer --concurrencies=2,4,8 --runs=3

The most consistent complaint in the HN thread was not that the videos looked bad. It was that they moved too fast to read. Slides appear, text animates in, and it is gone before a human finishes the sentence. This is a bug with a formula, not a matter of taste. Adult reading speed for unfamiliar screen text sits around 200–250 words per minute, and a viewer also needs time to find the new text before starting to read it. So: # minimum dwell time for a text block, in frames words = number of words in the block wpm = 200 # conservative for unfamiliar on-screen text settle = 0.4 # seconds to notice and locate the new text exit = 0.3 # seconds of breathing room before it leaves dwell_seconds = settle + (words / wpm) * 60 + exit dwell_frames = ceil(dwell_seconds * fps) # worked example: a 14-word bullet at 30 fps # 0.4 + (14 / 200) * 60 + 0.3 = 4.9 s -> 147 frames Two notes that make this actually useful: Animate in fast, hold long. The entrance transition should be 200–400 ms; the hold is where the dwell budget goes. Models tend to do the opposite — a long elegant fade, then a short hold. If narration exists, the dwell floor is the narration length. Text must stay up at least as long as the sentence describing it. Which is why deriving scene duration from the synthesised audio (step 4 above) fixes pacing almost for free. Clamp every scene to max(dwell_frames, narration_frames) and a large fraction of the "AI slop video" feeling disappears, with no change to the visuals at all.
documents.s: Pacing: the reason most AI explainers are unwatchable

documents.t: Community reports from the HN thread put a complete generated explainer at roughly $3–$4 in API spend, with the notable detail that the cost was dominated by image-model calls, not by the language model. One commenter reported generating a 5-minute video on an M4 MacBook Air in about 5 minutes of wall-clock time using an orchestrated pipeline. Treat the absolute numbers as perishable, but the shape is structural and worth planning around: The LLM is cheap here. A storyboard plus a few hundred lines of animation code is a small number of tokens. Even at flagship pricing it is cents. See what AI costs across providers. Per-asset generative calls dominate. Every generated image or b-roll clip is a separate paid call, and they multiply by scene count. This is the line item to cap. Compute is yours. Rendering runs on your machine or your CI, so it is time and electricity rather than API spend — until you move it to a serverless renderer, at which point it becomes both. Re-renders are nearly free, which is the whole structural advantage. Fixing a typo on slide 4 costs one render, not one regeneration. Localising into twelve languages costs twelve TTS runs and twelve renders, not twelve videos. The practical budgeting move: generate images once, commit them as assets, and keep re-renders asset-free. A pipeline that re-generates imagery on every render is the one that produces a surprising bill.
documents.s: What it costs, and which line item dominates

documents.t: The sharpest criticism in the thread is the one worth taking seriously: within weeks of these tools spreading, the outputs became recognisable. Same gradient backgrounds, same spring-in cards, same three-word bullets, same brisk voice. Several commenters also flagged repetitive copy and, in one case, a video confidently about the wrong subject entirely — a Twilight Imperium reference site described as an AI data startup. If you use this seriously, the levers that measurably de-generify output: Supply the design system, don't let it be invented. Pass your real palette, type scale, spacing scale and logo as constants the components import. Underspecified prompts are exactly where a model's house style leaks in. Write the copy yourself, or edit it hard. The visuals are the part models are good at. The narrative is the part that reads as generated. Use your own screen recordings as the hero asset. Real product footage composited into a generated scene is the single strongest anti-sameness move, and it also fixes the hallucination risk — the video cannot misdescribe your product if the product is on screen. Verify the claims like documentation. Anything factual in an explainer is a factual claim being published in your name, with none of a text page's easy correction path. Check it before you render, not after it is on YouTube. Break one convention on purpose. One deliberate choice that the default template would not make — an odd aspect ratio, silence where music is expected, a hand-drawn asset — is usually enough to stop the output reading as machine default.

Worth being honest, because the sceptics in that thread had a point: much of what gets produced is an animated slide deck with a voiceover. That is a perfectly good artefact for a changelog, a launch, a release note or an onboarding walkthrough — and a poor substitute for actual teaching, which needs a worked example, a wrong turn, and a reason to care. Reach for the code-driven pipeline when: The content must be exactly right — real UI, real numbers, real diagrams. You will need to change it later, or ship it in several languages. The same template will produce many videos from different data. Reach for something else when the goal is photographic footage (use a video model), or when the value is in a human explaining a hard idea badly and then well — which is still the thing no pipeline produces. Check yourself 0/5
documents.s: What this is good at, and what it isn't

documents.t: Opus 5.5 is good at explainer videos — Hacker News discussion — the thread this page is built around: 319 points, 175 comments, the reported workflows (HTML + JS timed animations captured with ffmpeg), the ~$3–$4 costs, the Manim weakness, the pacing complaints and the sameness criticism. Community reports, not vendor claims — treated as such throughout. Remotion — the React-based renderer. See useCurrentFrame() and interpolate() for the determinism model, random() for why Math.random() is banned and what the seeded PRNG returns, and the licence pages for the Company Licence, the Creators/Automators split and the v5.0 telemetry requirement. remotion-dev/skills — Remotion's twelve official Agent Skills for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others, installable with npx skills add remotion-dev/skills. The clearest current example of a vendor shipping agent-facing docs to fix stale model knowledge. @remotion/install-whisper-cpp — local transcription for captions: installWhisperCpp(), downloadWhisperModel(), transcribe() with token-level timestamps, and toCaptions() for post-processing. npx remotion benchmark — measures render time across concurrency values instead of guessing a flag. Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम Once your product talks to more than one model, the direct-SDK approach cracks. Each provider has its own key, its own rate limits, its own outage schedule, and its own bill. An AI gateway is the small piece of infrastructure that sits between your code and every model — Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Kimi, DeepSeek, your local Ollama — and turns "N brittle integrations" into "one endpoint you control." This page compares the four gateways that actually get deployed in production in 2026 — LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, and Vercel AI Gateway — and shows the killer workflow: point Claude Code at your own gateway so a single proxy handles routing, budgets, logging, and fallback for the whole team. What you'll learn Understand what an AI gateway is and the five problems it solves (many providers, one API; fallback; virtual keys; spend caps; observability) Compare LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, and Vercel AI Gateway on latency, pricing, self-hostability, and where each shines Wire Claude Code through your own LiteLLM proxy with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and a virtual key so the team gets shared limits and logs Configure OpenRouter fallback so a Claude outage silently promotes GPT or Gemini instead of showing users a 5xx Understand the March 2026 LiteLLM supply-chain incident and how to pin versions safely in production
documents.s: AI Gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel

documents.t: The first Claude integration is a two-line change: pip install anthropic, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, done. The second — say you want to fall back to GPT-5.4 when Anthropic throttles — is where the abstraction breaks. Now you have two SDKs with different request shapes, two dashboards, two bills, two rotation cadences for API keys, and two sets of retry logic. Add a third for Gemini and a fourth for your local Ollama, and every product decision ("cap this team at $500/month", "log every prompt for review", "let a customer bring their own key") becomes N implementations instead of one. An AI gateway concentrates that plumbing in a single place. Concretely, a production gateway gives you: One request shape for every provider. Most gateways speak the OpenAI Chat Completions API (or Anthropic Messages, or both) and translate to the real provider under the hood. Fallback and routing. Try Claude first; on 429 or 5xx, retry against GPT or Gemini without the caller knowing. Same for latency ceilings and content-moderation rejections. Virtual keys. Issue a per-user or per-service key that maps to a subset of models, its own budget, and its own rate limit — so a rogue script can't drain the whole account. Spend caps and logging. Every request is tagged, priced, and stored. You can revoke a key without touching Anthropic or OpenAI, and you can prove to compliance what was sent where. Caching. Prompt caching (exact-match) and semantic caching (near-match) turn repeat traffic into free hits. Not every team needs all five. But the moment two of them are on your roadmap, running a gateway is cheaper than reinventing them per provider.
documents.s: The problem: one direct SDK per provider does not scale

documents.t: There isn't one "winner" — the four leaders occupy different corners of the design space (self-hosted vs. hosted, open-source vs. proprietary, minimalist vs. control-panel). Gateway Deploy Pricing model Best at Not for LiteLLM Self-hosted (Docker) or SDK Free (OSS); Enterprise tier for SSO/audit Team proxy with virtual keys, budgets, no per-token markup, works with 100+ providers via one config Teams with no DevOps to run Postgres + Redis OpenRouter Hosted only Provider price + ~5.5% credit-purchase fee, no per-request markup Zero-ops access to 300+ models under one key; ideal for products that let users pick a model Compliance shops that need self-hosting or data residency Portkey OSS gateway (npx) or hosted cloud OSS free; cloud has usage tiers Sub-ms gateway latency, semantic caching, guardrails, canary testing — the "control panel" angle Teams who just want the simplest possible key aggregator Vercel AI Gateway Hosted only Provider price, no token markup; free with Vercel plans Devs already on Vercel who want AI SDK v5/v6 + Anthropic Messages + OpenAI Responses APIs unified Non-Vercel infrastructure or air-gapped deployments The important axis to pick on first: self-hosted vs. hosted. If your data cannot leave your VPC (regulated industries, EU residency, enterprise privacy reviews), you need a self-hostable gateway — LiteLLM or Portkey OSS. If you'd rather pay someone to run it, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway is a one-click affair. The second axis: how much control plane you actually need. If you're a one-person product that just wants to try Kimi K3 and Claude and Grok side-by-side without three signups, OpenRouter is the whole story. If you're a 20-person org where finance wants monthly spend by team, security wants virtual keys with rotation, and platform wants Grafana metrics, you're building on LiteLLM or Portkey. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-07-27। Gateway feature sets and pricing change quickly. Two examples measured on the verification date: OpenRouter charges a 5.5% platform fee on credit purchases (not per request), and Portkey's OSS gateway advertises sub-1ms overhead while hosted OpenRouter typically adds 100–150ms. Confirm against each vendor's current pricing and status page before committing. The categorisation above (self-hosted vs. hosted, minimalist vs. control-panel) is stable; the exact numbers behind it are not. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
