Securing local and hybrid agents — what to put around any harness whose own safety file tells you not to trust its sandbox. यह पेज साझा करें X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News लिंक कॉपी करें

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम लंबे समय तक "अच्छे AI" की कहानी कुछ गिने-चुने क्लोज़्ड, फ़्रंटियर मॉडलों की कहानी थी जिन्हें आप सिर्फ़ किसी API के ज़रिए किराए पर ले सकते थे। अब यह पूरी कहानी नहीं रही। ओपन-वेट मॉडलों की एक लहर — इनमें से कई DeepSeek जैसी चीनी लैब और Alibaba की Qwen से, साथ ही Meta की Llama और फ़्रांस की Mistral से — इतनी अच्छी, इतनी सस्ती, और इतनी छोटी हो गई कि अपना खुद का सक्षम मॉडल डाउनलोड करके चलाना एक असली विकल्प बन गया। यह पेज उस परिदृश्य का टिकाऊ नक्शा है: ऐसा क्यों हुआ, "ओपन वेट" का असल में क्या मतलब है, क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर मॉडलों की तुलना में ईमानदार ट्रेड-ऑफ़, और आज इन मॉडलों को वाकई कैसे इस्तेमाल करें। What you'll learn समझें कि ओपन-वेट मॉडल प्रतिस्पर्धी क्यों बने — प्रति-लागत क्षमता और ओपन रीज़निंग साफ़ करें कि 'ओपन वेट' का असल में क्या मतलब है — ओपन-सोर्स बनाम, और ओपन-डेटा बनाम आर्केटाइप पहचानें: जनरल चैट, रीज़निंग, कोडिंग, और छोटे/किफ़ायती मॉडल क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर बनाम असली ट्रेड-ऑफ़ तौलें — सबसे कठिन कामों पर क्षमता का फ़ासला, और अपनी खुद की infra व सुरक्षा संभालना इन्हें वाकई इस्तेमाल करने के दो तरीके जानें: एक होस्टेड API, या Ollama के ज़रिए सेल्फ़-होस्टिंग

लगभग एक ही समय पर तीन चीज़ें बदलीं, और मिलकर उन्होंने रोज़मर्रा का ज़्यादातर फ़ासला पाट दिया। प्रति-लागत क्षमता ढह गई। बेहतर ट्रेनिंग रेसिपी, डेटा क्यूरेशन, और mixture-of-experts (MoE) आर्किटेक्चर (जहाँ किसी बड़े मॉडल के पैरामीटरों का सिर्फ़ एक अंश ही प्रति टोकन सक्रिय होता है) ने लैब को ऐसे मॉडल भेजने दिए जो अपनी लागत से कहीं ऊपर का प्रदर्शन करते हैं। असली कामों के एक बड़े हिस्से के लिए — ड्राफ़्टिंग, सारांश बनाना, एक्सट्रैक्शन, वर्गीकरण, नियमित कोडिंग — एक अच्छा ओपन मॉडल अब फ़्रंटियर-API लागत के एक अंश में "काफ़ी अच्छा" है। ओपन रीज़निंग मॉडल आ गए। DeepSeek की रीज़निंग शृंखला एक मोड़ थी: इसने दिखाया कि "जवाब देने से पहले कदम-दर-कदम सोचो" वाली क्षमता — जो पहले चंद क्लोज़्ड मॉडलों की खाई थी — ओपन वेट के साथ ट्रेन और रिलीज़ की जा सकती है। एक बार एक लैब ने साबित किया, तो बाक़ी ओपन इकोसिस्टम ने पीछा किया। छोटे मॉडल वाकई इस्तेमाल-योग्य हो गए। 10B से कम और यहाँ तक कि 1B से कम मॉडल सुसंगत और उपयोगी हो गए, जिसका मतलब है कि आप किसी लैपटॉप या सस्ते सर्वर पर कुछ सक्षम चला सकते हैं। यह गोपनीयता, विलंब (latency), और पैमाने के अर्थशास्त्र को बदल देता है। कुल असर: क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर से फ़ासला ग़ायब नहीं हुआ, पर ज़्यादातर काम के लिए यह निर्णायक कारक नहीं रहा। निर्णायक कारक बन गए लागत, नियंत्रण, और आपका डेटा कहाँ रहता है।
documents.s: ओपन-वेट मॉडल अचानक प्रतिस्पर्धी क्यों हो गए

documents.t: पूरे क्षेत्र में यह इकलौता सबसे भ्रमित करने वाला बिंदु है। "ओपन" तीन अलग-अलग तरीकों से बहुत काम कर रहा है, और वे एक ही चीज़ नहीं हैं। शब्द आपको असल में क्या मिलता है आपको आमतौर पर क्या नहीं मिलता ओपन वेट ट्रेन किया हुआ मॉडल फ़ाइल (weights)। आप इसे डाउनलोड, चला, फ़ाइन-ट्यून, और सेल्फ़-होस्ट कर सकते हैं। ट्रेनिंग डेटा, और कभी-कभी पूरा ट्रेनिंग कोड। इस्तेमाल किसी कस्टम लाइसेंस से नियंत्रित हो सकता है। ओपन सोर्स (सख़्त) Weights साथ ही OSI-शैली लाइसेंस के तहत ट्रेनिंग/इन्फ़रेंस कोड, इस्तेमाल, संशोधन और पुनर्वितरण की स्वतंत्रता के साथ। फिर भी अक्सर ट्रेनिंग डेटा नहीं। ओपन डेटा असल डेटासेट जिन पर मॉडल ट्रेन हुआ, खुलेआम प्रकाशित। फ़्रंटियर-पैमाने के मॉडलों के लिए दुर्लभ; ज़्यादातर "ओपन" मॉडल ओपन-वेट हैं, ओपन-डेटा नहीं। व्यावहारिक निष्कर्ष: जिन्हें लोग "ओपन सोर्स" कहते हैं वे ज़्यादातर मॉडल असल में ओपन-वेट हैं। आप उन्हें चला और अनुकूलित कर सकते हैं, पर आमतौर पर उन्हें शून्य से पुन: नहीं बना सकते, और आपको लाइसेंस पढ़ना ज़रूरी है। लाइसेंस अलग-अलग होते हैं: कुछ अनुज्ञेय (permissive) लाइसेंसों (Apache 2.0, MIT) के तहत आते हैं जो व्यावसायिक इस्तेमाल के लिए साफ़-सुथरे हैं — मसलन Qwen और Mistral मॉडलों ने ऐतिहासिक रूप से Apache 2.0 इस्तेमाल किया है, और DeepSeek ने प्रमुख रिलीज़ों के लिए MIT इस्तेमाल किया है। कुछ शर्तों वाले कस्टम कम्युनिटी लाइसेंसों के तहत आते हैं — मसलन Meta के Llama लाइसेंस में ऐतिहासिक रूप से एक क्लॉज़ रहा है जो सबसे बड़ी कंपनियों (मासिक सक्रिय उपयोगकर्ताओं के आधार पर) को इसे स्वतंत्र रूप से इस्तेमाल करने से रोकता है। किसी मॉडल पर निर्माण करने से पहले हमेशा उसके विशिष्ट मॉडल कार्ड में लाइसेंस जाँचें। तटस्थ पर महत्वपूर्ण: किसी मॉडल का ओपन-वेट होना आपको बताता है कि आप इसे खुद होस्ट कर सकते हैं; यह आपको क़ानूनी शर्तें नहीं बताता, और यह लाइसेंसिंग या डेटा-रेज़िडेंसी के सवालों को ग़ायब नहीं करता — यह उन्हें आप तक स्थानांतरित कर देता है। आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-06-28। सटीक मौजूदा मॉडल संस्करण, पैरामीटर गिनती, बेंचमार्क स्कोर, और प्रति-टोकन क़ीमतें तेज़ी से बदलती हैं और यहाँ जानबूझकर स्थायी के रूप में नहीं बताई गई हैं। परिदृश्य का टिकाऊ स्वरूप — लैब, आर्केटाइप, और ओपन-वेट बनाम ओपन-सोर्स बनाम ओपन-डेटा का भेद — स्थिर है; विशिष्ट लीडरबोर्ड संख्याएँ नहीं। जो मौजूदा है उसके लिए लिंक किए गए संगठन पेज देखें। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: "ओपन वेट" का असल में क्या मतलब है

documents.t: ओपन-वेट परिवार लगभग हमेशा एक ही मॉडल के बजाय वैरिएंट के एक फैलाव के रूप में आते हैं। चार आर्केटाइप सीख लें और आप किसी भी लैब की लाइनअप एक नज़र में पढ़ सकते हैं। एक ही परिवार — Qwen सबसे साफ़ उदाहरण है — आमतौर पर आपको पूरी सीढ़ी देता है: edge और लैपटॉप के लिए छोटे मॉडल, सर्वरों के लिए मध्यम-आकार के मॉडल, सबसे कठिन कामों के लिए एक बड़ा फ़्लैगशिप, साथ ही कोडिंग- और रीज़निंग-विशेष वैरिएंट। आप उस पायदान को चुनते हैं जो आपके हार्डवेयर और काम में फ़िट हो, न कि "the model"।

ओपन-वेट मॉडल कोई सीधा अपग्रेड नहीं हैं। वे एक अलग सौदा हैं। यहाँ यह अदला-बदली तटस्थ रूप से है। आयाम ओपन-वेट (सेल्फ़-होस्ट या सस्ता होस्ट) क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर (होस्टेड API) सबसे कठिन-काम की क्षमता मज़बूत और तेज़ी से फ़ासला पाटती हुई, पर क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर आमतौर पर सबसे कठिन रीज़निंग, लंबी-अवधि के agentic, और विशिष्ट कामों पर अब भी आगे रहता है सबसे मुश्किल कामों पर आमतौर पर छत पैमाने पर लागत नाटकीय रूप से सस्ता हो सकता है, ख़ासकर सेल्फ़-होस्टेड या बजट होस्ट के ज़रिए प्रति-टोकन प्रीमियम; अनुमानित पर जुड़ता जाता है गोपनीयता / डेटा रेज़िडेंसी आप डेटा को पूरी तरह अपने वातावरण के भीतर रख सकते हैं डेटा आपके नेटवर्क से निकलकर प्रदाता के पास जाता है नियंत्रण और अनुकूलन पूर्ण: फ़ाइन-ट्यून, quantize, किसी संस्करण को पिन करना, ऑफ़लाइन चलाना जितना API उजागर करे उतने तक सीमित; संस्करण आपके नीचे बदल सकते हैं सुरक्षा और ऑप्स का मालिक कौन आप हैं — गार्डरेल, दुरुपयोग फ़िल्टरिंग, अपटाइम, स्केलिंग, और पैचिंग आपका काम है प्रदाता infra चलाता है और बेसलाइन सुरक्षा भेजता है वह आख़िरी पंक्ति ही वह है जिसे लोग कम आँकते हैं। जब आप किसी ओपन-वेट मॉडल को सेल्फ़-होस्ट करते हैं तो आप वे ज़िम्मेदारियाँ भी विरासत में लेते हैं जिन्हें कोई फ़्रंटियर लैब सामान्यतः आपके लिए सोख लेती है: कंटेंट सुरक्षा और दुरुपयोग शमन, डिप्लॉयमेंट को पैच रखना, क्षमता और अपटाइम, और हर नए मॉडल संस्करण का ख़ुद मूल्यांकन। "ओपन वेट" आपको नियंत्रण दिलाता है, और नियंत्रण जितना फ़ायदा है उतना ही लागत भी। इस अदला-बदली के API पक्ष पर लागत की समझ के लिए, देखें टोकन अर्थव्यवस्था।

बिल्कुल दो रास्ते हैं, और ज़्यादातर टीमें अलग-अलग चरणों में दोनों का इस्तेमाल करती हैं। होस्टेड API — कई प्रदाता (ख़ुद लैब और तीसरे-पक्ष के इन्फ़रेंस होस्ट समेत) ओपन-वेट मॉडलों को किसी API के पीछे परोसते हैं, अक्सर OpenAI-compatible। आपको ओपन-मॉडल अर्थशास्त्र मिलता है, इन्फ़्रास्ट्रक्चर का शून्य काम। तब सबसे अच्छा जब आप सर्वर चलाए बिना कम लागत चाहते हैं, पर ध्यान रहे कि आपका डेटा तब भी आपके नेटवर्क से निकलता है। सेल्फ़-होस्ट — weights डाउनलोड करें और उन्हें अपने वातावरण में चलाएँ। अधिकतम गोपनीयता और नियंत्रण, और तब इकलौता विकल्प जब डेटा वाकई आपके नेटवर्क से नहीं निकल सकता। सबसे आसान शुरुआत है Ollama, जो ओपन मॉडलों को एक ही कमांड से खींचकर चलाता है।
documents.s: किसी ओपन मॉडल को वाकई कैसे इस्तेमाल करें

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Ollama इंस्टॉल करें⌄ इसे ollama.com/download (macOS/Windows) से डाउनलोड करें या Linux इंस्टॉल स्क्रिप्ट इस्तेमाल करें। यह आपको ollama कमांड और एक लोकल बैकग्राउंड सर्विस देता है। पूरा वॉकथ्रू Run models locally पेज पर। ←PreviousNext→ 2ऐसी साइज़ चुनें जो आपकी मशीन चला सके⌄ छोटे मॉडलों को कम RAM/VRAM चाहिए। एक लैपटॉप आराम से छोटे वैरिएंट (कुछ GB) चलाता है; बड़े फ़्लैगशिप को असली GPU या सर्वर चाहिए। पहले छोटे से शुरू करें ताकि पुष्टि हो सब काम कर रहा है, फिर अगर गुणवत्ता पर्याप्त न हो तो बड़ा करें। ←PreviousNext→ 3इसे एक कमांड से चलाएँ⌄ ollama run <model> पहले इस्तेमाल पर weights डाउनलोड करता है (कई GB), फिर आपको एक इंटरैक्टिव चैट में छोड़ देता है। पहला रन धीमा होता है क्योंकि यह खींच रहा होता है; बाद के रन कैश से तुरंत होते हैं। ←PreviousNext→ 4इसे अपने कोड से कॉल करें⌄ Ollama एक OpenAI-compatible लोकल endpoint उजागर करता है, तो आप किसी मौजूदा OpenAI-शैली SDK को क्लाउड के बजाय localhost की ओर इशारा कर सकते हैं। अब वही कोड एक निजी, लोकल मॉडल पर चलता है। ←PreviousNext→ Ollama के साथ एक ओपन मॉडल को लोकल खींचें और चलाएँ CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ ollama run qwen3 वह एक कमांड एक Qwen ओपन-वेट मॉडल डाउनलोड करता है और एक लोकल चैट शुरू करता है — कोई API key नहीं, आपकी मशीन से कोई डेटा नहीं निकलता। किसी और परिवार पर उनकी तुलना करने के लिए qwen3 को बदल दें (मसलन कोई Llama, Mistral, या DeepSeek टैग)। किसी दिए गए काम के लिए सही मॉडल चुनना अपने आप में एक कौशल है: देखें मॉडल चुनना।
documents.s: किसी मॉडल को चार चरणों में लोकल आज़माएँ

documents.t: लीडरबोर्ड से मत चुनें। बाधा से चुनें: डेटा आपके नेटवर्क से नहीं निकल सकता → सेल्फ़-होस्टेड ओपन-वेट ही जवाब है, बात ख़त्म। ज़्यादा वॉल्यूम, लागत-संवेदनशील, "काफ़ी अच्छी" गुणवत्ता → ओपन-वेट (होस्टेड या सेल्फ़-होस्टेड) आमतौर पर लागत पर जीतता है। आपको सबसे कठिन कामों पर एकदम बेहतरीन चाहिए → क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर अब भी आगे रहता है — जहाँ मायने रखता है वहाँ इसका इस्तेमाल करें और आसान ट्रैफ़िक को सस्ते ओपन मॉडलों पर रूट करें। आप फ़ाइन-ट्यून, quantize, किसी संस्करण को पिन, या ऑफ़लाइन चलाना चाहते हैं → वह नियंत्रण सिर्फ़ ओपन weights ही देते हैं। सबसे टिकाऊ चाल यह है कि अपने ही असली डेटा पर एक ओपन और एक क्लोज़्ड उम्मीदवार के बीच एक छोटा-सा मूल्यांकन चलाएँ। बेंचमार्क किसी और के काम का वर्णन करते हैं; आपका eval आपके काम का वर्णन करता है। ख़ुद को जाँचें 0/3 Key takeaways ओपन-वेट मॉडलों ने रोज़मर्रा का ज़्यादातर फ़ासला पाट दिया — प्रति-लागत क्षमता, ओपन रीज़निंग मॉडल, और वाकई इस्तेमाल-योग्य छोटे मॉडलों की बदौलत 'ओपन वेट' = डाउनलोड-योग्य weights जिन्हें आप चला और फ़ाइन-ट्यून कर सकते हैं — ज़रूरी नहीं कि ओपन-सोर्स कोड, ओपन ट्रेनिंग डेटा, या अनुज्ञेय लाइसेंस; हमेशा मॉडल कार्ड पढ़ें किसी भी लाइनअप को आर्केटाइप से पढ़ें: जनरल चैट, रीज़निंग, कोडिंग, और छोटा/किफ़ायती — ज़्यादातर परिवार पूरी साइज़ सीढ़ी भेजते हैं अदला-बदली असली है: ओपन लागत, गोपनीयता और नियंत्रण दिलाता है, पर क्लोज़्ड फ़्रंटियर आमतौर पर सबसे कठिन कामों पर आगे रहता है और आप सुरक्षा व infra विरासत में लेते हैं इन्हें इस्तेमाल करने के दो तरीके: एक होस्टेड (अक्सर OpenAI-compatible) API, या एक कमांड से Ollama के ज़रिए सेल्फ़-होस्ट — फिर लीडरबोर्ड पर नहीं, अपने डेटा पर मूल्यांकन करें
documents.s: व्यवहार में, ओपन और क्लोज़्ड के बीच चुनना

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम At 04:00 UTC on September 10, 2026, DeepSeek flipped its API to a new model and published the weights the same day: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served as deepseek-flash. It is the smallest member of a new architecture family, but it is not a small model: 552 billion parameters, a 1-million-token context, native vision, and a KV cache that costs 890 bytes per token. On DeepSWE v1.1, the long-horizon software-engineering benchmark both Google and Anthropic now headline, DeepSeek reports 74.2, one-fifth of a point above Claude Opus 5. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reports 31.2 against Opus 5's 51.8. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them is the whole story. This page is the field guide for a Claude user: what actually changed, the routing change that quietly re-pointed every deepseek-v4-pro request, the effort dial and what it does to your bill, how to run the weights, and the workloads where Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Read the V4.1-Flash launch numbers the way they deserve: tied with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, far behind on Terminal-Bench, and why that split is not a contradiction Understand the new Causal Encoder-Decoder + CSA2 design well enough to know what the 890-byte KV cache buys you (and what DeepSeek says it has not yet characterized) Use the 1–100 reasoning_effort dial deliberately — 25 vs 100 is an 8-point DeepSWE swing for ~2.5× the output tokens Do the honest cost math: $0.30 / $1.20 peak, half that off-peak, $0.003 per million on an off-peak cache hit — and the UTC peak window that decides which rate you pay Know the September 14 routing change: deepseek-v4-pro now silently serves V4.1-Flash until V4.1-Pro ships Pick a serving path (hosted API, vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner) and the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-15। Model ID, routing dates, and pricing from DeepSeek's September 10 announcement and the API pricing page. Architecture, license, reasoning-effort range, and sampling defaults from the Hugging Face model card. Benchmark comparisons against Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol are DeepSeek's own launch table as reported by VentureBeat on September 10; treat them as vendor-run until an independent harness publishes. The 3.0/4.0 Terminal-Bench gaps come from the same table. DeepSeek's statement that the architecture has "robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized" is quoted from the same coverage. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026)

documents.t: V4.1-Flash is DeepSeek's first model on a new architecture (a "Causal Encoder-Decoder" with Compressed Sparse Attention 2), released MIT-licensed with native vision, a 1M-token window, 384K max output, and a continuously controllable reasoning effort from 1 to 100. It replaces every V4-era Flash endpoint immediately and, since September 14, also answers every deepseek-v4-pro call at Flash prices until V4.1-Pro lands.

DeepSeek's launch table, in the columns that matter for an agent shop: Benchmark DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Claude Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (resolved) 74.2 74.0 73.0 Terminal-Bench 3.0 30.0 43.3 — Terminal-Bench 4.0 31.2 51.8 — CyberGym 88.1 — — AutomationBench 54.8 — — DeepSWE rewards a model that reads a repository, plans a patch, and lands it: long context, careful retrieval, a few large edits. Terminal-Bench rewards many short, adaptive shell turns where each decision depends on the last tool result. V4.1-Flash has 1M tokens of context and a cheap cache, so the first shape suits it. It runs 8B active parameters per token at prefill and 16B at decode, which is a lot less "thinking per step" than a dense frontier model, so the second shape hurts. If your work looks like a pull request, the parity claim is credible and worth an eval. If your work looks like an interactive terminal session, the 20-point Terminal-Bench gap is the number to budget around. The same split shows up in Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash launch a week earlier, and for the same architectural reasons. The base-model rows tell a quieter story: MMLU-Pro 74.1 (V4-Flash 68.3, V4-Pro 73.5), HumanEval 79.4 (V4-Flash 69.5), GSM8K 93.0 (V4-Flash 90.8). The new "Flash" is a better base than last month's "Pro", which is why DeepSeek was comfortable routing Pro traffic onto it.
documents.s: 1. DeepSWE parity and Terminal-Bench deficit are the same fact seen twice

documents.t: Unlike Claude's effort (low/medium/high/max), V4.1-Flash exposes an integer from 1 to 100. DeepSeek's own ablation on DeepSWE v1.1: effort 25 scores 66.0%, effort 100 scores 74.2%, and the top setting emits roughly 2.5× as many output tokens. They also say the 60–80 band delivers most of the maximum-effort accuracy at less than half the token budget. Every benchmark row above was run at reasoning_effort=100. So the parity number is the expensive number. Reproduce it at 100 first, then walk down to the cheapest setting your evals still pass at. That is the same discipline we recommend for thinking_level on Gemini and effort on Claude in Reasoning models compared.
documents.s: 2. The reasoning-effort dial is a real dial, and it is on your bill

documents.t: From September 10, deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp route to V4.1-Flash, billed at Flash rates. The V4-Flash-Vision-Exp page's numbers now describe the open weights, not the hosted endpoint. From 04:00 UTC September 14, every deepseek-v4-pro request also routes to V4.1-Flash at Flash rates, "until V4.1-Pro launches". If you have evals pinned to deepseek-v4-pro, your production model changed under you on Sunday morning. Re-run the suite. The upside is that the same call now costs roughly a quarter of the Pro rate; the downside is that any Pro-specific behavior you tuned for is gone. This is exactly the failure mode Porting prompts across models warns about when a provider aliases model IDs.
documents.s: 3. Two routing changes happened without a client-side change

documents.t: Spec DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash API model ID deepseek-flash Release September 10, 2026 (API + open weights same day) Parameters 552B total; 8B active at prefill, 16B at decode MoE layout 384 routed + 1 shared expert per MoE layer; 6 routed experts active per token Architecture Causal Encoder-Decoder, Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2) KV cache 890 bytes per token (FP4, E2M1): ~1/4 of V4-Flash in HBM, ~1/8 in SSD storage; global KV cache lifetime at least 72 hours Context / max output 1M tokens / 384K tokens Vision Native; DeepSeek-ViT trained from scratch, 2D-RoPE, 3×3 pixel-unshuffle downsampling Reasoning control reasoning_effort integer 1–100 License MIT Weights Safetensors in BF16, F32, F8_E4M3, I8 Serving vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, Transformers; reference inference code in the inference/ folder Recommended sampling temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context 1M API concurrency 2,500 The KV-cache line is the architectural headline. A 1M-token conversation at 890 bytes per token is under a gigabyte of cache, which is why DeepSeek can promise a 72-hour cache lifetime and price cache hits at fractions of a cent. Anthropic's answer to the same problem is a cheaper cache-read rate on Claude Fable 5.1; DeepSeek's is to make the cache physically small. Both push you toward the same habit: put the stable prefix first and never edit it mid-run. See Prompt caching.

DeepSeek keeps a two-rate schedule. Peak hours are 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC, Monday through Friday; everything else is off-peak at exactly half the peak rate. Per 1M tokens Peak Off-peak Input, cache hit $0.006 $0.003 Input, cache miss $0.30 $0.15 Output $1.20 $0.60 Two things follow. First, the "$0.003 per million" headline is the off-peak cache-hit price, the cheapest of six cells; a cold, peak-hour agent run pays 100× that on input. Second, the peak window is defined in UTC and covers the European morning and the tail of the U.S. night. A batch job scheduled at 09:00 UTC pays double what the same job pays at 11:00 UTC. If you can shift, shift. For a framework that puts these cells beside Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google list prices, use What AI costs across providers; current Claude list prices live on Models and pricing.

Hosted is right for almost everyone: the model is enormous, and the API is the cheapest thing on this page. Self-host when data cannot leave your network or when you want the effort dial and 1M window without a rate limit. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide hosted vs self-hosted honestly⌄ 552B parameters in BF16 is over a terabyte of weights; the F8_E4M3 and I8 safetensors halve or quarter that but still need a multi-GPU node. If you do not already run Kimi K3 or Colibrì-class MoEs, the hosted endpoint at $0.30 / $1.20 peak will beat your amortized hardware bill. See the hardware math on Running Kimi K3 locally. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a serving stack the card actually names⌄ vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, and Transformers are the four listed. The card ships no Jinja chat template; it uses a custom encoding implementation, so use the reference code in the repo's inference folder (or the deepseek-recipe toolkit) rather than hand-rolling the prompt format. ←PreviousNext→ 3Set the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends⌄ temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context window 1M. These are the settings the benchmark rows were produced with. Do not port a Claude-tuned temperature of 0.2 over blindly. ←PreviousNext→ 4Start at reasoning_effort=100, then walk down⌄ Reproduce DeepSeek's number on your own eval first. Then try 80, 60, 40 and record accuracy vs output tokens. Most teams will land in the 60–80 band the vendor itself points at. ←PreviousNext→ 5Test long-context retrieval before you trust it⌄ DeepSeek says the new architecture has robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized, specifically sparse retrieval over very long contexts. Run a needle-in-haystack and a multi-hop retrieval test at the context length you will actually use. Treat the 1M number as a ceiling, not a promise. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted call with the effort dial (OpenAI-compatible endpoint) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ curl https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-flash", "reasoning_effort": 70, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Here is the log and the relevant module: ..."} ] }' Self-hosted with vLLM (shape only; check the model card for the exact flags) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # One node, tensor-parallel across all visible GPUs. # The card names vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner and Transformers as supported. vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --max-model-len 1000000 \ --trust-remote-code # Then hit http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions with the same body as above.

Pro tip Reach for V4.1-Flash: repository-scale coding tasks that look like DeepSWE (read a lot, edit a little), where you can run at effort 60–100 and the cost per resolved issue still undercuts Claude by an order of magnitude. Reach for V4.1-Flash: anything that needs a 1M-token window and a warm cache for days — a 72-hour global cache lifetime and 890-byte-per-token KV make 'keep the whole codebase in context' cheap. Reach for V4.1-Flash: self-hosted or data-residency workloads where MIT licensing matters and you already run a multi-GPU MoE stack. Stay on Claude: interactive terminal agents and any many-short-turns loop. A 20-point Terminal-Bench 4.0 gap (31.2 vs 51.8) is not noise, and it is the shape of most real Claude Code sessions. Stay on Claude: work that needs Anthropic's tool-use loop, prefilled assistant turns, structured-output strictness, or the safety and retention guarantees of a first-party API. The DeepSeek API is OpenAI-shaped and the model has documented, uncharacterized long-context failure modes. Cross-check both: for a coding agent, run your own eval at DeepSeek's effort=100 and Claude's default effort, then at the cheapest passing setting on each. The vendor tables were run at maximum effort; your bill will not be. For the durable framework behind that list, How to choose a model. For what changes when you move a prompt between an Anthropic-shaped and an OpenAI-shaped API, Porting prompts across models. For the Claude-side reference these comparisons hang off, Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.
documents.s: When to reach for V4.1-Flash, and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways V4.1-Flash is a repository-shaped model: parity with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, a 20-point deficit on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Match it to work that reads a lot and edits a little. The 1–100 effort dial is the price lever. Every launch number is at 100; DeepSeek's own guidance is that 60–80 keeps most of the accuracy at under half the tokens. Six price cells, not one. The $0.003 headline is off-peak cache-hit input; a cold peak-hour token is 100× that. Peak is 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays. Two silent routing changes: V4-Flash endpoints on Sept 10, deepseek-v4-pro on Sept 14. If you pinned Pro, your model changed — re-run evals. The 890-byte KV cache and 72-hour cache lifetime make long-lived 1M-token contexts cheap, but DeepSeek itself flags long-context sparse retrieval as uncharacterized. Test before you trust.

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम At 00:00 UTC on August 31, 2026, DeepSeek quietly pushed a new repository to Hugging Face: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp. Ten days after the same model went live on their API (August 21), the weights are now MIT-licensed and public. This is the first V4-family model with native vision — not a text model with a bolt-on adapter, but a joint-trained multimodal MoE — and its agent scores on the vision side jumped from 26.2 to 36.5 on ApexBench without moving the text-only agent scores at all. On several agent benchmarks it now matches or edges past Claude Opus 4.8 while the API costs $0.22 per million input tokens. This page is the practical field guide the launch didn't come with: what changed architecturally, the numbers that matter, the one hard limit nobody warns you about, how to run it, and when Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Understand what 'native vision' means here — the V4-Flash backbone plus a vision encoder + aligner trained together, not stapled on after Read the benchmark table the way the release intends: text-only agents preserved, vision agents up sharply, both within striking distance of Claude Opus 4.8 Know the hard 384-tokens-per-image architectural cap and why it changes how you prompt Do the honest cost math: $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 (cached) per million tokens vs Claude Opus 4.8 at $15 / $75 Pick the right serving path — hosted API for almost everyone, vLLM + DSpark for a real self-hosted run

documents.t: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is a 305-billion-parameter sparse-MoE multimodal model — 13B active per token, 1.048M-token context — that adds joint-trained vision to the V4-Flash text backbone, ships open under MIT on Hugging Face on August 31 2026, and delivers agent-tier multimodal performance at roughly one-fortieth of Claude Opus 4.8's per-token price.

Every open lab that has bolted vision onto a strong text model has paid a tax on text benchmarks. DeepSeek's release table is the flex: on Terminal Bench 2.1 the vision model scores 83.9 (vs 82.7 for the text-only V4-Flash-0731); on DeepSWE it climbs to 59.3 (from 54.4); on Toolathlon-Verified to 75.9 (from 70.3). None of these are vision tasks — they're pure code and tool-use agent evals. The vision variant is better on text-agent work than the text-only checkpoint, not worse. This matters because it's the "prove-out" the field has been waiting for since Chameleon: you can jointly train a giant MoE for text and vision without the multimodal add causing text regression, as long as the vision head lands late enough and the router gets to keep specializing text experts.
documents.s: 1. Vision was added without breaking the text agents — that's the whole point

documents.t: This is the single most important thing to learn before writing your first prompt. The vision encoder in V4-Flash-Vision-Exp allocates at most 384 tokens per image — and that ceiling is architectural, not a commercial policy. There is no "high-detail" mode that unlocks more. Practical consequences: Big screenshots lose fine text. A 2560×1440 dashboard, a dense CSV rendered as an image, or a long PDF page will be encoded at whatever resolution 384 tokens of visual features can express — meaning small-font text will not survive round-trip. Crop, don't scale. If you need to read numbers off a chart, send the chart cropped to the region of interest, not the whole page. Multi-image beats one giant image. Split large documents into per-region tiles; each tile gets its own 384-token budget. This is why Chartography lands at 64.3 (competitive with Claude Opus 4.8's 65.0) but why the model will still miss a footnote in a 12-point font on a full-page screenshot. Every vision-agent workflow you build should assume this ceiling. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-01। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: 2. The vision encoder has a hard 384-tokens-per-image budget

documents.t: Most published MoE recipes activate 8 experts of 32 or 64. V4-Flash-Vision-Exp uses a much wider expert bank: 256 routed experts + 1 shared expert, with only 6 routed experts firing per token — a 2.3% activation ratio. The model has 43 layers, hidden size 4,096, and the hybrid attention stack combines two mechanisms: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) — sparse patterns for long-range reads. Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) — an aggressively compressed form for the deep-context tail. Wrapped over that, Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) replace the standard residual with a constrained-manifold projection, which the paper reports stabilizes signal propagation through the 43-layer stack. Together these are the reason the model can advertise a 1,048,576-token context window without the quadratic attention bill.
documents.s: 3. The MoE routing is unusually sparse — 6 of 256 experts fire per token

documents.t: Sticker prices, all per million tokens: Model Input Output Cached read DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (API) $0.22 $0.66 $0.007 Claude Opus 4.8 $15.00 $75.00 $1.50 Kimi K3 (cache-miss / cache-hit) $3.00 / $0.30 $15.00 $0.30 Cached-read at $0.007/M is not a typo — that is roughly one two-hundredth of a cent per thousand tokens. For any workload where a repeating system prompt or long context is re-sent (agent loops, RAG over a static corpus, chat with a fixed persona) the effective input price collapses. This is the reason V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is showing up in agent-cost tables at a fraction of what Claude Opus 4.8 costs per task, even when the raw quality is within a few points. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-01। Prices, context window and MoE routing are from the official model card at release. See Freshness half-life for how quickly these numbers move. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

Benchmark V4-Flash-Vision-Exp V4-Flash-0731 Claude Opus 4.8 Text agents Terminal Bench 2.1 83.9 82.7 85.0 NL2Repo 57.7 54.2 69.7 DeepSWE 59.3 54.4 58.0 Toolathlon-Verified 75.9 70.3 76.2 Multimodal agents ApexBench (Pass@1) 36.5 26.2† 39.4 Agents' Last Exam 27.3 25.2† 25.7 Chartography 64.3 — 65.0 ZeroBench (Pass@5) 35.0 — 34.0 † Prior text-only checkpoint scored on images it couldn't natively read — a floor, not a fair fight. Reading the table straight: On text-agent work, V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is within a few points of Claude Opus 4.8 across the board, and actively beats V4-Flash-0731 on every eval. Vision was added without regression. On multimodal agents, it beats Claude Opus 4.8 on Agents' Last Exam and ZeroBench Pass@5, trails narrowly on ApexBench and Chartography. This is the first open-weight release where "matches Opus on multimodal agents" is not a marketing line. The one benchmark that's not close is NL2Repo (57.7 vs 69.7). Whole-repository code translation is still a place where the closed frontier holds a real gap. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-01। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

documents.t: V4-Flash-Vision-Exp launched on the DeepSeek API on August 21, 2026, and only landed on Hugging Face as open weights on August 31. This ten-day gap is DeepSeek's new default. Compare Z.ai (GLM), which has been shipping API + weights simultaneously; DeepSeek is deliberately sequencing. The industry read: labs now agree that big open MoEs are shipping. The remaining question is when in the release cycle the weights arrive. For production planning that means: If you need on-prem from day zero, watch for GLM-family releases. If you can start on the API and cut over to self-hosted a week or two later, DeepSeek is the pattern.
documents.s: The release pattern — API first, weights ten days later

documents.t: There are three realistic paths. Pick by the two constraints that actually matter: whether the weights need to live on your infrastructure, and how much VRAM (or RAM) you can pay for. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Path A — DeepSeek's hosted API (default for almost everyone)⌄ OpenAI-compatible endpoint at api.deepseek.com. Model ID is deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp. Pricing is $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 per million tokens. This is the right answer unless you have a data-residency or air-gap constraint. ←PreviousNext→ 2Path B — vLLM on 4× GB300 (single-node self-host)⌄ The vLLM container ships day-0 support and the deepseek_v4 tool-call parser. You need one node with 4× GB300 (or equivalent B300 config). DSpark speculative decoding is enabled via --speculative-config. FP8 KV cache and block-size 256 are both required for the throughput numbers DeepSeek published. ←PreviousNext→ 3Path C — Community GGUF via llama.cpp / Ollama (workstation-class)⌄ unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF ships two dynamic quants: UD-Q4_K_XL at 155 GB and UD-Q8_K_XL at 162 GB. Neither fits a single 24/48/80 GB GPU. What works is a fat workstation with 192 GB+ system RAM and offload, or a small multi-GPU rig with CPU spillover. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted API — Python (OpenAI-compatible) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_DEEPSEEK_KEY", base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp", messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "What does this chart claim, and what's the one thing it hides?"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/chart.png"}}, ], } ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) Self-host — vLLM on 4× GB300 with DSpark CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv4-flash-vision \ deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 256 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' Local — Ollama with the community GGUF CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ ollama run hf.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL # Compact image syntax the model was trained to accept: # <image>path/to/screenshot.png</image> followed by your prompt

Reach for V4-Flash-Vision when: You need multimodal agent quality at roughly Opus-4.8 tier and cost is a factor. Cached-read pricing crushes anything on the closed frontier. The workload benefits from a 1M-token context (long-document VQA, whole-video-frame analysis, big-repo review with screenshots). You need open weights for compliance, air-gapped work, or fine-tuning, and you have (or rent) frontier-class hardware. You're building a chart-heavy or dashboard-parsing pipeline where you can control image tiling. Stay on Claude Opus 4.8 (or Sonnet 5) when: The job is whole-repository code translation or synthesis — NL2Repo is the outlier where the gap is real (57.7 vs 69.7). You need Claude-specific features: Extended thinking under budget, Skills, Sub-agent orchestration in Claude Code, or the Managed Agents session-budget controls. Your prompts contain images with tiny critical text and you cannot tile — you'll hit the 384-token cap and lose accuracy. You want a single vendor / SLA / support contact and are already invested in Anthropic tooling. For a broader model-choice framework, see How to choose a model. For a side-by-side of the whole open-weight wave, DeepSeek, Qwen & the Open-Weight Wave is the durable overview.
documents.s: When to reach for V4-Flash-Vision — and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: You will forget the 384-token cap. The first three vision agents you build will overshoot resolution and quietly lose accuracy on small text. Instrument for it: log per-image dimensions and downscale + tile deliberately. DSpark drops silently if you skip --speculative-config. Without the flag, vLLM will happily serve the model at 1/3 the throughput the release announced. Always pass the speculative config in production. The GGUF is not a laptop model. UD-Q4_K_XL is 155 GB. Community threads that show it "running" on smaller boxes are running it at fractional tokens/s via SSD swap — technically working, not usable. API vs weights version parity is not guaranteed. The API model can be silently updated; the Hugging Face weights are pinned to Vision-Exp. If a benchmark shifts a few points month-to-month on the API, that's why. Exp means experimental. The vision variant is not guaranteed to survive into production V4 releases. Do not build a critical pipeline on the assumption that this specific checkpoint will be around in a year.

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-11-02। agent-desktop reached v1.0.0 on 28 October 2026 and v1.0.2 two days later. A project moving at that cadence will change command names, flags and error codes. Everything below is read from the repository's own README.md and CONCEPTS.md at the start of November 2026 — check agent-desktop --help and the CHANGELOG before you depend on a specific flag. The design model in the second half is the durable part and is worth reading even if you never install this tool. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत. What you'll learn Understand what an accessibility-tree agent reads, and how it differs from a screenshot agent at the protocol level Learn the retry rule that most computer-use harnesses get wrong — and why 'did it fail?' is the wrong question See why refs are scoped to a snapshot, and what a harness should do instead of guessing when one goes stale Know the three-state property model that stops an agent acting on a failed read Spot the two failure modes this approach does NOT fix: truncated trees and apps with no accessibility surface Understand the security surface: everything on screen becomes agent input On 28 October 2026 Vercel Labs tagged v1.0.0 of agent-desktop, and by 31 October it was at the top of GitHub's trending list. It is a Rust CLI and C library, Apache-2.0, that gives an agent computer use on macOS, Windows and Linux by reading the operating system's accessibility tree — the same structure a screen reader consumes: AX API on macOS, UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux. Vercel's own framing is "agent-browser, for your whole computer." Every write-up so far stops at the headline: trees instead of pixels, so clicks land where they should. That is true and it is the least interesting half. The interesting half is that the repository ships a CONCEPTS.md which is, in effect, a specification for how a computer-use harness should handle uncertainty — and it answers questions that the mainstream computer-use APIs leave entirely to you. If you build agent loops, read this page for the model even if you never install the tool. Our computer-use agents compared page covers the screenshot-based APIs from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google; this is the other architecture.

A screenshot agent gets an image and returns coordinates. The contract is: here are some pixels, tell me where to click. Everything the agent knows about the UI it has to infer visually, and every action is a bet on a coordinate. A tree agent gets structure. A snapshot returns JSON with a ref for every element the agent can act on, and actions name a ref rather than a point. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Observe⌄ Snapshot the accessibility tree of a window, app or surface. You get back JSON — roles, names, states — with a ref per actionable node, and a snapshot ID that the refs belong to. ←PreviousNext→ 2Resolve⌄ Before the action fires, the ref is re-matched against the CURRENT live tree using identity evidence stored at snapshot time. This step is the whole ballgame and is covered below. ←PreviousNext→ 3Act⌄ Dispatch under an interaction lease — machine-wide exclusivity over desktop input, held by one process at a time, so two callers cannot interleave synthetic input into each other's actions. ←PreviousNext→ 4Verify⌄ Re-read the element to confirm the change actually reached it. A mutation is only 'delivered' once a re-read says so. ←PreviousNext→ The practical differences that follow from this are larger than they look: Refs survive layout changes that break coordinates. A button that moves 200 px down the window is the same node in the tree. For a screenshot agent it is a new bet. It is headless by default. Input goes through the accessibility API without moving the system pointer or stealing focus, so the agent can drive apps while you keep using the machine. A --headed mode exists for physical input synthesis when an app ignores programmatic input. This is a genuinely different operating model from screenshot agents, which fight you for the cursor. Snapshots are text, not images. That matters for your bill and your context window — see why agents burn tokens. But it is not a free win, because dense trees get large; the repo's own answer is to map coarsely first (--skeleton --compact) and then drill into a region with --root. You still need screenshots sometimes. The tool ships screenshot alongside snapshot. Canvas-rendered apps, custom-drawn UIs and games have little or no accessibility surface, and no amount of tree-reading invents one. The minimal observe / act / verify loop CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop version # macOS only: accessibility permission must be granted first agent-desktop permissions --guide # 1. observe — -i limits output to interactive elements agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # 2. act — the ref MUST carry its snapshot ID; a bare @e8 is rejected agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # 3. verify — re-snapshot and confirm the change landed agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # dense UI? map coarsely, then drill into one region agent-desktop snapshot --app Slack --skeleton --compact agent-desktop snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e42 Output is JSON with an ok boolean and either data or an error carrying a code, a disposition and a suggestion. The commands group into observe (snapshot, find, get, screenshot, list-surfaces), act-on-ref (click, type, set-value, scroll, toggle, expand), raw keyboard and mouse (press, hover, drag, key-down), window and app management (launch, focus-window, resize-window, list-apps), and system (permissions, status, batch, skills).
documents.s: What changes when you read the tree instead of the screen

documents.t: Here is the rule, and it is the single most useful thing in the repository: The distinction that matters is not success versus failure. It is delivered versus not delivered. Think about what an agent does when a type command returns an error. The instinctive harness behaviour — retry on error — is actively dangerous, because "error" conflates two completely different situations: The keystrokes never reached the field. Retrying is free. The keystrokes may have landed and the confirmation read failed. Retrying types everything twice. A harness that cannot tell these apart will silently double-submit forms, double-click Send, and duplicate rows. So agent-desktop classifies every mutation into three delivery states instead of a boolean: Delivery state Meaning Retry? Not delivered Argument error, access denial, or a read-only command — the action demonstrably never reached the target Safe. Retry freely Delivered unverified Input was posted but the effect is unconfirmed — the typical outcome of physical input synthesis Unsafe. Re-reading state is the only correct move Delivered Effect confirmed by re-reading the element Done; nothing to retry Reads get a parallel four-way classification, and the first one is the subtle one: Settled absence — the provider was asked and the target genuinely lacks that property or pattern. A final answer, never retried. Retryable failure — a transport fault such as a timeout or dropped connection. Worth repeating within a budget. Unavailable element — it disappeared. Settles as a stale ref if the element had been resolved; retryable if hit mid-walk. Terminal failure — a denial or an unclassified code. Final, surfaced as-is. The tool exposes this directly: you retry only when error.disposition.retry says safe. Key takeaways If you are writing your own computer-use loop today, port this one idea even if you port nothing else. Classify every action by whether it could have landed, and make 'may have landed' a distinct branch that re-reads state instead of retrying. Idempotency is not a property of your retry code — it is a property of each individual action, and only the tool layer knows which is which.
documents.s: The idea worth stealing: delivered, not successful

documents.t: In agent-desktop a ref looks like @e8, but you may never use it bare — a bare ref fails with INVALID_ARGS. It must be qualified by its snapshot ID: @s8f3k2p9:e8. That looks like friction. It is a deliberate type system. The stated reason: refs are deterministic inside one snapshot but are not stable across UI changes. The snapshot ID is a namespace, and every lookup is confined to the namespace it was created in — a snapshot taken under a session needs that same session scope later. So the awkward syntax makes a real category error unrepresentable. You cannot accidentally carry an identifier from an observation three actions ago and have it silently resolve to whatever now occupies that slot. Compare the screenshot world, where a coordinate from a stale screenshot is syntactically indistinguishable from a fresh one and resolves to something every time.
documents.s: Why refs are scoped to a snapshot

documents.t: When the action fires, the ref is resolved against the live tree through a graded sequence, and the ordering encodes a judgement about which evidence is trustworthy: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Walk the stored positional path⌄ Follow the path recorded at snapshot time down the current tree. ←PreviousNext→ 2Verify against stored identity evidence⌄ Check the candidate against what was recorded: native ID first, then role-conditional stable text. Position gets you to a candidate; identity decides whether it is the right one. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fall back to a bounded broad search⌄ If the path no longer exists, search more widely — but with a bound, not indefinitely. ←PreviousNext→ 4Only then, geometry⌄ Resolve by unique geometry as a last resort, and only when the ref has NO meaningful identity to match on. On Windows and Linux the stored bounds must be a positive-area rectangle — a zero-extent stored hash never promotes to a geometric match. ←PreviousNext→ The design commitment is in what happens when none of that produces a confident match: the resolution fails closed. Missing, stale and ambiguous matches are rejected — STALE_REF, AMBIGUOUS_TARGET — rather than resolved to a best guess. On macOS the implementation retains the native accessibility objects specifically so an element cannot be silently misidentified when tree ordering shifts underneath it. This is the opposite of how a pixel agent degrades. A stale coordinate always hits something; a stale ref returns an error. Trading a silent wrong action for a loud failure is the entire reliability claim, and it is the right trade for anything an agent does unsupervised. What you'll learn The same reasoning shows up in the repo's two-sided treatment of partial results: if a snapshot runs out of its time budget mid-walk, it returns what it observed rather than discarding the walk — but it reports completeness per node. A harness that ignores that field will confidently reason over a truncated tree and conclude a button does not exist. Check completeness before you conclude absence.

A smaller mechanism with outsized consequences. Properties are never collapsed to a boolean. Three states stay distinct: Known — a value was read. Absent — the provider was asked and genuinely has no value. Unknown — the read itself failed. Most harnesses flatten Unknown into false or null, and an agent then acts on a failed read as if it were a negative result: the checkbox "isn't checked" (we could not read it), the field "is empty" (the query errored). The repo's phrasing is that uncertainty must travel — when a higher-priority evidence source fails, that failure is carried forward rather than smoothed away. Accessible names are computed in the core from ranked slots rather than in each platform adapter, so shared logic never sees a platform-specific token and the same uncertainty rules apply everywhere. If you take two things from this page, take delivery semantics and this. They are both cases of the same discipline: do not let a failure to know masquerade as knowledge.

The interaction lease covers dispatch only. Input exclusivity is machine-wide and held by one process at a time, but the lease deliberately does not cover the waiting that precedes an action, because waiting for an element to become actionable can run long. The practical consequence: an element can become actionable and then change again between your wait and your dispatch. That is exactly why the verify step is not optional. Platform support is not uniform, and Linux is the ragged edge. Accessibility tree, clicking and typing work across all three OSes, but on Linux clicking and typing run through AT-SPI with X11/GNOME caveats, screenshots need X11 or a Wayland portal, the clipboard needs wl-clipboard under Wayland, app management is launch-and-list only, and notifications are GNOME Shell. macOS needs accessibility permission granted explicitly, plus a TMPDIR that is user-owned with mode 0700. Windows needs no special permission at matching terminal integrity level. Of roughly 60 commands, not all are operational on every platform — check agent-desktop status on the machine you actually plan to run on.

This needs stating plainly, because the convenience is seductive. An accessibility-tree agent reads the text content of applications, which is a strictly richer capture than a screenshot of the focused window — including, potentially, content that is on screen but not what you were looking at. The repo is explicit that snapshots, screenshots and clipboard contents can contain sensitive data and should be kept out of public logs. It does build in one real mitigation: secure fields. Once a platform marks an element secret, the read path withholds both its value and related text evidence, and the action path may write into it but never echoes the attempted or observed value. That protects passwords. It does not protect the open email, the Slack DM, or the customer record in the next window. Two consequences: Transcripts become sensitive artifacts. Agent logs from a desktop session are closer to a screen recording than to a terminal history. Treat them accordingly — see what your agent uploads. Every readable surface is an injection surface. Any text an app displays becomes agent input, so a crafted calendar invite, filename or chat message is a prompt-injection vector with no network request involved. The same reasoning as the web your agent reads applies to the desktop, and prompt injection is the primer. An agent with machine-wide input exclusivity and no pointer movement is also, by construction, one whose actions you will not see happening. Watch out Headless-by-default is a usability feature and a supervision hazard at the same time. Because the agent does not move your pointer or steal focus, there is no ambient signal that it is acting. If you run this unattended, the compensating control has to be the log and a scoped-down target app — not your attention. Our hardening-autonomous-runs page covers the general pattern.
documents.s: The security surface is the whole screen

documents.t: Situation Reach for Native desktop app with real accessibility support (Finder, Office, most Cocoa/WinUI apps) Tree agent. Stable refs, cheap text snapshots, no coordinate math Web app in a browser A browser-specific harness first — the DOM is a better tree than the browser's AX projection. See computer-use agents compared and shared-login browsers Canvas/WebGL app, game, custom-drawn UI, remote desktop Screenshot agent. There is no accessibility surface to read Agent must run while you keep working Tree agent, headless mode — no focus stealing, no pointer fight Unsupervised, repeated, mutating actions Tree agent, and honour the delivery semantics. This is the case the whole design exists for Visual verification ("does this look right?") Screenshot, regardless of harness. A tree cannot tell you the layout is broken Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways Accessibility trees replace a coordinate bet with a named reference, so layout changes that break a screenshot agent are a non-event — but canvas, games and custom-drawn UIs have no tree to read. Steal the delivery model: classify actions by whether they COULD have landed, not by whether they returned an error. 'May have landed' deserves a re-read, never a retry. Scoping refs to a snapshot is a type system, not friction — it makes stale-identifier bugs impossible to express rather than silently wrong. Fail-closed resolution is the reliability claim: a stale coordinate always hits something, a stale ref returns STALE_REF. Prefer the loud failure for anything unsupervised. Keep Unknown distinct from Absent. An agent that reads a failed query as a negative result will act confidently on nothing. Headless operation removes the ambient signal that an agent is working. If you run it unattended, logs and a scoped target app are the control — not your attention.

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत Every model on AILmanac so far generates text the same way: one token, then the next, left to right, forever. A different family of models does not. It starts with a blank canvas of masked positions, predicts all of them at once, keeps the ones it is confident about, and repeats. Position 40 can be decided before position 7. The numbers are the reason anyone cares. Inception's Mercury 2 — a reasoning model — reportedly runs at 1,009 tokens/sec on Blackwell GPUs with 1.7 s end-to-end latency, roughly 8–14× faster than comparable reasoning-enabled competitors (The Decoder). Google's experimental Gemini Diffusion samples at 1,479 tokens/sec excluding overhead, against Gemini 2.5 Flash's 272.4 (Techmeme roundup). And yet the README of LLaDA — the 8B open-weight model that proved the approach at scale — tells you its quality peaks when the number of sampling steps equals the response length. One forward pass per token. Exactly like an autoregressive model, but without a KV cache, so slower. Both facts are true. This lesson is the bridge between them: what the algorithm actually does, which knob buys the speed and what it costs, the two structural limits that made early diffusion LLMs unusable and the fix that shipped, and the three gotchas (streaming, length billing, and a jailbreak class that does not exist on autoregressive models) you need before you put one in production. What you'll learn Describe masked-diffusion generation in terms of a canvas, a denoising pass, and a commit decision — and say what bidirectional attention buys and costs Use the steps knob correctly: compute tokens-per-forward-pass, and explain the conditional-independence failure that makes aggressive parallelism wrong rather than merely worse Explain why block diffusion is on every dLLM you can actually call today — it is what restored the KV cache, variable-length output, and token streaming Pick the jobs where a dLLM genuinely wins: infilling and any-order edits, latency-bound voice, and bounded decisions — not 'everything, but faster' Treat an open dLLM endpoint as unaligned at the boundary, because masked-infill prompts bypass alignment in a way autoregressive refusals cannot आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-10-02। Every price, context window, tokens-per-second and latency figure here is perishable — this field is moving monthly and Inception's rate card currently carries promotional discounts. Check the vendor's own model page and the independent leaderboards before quoting any number in a decision. Research claims are cited to their papers; several are preprints, not replicated results. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: Diffusion LLMs: The Models That Don't Write Left to Right

documents.t: An autoregressive (AR) model's loop is: read the whole prefix, emit a probability distribution over one position (the next one), sample, append, repeat. The KV cache is what makes this cheap — the keys and values for every earlier token were computed once and never change, because attention is causal and nothing to the right exists yet. A masked diffusion LLM inverts that. Attention is bidirectional: every position attends to every other position, in both directions. So in a single forward pass the model produces a distribution for every masked position simultaneously. Generation becomes an iterative refinement of a whole answer, not a walk along it. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Lay out a canvas⌄ Decide a generation length L. Fill all L positions with a special mask token. On a pure masked dLLM (LLaDA, Dream), L is fixed before the first forward pass — the model does not grow the sequence as it goes. ←PreviousNext→ 2One denoising pass predicts everything⌄ The transformer runs once over prompt + canvas and returns a distribution for every masked slot at once. Not 'the next token' — slot 3, slot 17 and slot 240, in the same pass. ←PreviousNext→ 3Commit a subset (this is the whole game)⌄ You unmask some of those predictions and freeze them as real tokens. Which ones, and how many, is the decoding policy: random order, highest top-1 confidence, largest top1−top2 margin, or lowest entropy. Everything else stays masked. ←PreviousNext→ 4Re-run with the committed tokens as context⌄ The next pass sees the frozen tokens and re-predicts the remaining masks — and because attention is bidirectional, a token committed at the END of the answer conditions the tokens still missing from the middle. This is what AR models cannot do. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stop when the canvas is full⌄ Total cost = (number of passes) × (one full forward pass). So tokens per forward pass = L / steps. That ratio, not the hardware, is where the headline tokens/sec comes from. ←PreviousNext→ That last line is the one worth memorising. An AR model is pinned at one token per forward pass. A diffusion LLM lets you choose. DiffusionGemma, Google's open-weight entry, reports roughly 20 tokens per forward pass while refining blocks of 256 in parallel, which is how it reaches ~1,500 output tokens/sec on a single H100 (DiffusionGemma Technical Report).
documents.s: The mechanism, in one diagram you have to imagine

documents.t: Dream 7B exposes the knob explicitly. Its diffusion_generate() documents steps as "diffusion timesteps" where max_new_tokens / steps tokens are produced per step, and notes plainly that fewer steps are faster but coarser (DreamLM/Dream, Apache-2.0). So why not always use few steps? Because the error it introduces is not noise — it is a specific, nameable bug. A single forward pass gives you, for each masked slot, a marginal distribution: the probability of a token at that position, averaged over everything still unknown. If you commit two slots from the same pass, you are sampling from the product of their marginals, not from their joint distribution. Any dependency between them is silently discarded. The Fast-dLLM authors state the root cause directly: generation quality degrades under parallel decoding because masked diffusion models sample tokens independently from marginal probabilities when the true joint distribution has dependencies (Fast-dLLM, arXiv:2505.22618). The intuition: ask for a city and two adjacent slots might score "New" and "Delhi" as the most likely token for their own position, because "New York" and "New Delhi" are both plausible. Commit both in one pass and you get neither. The failure mode of over-parallel decoding is not vaguer prose, it is confidently assembled nonsense at the seams. The fix that made the field practical is confidence-aware parallel decoding: compute a confidence per masked slot (typically the max softmax probability), commit only the slots above a threshold, and if none clear it, commit the single highest so the loop still makes progress. Tokens that are nearly independent get decoded together; tokens that depend on each other wait. Fast-dLLM reports up to 27.6× throughput improvement on LLaDA and Dream across benchmarks with minimal accuracy loss — training-free, just a decoding change. That is the shape of this entire research area: the parallelism is free, the independence is not, and the work is in detecting which tokens can safely go together. What you'll learn A confidence threshold is a quality dial you can actually reason about: higher threshold means fewer tokens committed per pass, more passes, slower, closer to AR quality. Fast-dLLM v2 reports a 2.6× speedup on GSM8K at threshold 0.9 with minimal accuracy loss — that is the kind of setting to start from, not 'commit everything'.
documents.s: The steps knob, and why cranking it is wrong rather than just lossy

documents.t: LLaDA's own repository lists its efficiency constraints without euphemism: fixed context length for sampling, no KV-cache support, and degraded performance when sampling steps drop below the response length. The authors frame it as deliberate — they wanted to find the ceiling of the approach before optimising it (ML-GSAI/LLaDA, MIT, ~4k stars, Base and Instruct weights plus LLaDA 1.5, LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B and iLLaDA variants). Stack those up and a pure masked dLLM is nearly unusable as a product: No KV cache. Bidirectional attention means every pass can change any token's context, so cached keys and values are invalid. You recompute the whole sequence every step. Fixed output length. You must pick L before generating. Too small truncates; too large wastes compute on positions you will throw away. Latency worse than AR. Points 1 and 2 together can make a "parallel" model slower end-to-end than the sequential one it replaces. Block diffusion resolves all three by refusing to be pure. Generate in blocks: condition on previous blocks autoregressively, run diffusion inside the current block. That gives flexible sequence length and KV caching between blocks — the BD3-LM formulation, an ICLR 2025 oral (arXiv:2503.09573, kuleshov-group/bd3lms). Fast-dLLM v2 (arXiv:2509.26328) shows what a tuned version looks like, and the details are worth knowing because they explain the vendor behaviour you will observe: Hybrid attention mask. Block-diagonal (bidirectional) within a block, block-causal (left-to-right) between blocks. Bidirectional context where it helps, AR semantics where the cache lives. Two cache levels. A block-level cache holding finished blocks as clean prefix context, plus a sub-block cache (DualCache) for the recomputation that intra-block decoding still needs. Complementary masking in training. Each sample is duplicated into two views with masks m and 1 − m, so every token is supervised both as a mask target and as context. Reported results. Up to 2.5× faster than standard AR decoding; 1.8× at batch size 64 on H100s; a 7B average benchmark score of 60.3 against Dream's 57.6, including HumanEval 63.4 vs 57.9 and GSM8K 62.0 vs 39.2. And the training cost is the detail that reframes the field: Fast-dLLM v2 reports fine-tuning from an AR model on roughly 1B tokens — about 500× less than Dream's 580B — a 7B trained in ~12 hours on 64 A100s.
documents.s: The two structural limits — and block diffusion, which is why you can call one today

documents.t: DiffusionGemma makes that point unmissable. It is not trained from scratch: it fine-tunes Gemma 4, a mixture-of-experts model with 3.8B activated and 25.2B total parameters, into a diffusion model using fewer than 10% of the starting AR model's total training token budget — supervised denoising fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning and sampler distillation (arXiv:2608.00146, CC-BY-4.0 weights). What survives the conversion is the surprising part. The report states it retains the base model's thinking mode, multimodal inputs and long contexts — and keeps the ability to generate autoregressively with only minor degradation. One set of weights, two decoding modes. If that result holds up, "diffusion LLM" stops being a distinct product category and becomes a serving option: the same family, with a parallelism dial on the inference side. That is a far more consequential claim than any single tokens-per-second record, and it is the reason to learn the mechanism now rather than when a provider flips a flag on a model you already use.
documents.s: Diffusion is a decoding mode you can retrofit, not a separate species

documents.t: Speed is the headline and the weakest part of the case, because speed is contested — specialised AR hardware is also delivering hundreds of tokens per second (see Token Speed). The durable advantages are the ones that follow from the shape of the algorithm. Any-order generation and native infilling. Because you choose which slot to commit, you can leave a hole in the middle of a sequence and have the model fill it with full context on both sides. Dream exposes this as the alg parameter — origin (random order), maskgit_plus (top-1 confidence), topk_margin (top1 − top2 margin), entropy — plus alg_temp to add randomness to those strategies. For code edits, template completion, or filling fields in a fixed JSON skeleton, that is a structurally better fit than asking an AR model to re-emit a whole file to change line 40. Latency-bound interaction. Inception's Mercury Voice advertises time-to-first-token under 170 ms on a 128K context, priced at $0.20/$1.50 per million input/output tokens at the time of writing. Voice is the clearest case where latency is the product; our full-duplex voice AI page covers why that threshold matters. End-to-end reasoning turnaround. Mercury 2's reported 1.7 s for a complete reasoning answer is a different claim from throughput — it is the number an agent loop actually feels, turn after turn. Bounded answers instead of prose. Inception's Mercury Decide returns a choice, a score, or a yes/no with a calibrated probability read off the model rather than written out as text — reported at up to 14 decisions per second, which makes "run it on every case and escalate the unsure ones" affordable. The category and its caveats are covered in depth on System One decision models; the diffusion backbone is an implementation detail there, not the point. Price pressure. Mercury 2.5 currently lists a 260K context at $0.04/$0.15 per million input/output tokens (promotional, off $0.20/$0.75) with cached input at $0.004 per million. Treat promo pricing as temporary and model your bill at list.
documents.s: What a diffusion LLM is actually better at

documents.t: Watch out Tokens/sec is measured at the vendor's chosen parallelism. Your quality bar may require more steps, which costs you the speedup. Benchmark on your own prompts at your own accuracy threshold. Output is not final left-to-right. Only block boundaries are monotonic; inside a block, slots can still be masked or revised. Any UI or parser that assumes 'token N will never change' is wrong. A pure masked dLLM bills and computes a length you chose in advance. Block diffusion reduces that to per-block granularity — it does not remove it. The third one deserves more than a bullet, because it is a security property and it has no autoregressive analogue. An AR model's alignment has a structural advantage: the refusal happens first. If the model decides to decline, every subsequent token is conditioned on "I can't help with that." A diffusion LLM has no such moment. There is no left-to-right point at which a refusal takes over the rest of the generation — masked slots get filled to be consistent with whatever is already on the canvas. DIJA ("The Devil behind the mask", ICLR 2026, arXiv:2507.11097, ZichenWen1/DIJA) turns that into an attack. The adversarial prompt puts the harmful intent in unmasked tokens and leaves masked spans for the model to complete in a contextually consistent way. The reported results: up to 100% keyword-based attack success rate on Dream-Instruct, surpassing the strongest prior baseline by up to 78.5% in evaluator-based ASR on JailbreakBench and by 37.7 points in StrongREJECT score — while requiring no rewriting or obfuscation of the harmful content. The authors' conclusion is that existing alignment mechanisms do not protect dLLMs against context-aware masked-input prompts, because the model cannot filter an unsafe generation mid-inference the way a sequential one can. A follow-up (arXiv:2602.00388) argues the picture is two-sided — diffusion confers a safety blessing in some settings that then breaks under context — which is a reason to measure rather than to assume either way. Practical takeaway: if you expose an open-weight dLLM, do not treat its instruction tuning as a guardrail. Filter and classify at the boundary, on both the request and the response, exactly as you would for a base model. Our securing local and hybrid agents page covers the boundary pattern.
documents.s: Three gotchas before you ship one

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Hosted, zero setup⌄ Inception serves Mercury through an OpenAI-compatible API, and the models are listed on OpenRouter (for example openrouter.ai/inception/mercury-2). Point an existing OpenAI-SDK script at it and change the model string — nothing about the request shape is diffusion-specific. ←PreviousNext→ 2Open weights, local⌄ LLaDA-8B-Instruct (MIT) and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B (Apache-2.0) both ship inference code on Hugging Face. DiffusionGemma's weights are CC-BY-4.0. Note that a pure masked dLLM has no KV cache, so plan VRAM for recomputing the full sequence every step. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the steps sweep⌄ The single most informative experiment: hold the prompt fixed, vary steps, and plot wall-clock against a task metric you care about. You will find your own quality cliff, and it will not be where a benchmark table put it. ←PreviousNext→ 4Then test the seams⌄ Use prompts whose answers contain multi-token units — proper nouns, numbers with units, identifiers, JSON keys. Those are where conditional-independence errors show up first, and where a confidence threshold earns its cost. ←PreviousNext→ Call a hosted diffusion LLM with the OpenAI SDK (nothing changes but the model string) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Inception serves an OpenAI-compatible API; OpenRouter also lists the models. # Check the provider's model list for the current slug before you hard-code one. curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "inception/mercury-2", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Rewrite this function to stream its output, and explain the two failure modes you introduced."} ], "stream": true }' # What to watch for, beyond the content: # - time to first token vs time to last token (the diffusion win is usually in the gap) # - whether the stream arrives in chunks that look like BLOCKS rather than words The steps sweep on Dream 7B — find your own quality cliff CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import time, torch from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer NAME = "Dream-org/Dream-v0-Instruct-7B" tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(NAME, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( NAME, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, trust_remote_code=True ).to("cuda").eval() PROMPT = "List the five largest cities in Germany with their populations." MAX_NEW = 256 # steps == MAX_NEW is the authors' best-quality setting: one token per # forward pass. Each halving doubles tokens-per-pass and doubles the # number of independence assumptions you are making. for steps in [256, 128, 64, 32, 16]: inputs = tok.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}], return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True, add_generation_prompt=True, ).to("cuda") t0 = time.perf_counter() out = model.diffusion_generate( inputs.input_ids, attention_mask=inputs.attention_mask, max_new_tokens=MAX_NEW, steps=steps, temperature=0.0, alg="entropy", # commit the lowest-entropy slots first alg_temp=0.0, ) dt = time.perf_counter() - t0 text = tok.decode(out[0][len(inputs.input_ids[0]):], skip_special_tokens=True) print(f"--- steps={steps} tokens/pass={MAX_NEW/steps:.0f} {dt:.2f}s ---") print(text.strip()[:400]) # Read the OUTPUTS, not just the timings. The numbers and the city names are # the multi-token units that break first when too many slots are committed # from one pass. That corruption is the conditional-independence bug, visible.

Key takeaways A diffusion LLM's speed comes from one ratio — generation length divided by denoising steps, i.e. tokens committed per forward pass. An AR model is fixed at 1. Everything else is a consequence of that dial. Over-parallel decoding is wrong, not just coarse: committing correlated slots from one pass samples the product of marginals instead of the joint. Confidence-threshold decoding is the fix, and Fast-dLLM reports up to 27.6x throughput with minimal accuracy loss. Pure masked diffusion has no KV cache and a fixed output length. Block diffusion (AR between blocks, diffusion inside) is what restored caching, variable length and streaming — it is why every callable dLLM today is a block model. DiffusionGemma converted an autoregressive Gemma 4 MoE into a diffusion model for under 10% of its original training token budget while keeping thinking mode, multimodality and AR generation. Diffusion is looking more like a decoding mode than a separate species of model. Pick it for infilling and any-order edits, sub-200 ms voice turns, fast bounded decisions and end-to-end turn latency — and assume its alignment does not hold, because masked-infill prompts reach up to 100% ASR on an aligned open dLLM. Check yourself 0/5 New to the underlying machinery? What is an LLM and Tokens and context cover the autoregressive baseline this page departs from, and Token Speed covers the hardware and software multipliers that attack the same latency problem from the other side.
