Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम On October 3, 2026, Simon Willison published a short argument that landed on the Hacker News front page with 615 points: usage-billed services need hard budget caps by default, with uncapped billing as the explicit opt-in. His framing is the one that matters — "Nobody wants to wake up to an email sent at midnight warning about a budget limit and find that, while they slept, their rogue service had consumed several hundred (or several thousand) more dollars." The reason this became a 2026 argument rather than a 2015 one is that agents changed the shape of the risk. A human misconfiguring a cron job is a slow leak. An agent that retries a failing tool call in a loop, or spawns subagents that spawn subagents, is a leak with a model behind it — and it runs at machine speed while you sleep. The good news: in the last four months, most of the stack quietly grew real caps. The bad news is what this page is actually about — the caps exist, but they announce themselves with four different HTTP status codes, and at least two of them will be swallowed by the retry logic you already wrote. What you'll learn Tell a soft cap (an email) from a hard cap (a blocked request) — and know which one each provider gives you Handle the four different error shapes a spend cap can return, including the one that arrives as a 400 your retry logic treats as a bug Understand why no cap on the market can be exact, and why every vendor disclaims liability for the overage Know where Anthropic's default safety net disappears, and what the Enterprise Spend Limits API replaces it with Put a real ceiling under a new project in about twenty minutes, at the layer that actually blocks
documents.s: Hard Spend Caps: Which AI Providers Actually Stop the Bill

documents.t: Strip away the marketing and every spend control is one of two things. A soft cap observes. It watches a cost signal, compares it to your number, and notifies — email, webhook, dashboard badge. Traffic keeps flowing. AWS Budgets, Anthropic's usage dashboard, and every "billing alert" you have ever configured are soft caps. They are genuinely useful, and they are not protection: a soft cap's only effect is to tell a human to intervene, which means its latency is your response time, not the system's. A hard cap enforces. It blocks new requests at the limit. Your code finds out through an error, not an inbox. The practical test: if every human on the team is asleep, does the spend stop? If the answer is no, it is a soft cap no matter what the UI calls it. Everything below is about hard caps. Keep your soft caps too — a cap that fires is an incident, and you want the warning at 60% as well as the block at 100%.
documents.s: Soft cap vs hard cap: the only distinction that matters

documents.t: Provider / layer Hard cap? Scope What you get when it fires Anthropic — tier cap Yes, by default Organization, monthly HTTP 429, rate_limit_error, no retry-after, details.error_code: enforced_spend_limit_reached Anthropic — limit you set Yes, opt-in Organization or workspace HTTP 400, invalid_request_error, message begins "You have reached your specified API usage limits" Anthropic — Claude Code workspace Yes That workspace Checked separately; can return a 429 that does carry retry-after OpenAI — hard spend limit Yes, opt-in Organization and/or project HTTP 429 OpenRouter — credits / key cap Yes, structurally Account balance, per-key HTTP 402, with error.metadata.limit_source Google Cloud — spend cap budget Yes, opt-in (Preview) One project × one service New usage for that service blocked until manually lifted AWS — project spend limit Yes, new accounts Per project Project paused rather than accruing further charges LiteLLM / self-hosted gateway Yes, pre-flight Key, user, team, model Auth-shaped error, raised before the provider is called Claude Code telemetry No — Observability only; exports cost, enforces nothing आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-10-05। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। स्रोत: Anthropic rate limits & Spend Limits API docs; OpenAI API rate-limits guide; OpenRouter limits reference; Google Cloud Billing spend-cap docs & July 27 2026 release note; LiteLLM proxy docs; Help Net Security on the AWS launch

This is the part that is documented in four separate places and assembled nowhere, and it is the thing most likely to bite you. Read the Anthropic behaviour carefully, because it is two different behaviours. When you cross your tier's monthly cap, the API returns HTTP 429 with error type rate_limit_error — the same type as an ordinary rate limit — but with no retry-after header. Anthropic's own documentation is blunt about the consequence: "Retrying, including the SDK's automatic retries, fails until access resumes." Access resumes at 00:00 UTC on the first of the next month unless you raise the limit. So a well-behaved client with exponential backoff will sit in a retry loop for up to 31 days, logging transient-looking errors. The distinguishing field is error.details.error_code, which is enforced_spend_limit_reached. When you cross a limit you configured — organization or workspace — the API returns HTTP 400 with type invalid_request_error. That inverts the usual assumption: a 400 means "your request was malformed, do not retry," so most clients log it as a bug and either crash or drop the work silently. It is not a bug; it is your own cap doing its job. And the Claude Code workspace is checked separately again: requests over that workspace's limit can receive a 429 that does carry retry-after. OpenRouter takes the third route. Because the model is prepaid credits, running out is a payment problem, so it returns HTTP 402 Payment Required, with error.metadata.limit_source naming which of the three limits you hit — account balance, per-key cap, or the in-flight budget hold. One detail worth knowing: when the account balance goes negative, requests to free models fail too. OpenAI's documentation states that requests affected by a hard spend limit return a 429. It does not state an enforcement latency, and it distinguishes two things that are easy to conflate: the approved monthly usage limit OpenAI sets for your organization, and the spend limits you configure yourself on an organization or a project. Both can apply to one request, so a project with headroom can still be blocked by the organization ceiling above it. Four shapes for one event. Which means the handler you want is not "retry on 429." Classify a cap error instead of retrying it CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # The three signals that mean "stop, this is a budget wall" — not "wait and retry" # # Anthropic tier cap -> 429, type=rate_limit_error, NO retry-after, # error.details.error_code == "enforced_spend_limit_reached" # Anthropic own limit -> 400, type=invalid_request_error, # message startswith "You have reached your specified API usage limits" # OpenRouter -> 402, error.metadata.limit_source present # OpenAI hard limit -> 429 (no documented discriminator field) def is_budget_wall(status, body, headers): err = (body or {}).get("error", {}) or {} detail_code = (err.get("details") or {}).get("error_code") if status == 429 and detail_code == "enforced_spend_limit_reached": return True # month-long wall; do NOT back off if status == 429 and "retry-after" not in {k.lower() for k in headers}: return True # 429 with no retry-after is not a rate limit if status == 400 and err.get("message", "").startswith( "You have reached your specified API usage limits" ): return True # your own cap, wearing a 400 if status == 402 and (err.get("metadata") or {}).get("limit_source"): return True # prepaid balance or key cap return False # Page a human, mark the work as blocked, and stop the loop. # Retrying a budget wall just burns your own CPU until the first of the month. The general rule that survives any provider's refactor: a 429 without a retry-after header is not a rate limit. Rate limits are temporary by construction and tell you how long to wait. A 429 that refuses to tell you how long is a different animal.
documents.s: The trap: four status codes, one event

documents.t: Every hard cap on the market fires on estimated cost, not billed cost. This looks like a shortcut and is in fact the only workable design: a billing pipeline that aggregates, rates, applies discounts and reconciles usage takes minutes to hours. A cap that waited for it would be useless against exactly the failure mode it exists to stop. Google Cloud states the trade-off plainly: "For faster enforcement, spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger alerts and enforce the spend cap" — and then, honestly, "Due to latency in usage and cost reporting, spend cap enforcement isn't instantaneous. Consider setting your budget slightly below your absolute limit." And the liability: "any cost overages are billed as normal." You remain responsible for what leaks through during the reporting lag. Three consequences you should design around: Set the cap below your real ceiling. If $500 is the number that genuinely hurts, cap at $400. The gap is your overshoot budget. How big it needs to be depends on your peak burn rate, not on the provider — an agent fleet that can spend $50/minute needs a wider margin than a chat app that spends $50/day. In-flight requests complete. A cap blocks new usage. Anything already in flight finishes and bills. With long-running agent turns this is not a rounding error. Pre-flight beats post-hoc. The only mechanism that structurally avoids overshoot is reserving the estimated cost before the call. LiteLLM's proxy does this by default: it estimates the maximum cost from the request body and the model's pricing, holds that amount against every applicable budget, rejects the request if the reservation would breach the budget, then swaps the reservation for the actual cost once the response lands. OpenRouter's in-flight budget hold is the same idea applied to a prepaid balance. Both are strictly stronger than measuring after the fact, and both are only approximate in the other direction — they over-reserve, which means they can refuse a request you could have afforded.
documents.s: Why no cap can be exact — and why that is not laziness

documents.t: Anthropic gives you a hard cap whether or not you ask for one. The Start, Build and Scale tiers each carry a monthly spend cap — the maximum your organization can spend on the API in a calendar month. Usage tier Monthly spend cap Start $500 Build $1,000 Scale $200,000 Custom None — arranged with your account team आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-10-05। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। स्रोत: platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits — Spend limits Read the last row again. The default safety net exists on every tier except the one occupied by the organizations spending the most. Graduating to Custom removes the automatic ceiling, which makes an explicitly configured limit mandatory rather than optional at exactly the point where people stop thinking about it. Two more things worth setting while you are in there: Set your own limit below the tier cap. The Billing page takes a number lower than your tier's cap. This is the control you actually want, because you choose it — and remember it surfaces as a 400, not a 429. Use workspaces as blast-radius boundaries. Workspaces take their own spend and rate limits, so an experimental agent and your production traffic do not share one pool. Organization-wide limits always apply on top, even if the workspace limits sum to more. One restriction: you cannot set limits on the default workspace — so do not put anything you care about there.
documents.s: Anthropic's tiers, and where the net disappears

documents.t: Claude Enterprise organizations get something the Console does not expose: a Spend Limits API, which treats per-person budgets as a resource you can read and write programmatically. It is the piece of this story that is barely written about anywhere, so it is worth knowing what it does. Eight endpoints across two resources. The first answers "what cap applies to each member, where did it come from, and how close are they to it": Read every member's effective cap and month-to-date spend CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ curl "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/organizations/spend_limits/effective?limit=20" \ --header "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY" \ --header "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" # Each row carries: # amount -> the effective cap, in MINOR UNITS ("50000" = $500.00) # null = unlimited; "0" = included plan usage only # source.type -> user | seat_tier | rbac_group | organization # period_to_date_spend -> spend since the period started, same minor-unit format # spend_limit_id -> the configured row this resolved from # # Requires an Admin API key with the read:spend_limits scope. Four details in there that will cost you an afternoon if you miss them: Amounts are decimal strings in minor units of the billing currency. "50000" is $500.00. Parse as a decimal and divide by 100 — the docs explicitly warn against binary floating point for large values. null and "0" are not the same. On a member's effective row, null means unlimited; "0" means the member cannot use Claude beyond their plan's included usage. Treat "0" as already at-limit. period_to_date_spend can read "0" when the reading is simply unavailable. The docs call it informational, not transactional — so do not build a gate that treats a zero reading as "no spend." A group limit is a per-member default, not a pooled budget. Each member inheriting it is gated against their own spend. The second resource is a review queue. When a member clicks "Request more usage" in claude.ai, a spend-limit increase request appears; you can list pending ones, and each carries a live spend_summary with that member's current cap and period-to-date spend, so a policy engine can decide without a second lookup. Approving writes the new per-user cap in the same call. Two asymmetries to know: setting a limit directly with POST /spend_limits does not resolve a pending request (use the approve endpoint), and all eight endpoints share one 60-requests-per-minute budget per organization. You can only write per-user overrides through this API. Seat-tier, group and organization defaults are configured in claude.ai settings. And the API is Enterprise-only — it is not available to Claude Platform (Console) organizations. For reporting rather than enforcement, the companion is the Usage & Cost Analytics API — GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, which groups spend by model, workspace, API key, actor, cost_type and token_type. That cost_type split is how you find out that your bill is not mostly inference. The older GET /v1/organizations/cost_report still works but Anthropic marked it legacy on October 29, 2026; it returns daily buckets (default 1d, at most 31 per page) with amounts in minor units, groupable by description or workspace_id. Two differences matter before you swap one for the other: the new API needs the anthropic-beta: analytics-usage-cost-2026-08-24 header, and its data lags 4–24 hours instead of ~5 minutes — so it reports, while the spend-limit endpoints above enforce.
documents.s: The Enterprise layer: per-member caps as an API

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Decide the number that would actually hurt — then cap below it⌄ Pick the figure at which you would want everything to stop, and set the cap 20-25% under it. That margin absorbs reporting lag and in-flight requests. Write the number down somewhere a future teammate will find it, because an unexplained cap gets raised during the first incident. ←PreviousNext→ 2Set the provider-level cap first — it is the only one that cannot be bypassed⌄ On Anthropic: Settings > Billing > Spend limits > Adjust limit, below your tier cap. On OpenAI: configure a hard spend limit on the organization, and a tighter one on the project. On OpenRouter: the prepaid balance IS the cap, so top up small and set a per-key credit limit with a reset schedule. Gateway and application limits are defence in depth; this layer is the wall. ←PreviousNext→ 3Give every risky workload its own key and its own workspace⌄ A cap you share with production is a cap you will raise under pressure. On Anthropic, create a workspace per workload with its own spend and rate limits (not the default workspace — it cannot take limits). Elsewhere, one API key per workload, each with its own ceiling. ←PreviousNext→ 4Teach your client to recognise a budget wall⌄ Add the classifier from earlier on this page. Specifically: stop retrying on a 429 with no retry-after, and stop treating a 400 as a code bug when its message starts 'You have reached your specified API usage limits'. Log a distinct event type for budget walls so they show up as incidents rather than as noise in your 4xx rate. ←PreviousNext→ 5Add a pre-flight budget at the gateway if agents are involved⌄ Put LiteLLM (or an equivalent) in front and set max_budget with a budget_duration per key, user and team. Budget reservation is on by default: it holds the estimated maximum cost before the provider is called and reconciles to actual afterwards, which is what stops a burst of concurrent agent calls from collectively blowing past a limit that each one individually respected. ←PreviousNext→ 6Cap the infrastructure too, not just the model⌄ The model API is rarely the whole bill. On Google Cloud, create a spend cap budget for the specific project and service. On AWS, set the project spend limit if your account is eligible. Then check what is NOT covered — on GCP, persistent compute and storage keep accruing while a cap is enforced. ←PreviousNext→ 7Keep the soft caps, and test the hard one⌄ Set alerts at 50/75/90% as well. Then verify the wall exists: set a throwaway key's cap to a few cents, run traffic through it, and read the actual status code, headers and body your stack receives. A cap you have never seen fire is a belief, not a control. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Put a ceiling under a project

documents.t: Google Cloud shipped spend cap budgets in its July 27, 2026 billing release notes — in Preview, with notably little fanfare for a feature that topped billing feature requests for a decade. The mechanics are worth reading closely, because the scope is narrower than "a hard cap on Google Cloud": Eligible services are a short list — as documented: Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions. Check the current list before you rely on it; a cap on a service that is not eligible does not exist. One cap covers one project × one service. Not an account-wide killswitch. Monthly periods only. It does not auto-resume. "When a spend cap is enforced, the usage block is reversed only when you manually lift the spend cap" — and services can take up to an hour to fully resume afterwards. For a production service, that is a deliberate outage you are choosing over a deliberate bill. Decide which one you want before you set the cap. Persistent resources keep charging. Fixed usage tied to compute and storage stays active and keeps accruing. The cap stops new requests, not your running infrastructure. Subscription costs are excluded — Gemini Enterprise licences, for example. AWS went the other way and attacked the problem at signup. Reported on September 17, 2026, new AWS accounts arrive structured as a project, start with $100 in Free Tier credits, and on moving to paid get a monthly spend limit per project starting at $20, with AWS suggesting a figure from prior usage. At the limit the project is paused rather than accruing charges, and it resumes when the owner raises the cap. Two caveats: the rollout is gradual and covers new customers only, and what a paused project does to a live public endpoint is not spelled out — which, for anything user-facing, is the question you need answered first. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-10-05। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। स्रोत: docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets-spend-caps and Cloud Billing release notes (2026-07-27); helpnetsecurity.com/2026/09/17/aws-spend-limit-agent-set-permissions/
documents.s: The cloud layer, and what it does not cover

documents.t: A hard cap is a ceiling on metered usage at one layer. Four things routinely sit outside it: Seats and subscriptions. Per-seat licences and plan fees are not metered usage and are not capped by a usage cap. Persistent infrastructure. Idle GPU instances, provisioned databases and storage keep billing while your API cap is enforced. The agent stopped; the machine it was running on did not. Coding agents on their own clock. Claude Code exports cost telemetry — claude_code.cost.usage in USD and claude_code.token.usage in tokens, both incremented after each API request, attributed by model, query source (main / subagent / auxiliary), speed and effort. That is genuinely good observability, and it enforces nothing: the metrics are read-only exports emitted after each request completes. The enforcement has to live at the API or gateway layer underneath. Set a Claude Code workspace limit, and remember that workspace is checked separately from the rest of your organization. The gap between layers. A gateway budget does not help if a service can reach the provider directly. The provider-level cap is the only one that cannot be routed around — which is why it goes first. Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways A soft cap's latency is your response time. If nobody is awake, it is not a control. One event, four status codes: 429-without-retry-after (Anthropic tier), 400 (your own Anthropic limit), 429 (OpenAI), 402 (OpenRouter). Generic retry logic mishandles at least two. A 429 with no retry-after header is never a rate limit. That one heuristic catches the worst failure mode — a client retrying a month-long wall. Every cap fires on estimated cost and every vendor disclaims the overage. Cap 20-25% below the number that would actually hurt. Anthropic's Custom tier has no default monthly cap — the safety net vanishes where the spend is biggest. Pre-flight reservation (LiteLLM, OpenRouter's in-flight hold) is the only design that holds under concurrent agent bursts. Post-hoc measurement always overshoots. Cap the provider first — it is the only layer that cannot be routed around. Gateway and app limits are defence in depth. A cap you have never watched fire is a belief. Set a throwaway key to a few cents and read the real status code your stack receives.
documents.s: What caps will not save you from

Most "agent memory" is a vector store with a nice wrapper: you dump conversation turns in, you cosine-similarity them back out, and the agent recites history it was never going to forget anyway. Hindsight is built around a different claim — that an agent should end the month believing things it did not believe at the start of it — and it is currently the fastest-growing project on GitHub because of it: roughly 4,500 stars in a single day on 2026-09-27, about 37,000 total, MIT-licensed, Python, with a peer-reviewable paper behind the architecture. This page is the practical read: what is actually inside a memory bank, why recall and reflect are two different cost classes, the benchmark result that should change how you budget your stack, and the four defaults that will bite you in production. What you'll learn Tell apart the three operations — retain, recall, reflect — and the third path most people miss: reading a mental model with no LLM call at all Understand why recall is four parallel retrievers fused by reciprocal rank fusion, not a vector search Read the benchmark numbers correctly, including the one where a competitor wins and the 3.2-point gap between the vendor's own two pages Stand a server up and wire it into Claude, an OpenAI-SDK agent, or a coding agent, in three commands Spot the four production defaults that are wrong for you — starting with the security policy that is off until you switch it on आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-28। Hindsight ships fast (last push the day before this page was written) and the live leaderboard changes. Treat every score, star count and pattern count below as a dated snapshot; the architecture and the gotchas are the durable part. स्रोत: github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight README and GitHub API (36,993 stars, MIT, Python, pushed 2026-09-26); github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight-benchmarks (LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo tables); vectorize.io/benchmarks (94.6% headline); arXiv:2512.12818 'Hindsight is 20/20'; hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/memory-defense, /developer/mcp-server, /developer/mental-models, /developer/observations, /developer/retrieval; hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/03/23/agent-memory-benchmark; GitHub trending (daily) 2026-09-27. Benchmark leaderboards here are continuously updated and every non-Hindsight score is vendor-self-reported — re-read the live tables before quoting a number in a decision.

Almost every mistake with Hindsight comes from treating its three verbs as interchangeable. They are not — they sit at wildly different points on the price/latency curve, and there is a fourth path that costs essentially nothing. Path What happens LLM calls Use it for retain An LLM extracts facts, timestamps, entities and relationships, then normalises them into canonical entities, time series and search indexes Yes, on write Ingesting a turn, a tool result, a document recall Four retrievers run in parallel, results are fused and reranked, then trimmed to a token budget No generation — retrieval and a cross-encoder "What do I know about X?" before a turn reflect Walks the hierarchy mental models → observations → raw facts and reasons over it, shaped by the bank's mission, directives and disposition Yes, and more than one "What risks am I missing on this project?" Read a mental model A stored standing answer is fetched from the database None Booting an agent with settled knowledge That last row is the mechanism most readers have never seen. A mental model is a question you register once ("What are this user's preferences?"); Hindsight writes the answer, stores it, and rewrites it in the background as the bank learns. Reading it is a database read — no retrieval, no inference, no tokens. So an agent's session can start already knowing, instead of spending its first three turns rediscovering. The practical rule: reflect is for thinking, recall is for looking up, and a mental model is for what you look up every single session. If you are calling reflect on every turn, you have built an expensive chatbot.
documents.s: The one idea: three operations, three cost classes

documents.t: A bank is one isolated brain — one user, one agent, or one project — with strict isolation and no cross-bank leakage. Inside it, memories are not one flat pile. Hindsight splits them along a biomimetic axis: World facts — how the world is. "The stove gets hot." Experiences — what this agent did and what happened. "I touched the stove and it hurt." Observations — consolidated, evidence-backed beliefs formed from many facts. Mental models — learned understanding synthesised from observations and facts. Knowledge pages — mental models with the mechanics hidden: living wiki-style documents the bank writes about itself, organised in folders, searchable, and projectable onto disk as plain markdown. The world/experience split is doing real work. "The deploy script needs sudo" and "I ran the deploy script and it failed" are different kinds of claim with different lifetimes, and collapsing them into one undifferentiated memories table is exactly what makes a naive vector store answer confidently about a fact it only ever observed once, two months ago, in a failed attempt. Observations are refined, not overwritten. Each one keeps its supporting evidence as exact quotes plus a proof count, and when new evidence arrives it strengthens, weakens or extends the existing belief rather than silently replacing it. This is the difference between a memory system and a cache: a cache's last write wins, and a belief's last write is evidence. Banks also carry a mission (a natural-language identity that directs what to prioritise), directives (hard rules never to violate) and disposition traits (skepticism, literalism, empathy) that shape how reflect reasons. Two banks over identical facts can reach different conclusions on purpose.
documents.s: What is actually inside a bank

documents.t: This is the part worth internalising even if you never run Hindsight. A single recall fires four retrieval strategies in parallel: Semantic — dense vector similarity Keyword — BM25 exact matching Graph — entity, temporal and causal links Temporal — time-range filtering Then the four result sets are merged by reciprocal rank fusion, reordered by a cross-encoder reranker, and trimmed to fit a token limit. Why bother? Because each arm fails in a way the others do not. Semantic search cannot answer "what happened in June" — a date is not semantically similar to anything. BM25 cannot match a paraphrase. A graph traversal is the only thing that answers "who replaced the person who owned the account the user complained about," and none of the three know that the answer must fit in 2,000 tokens. Reciprocal rank fusion is the cheap trick that makes this composable: it scores by rank position, not by each retriever's own score, so you never have to normalise a cosine distance against a BM25 score. If you are hand-rolling hybrid retrieval anywhere in your stack, that one detail is the takeaway. The reranker matters more than the retrievers. Fusion gets the right memory into the top 50; the cross-encoder is what gets it into the top 5 that actually reach the model.
documents.s: Recall is not a vector search

documents.t: On LongMemEval-S (500 questions), the project's own harness reports: System Score Hindsight (Gemini 3) 91.4% Hindsight (OSS-120B) 89.0% Supermemory (Gemini 3) 85.2% Supermemory (GPT-5) 84.6% Hindsight (OSS-20B) 83.6% Full context (GPT-4o) 60.2% Full context (OSS-20B) 39.0% Look at the two bold rows. Same 20B open-weight model, same questions. With Hindsight in front of it: 83.6%. With the whole history stuffed into its context: 39.0%. That is +44.6 points from architecture alone, and it puts a 20B model 23 points above full-context GPT-4o. The paper's framing — memory as "a structured, first-class substrate for reasoning" rather than a retrieval add-on — is exactly this result. If your memory layer is losing, buying a bigger model is the expensive way to not fix it. Now the honest caveats, because they matter more than the headline: A competitor wins the other benchmark. On LoCoMo, Hindsight (Gemini 3) scores 89.61% — and Backboard reports 90.00%. Memobase 75.78%, Zep 75.14%. The ranking flips depending on which benchmark you pick, which is the whole reason to read two. Only one row is independently reproduced. Per the project's own README, Hindsight's figures were reproduced by research collaborators at Virginia Tech's Sanghani Center and The Washington Post; every other system's score is self-reported by its vendor. A table of self-reported numbers is a table of best days. The vendor's two pages disagree. vectorize.io/benchmarks headlines 94.6% on LongMemEval; the benchmarks repo's LongMemEval-S table says 91.4%. Both are Hindsight's own publications. The leaderboard is continuously updated and the configurations differ, but a 3.2-point spread between a marketing page and a repo is a reason to run the harness yourself before you quote either. And then the most interesting critique — which comes from Hindsight's own team. Their benchmark manifesto argues that LoCoMo and LongMemEval were designed for the 32k-context era, when retrieval was the hard part. With million-token windows, stuffing everything in scores competitively, so these benchmarks increasingly measure a model's reading comprehension rather than a memory architecture. Worse, they collapse everything to one axis. Their line is the one to steal: A system that scores 90% and costs $10 per user per day is not better than one that scores 82% and costs $0.10. Which is the correct way to evaluate any memory layer, including the one you already have: accuracy per dollar per user per day, on your own traffic. See Evaluating Agents for how to build that harness.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 11. Run the server⌄ One Docker command, one LLM key. It ships an embedded Postgres (pg0) in a named volume, so there is nothing else to provision. API on 8888, UI on 9999. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Pick the provider deliberately⌄ HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER accepts 25+ values — openai, anthropic, gemini, groq, bedrock, vertexai, deepseek, minimax — plus fully local ollama, lmstudio and llamacpp, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and litellm gateways. Existing subscriptions work with no API key at all: claude-code (Claude Pro/Max), openai-codex (ChatGPT Plus/Pro), cursor, github-copilot. Retain calls an LLM on every write, so this choice is your bill. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Retain, recall, reflect from a client⌄ pip install hindsight-client (or npm, Go, CLI). Three methods, one bank_id. Pass a real timestamp on retain — temporal recall is one of the four arms and it cannot filter on a time you never supplied. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Register the questions you ask every session⌄ Turn the lookups your agent repeats into mental models or knowledge pages. Each one converts a recall into a database read. This is the single biggest cost lever in the system. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Turn Memory Defense on before the first real write⌄ It is opt-in, disabled by default, and it does not scan retroactively. Enable it at bank creation — see the gotchas below for why 'later' is the wrong answer. ←PreviousNext→ Server, client, first three calls CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Server — API on :8888, UI on :9999, embedded Postgres in a volume export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-xxx docker run -it --pull always --name hindsight --restart unless-stopped \ -p 8888:8888 -p 9999:9999 \ -e HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_API_KEY=$OPENAI_API_KEY \ -v hindsight-data:/home/hindsight/.pg0 \ ghcr.io/vectorize-io/hindsight:latest # 2. Client pip install hindsight-client -U Python: the three operations CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from hindsight_client import Hindsight client = Hindsight(base_url="http://localhost:8888") # Retain — an LLM extracts facts, entities, relationships, time. # Always pass a real timestamp: temporal recall filters on it. client.retain( bank_id="user-123", content="Alice got promoted to senior engineer", context="career update", timestamp="2026-06-15T10:00:00Z", ) # Recall — 4 parallel retrievers, RRF, cross-encoder, token trim. No generation. client.recall(bank_id="user-123", query="What does Alice do?") client.recall(bank_id="user-123", query="What happened in June?") # temporal arm # Reflect — walks mental models -> observations -> raw facts and reasons. # Costs several LLM calls. Not a per-turn operation. client.reflect(bank_id="user-123", query="What should I know about Alice?") No Docker, or you want it inside a test suite? There is an embedded mode that starts and stops the server in a context manager: Embedded — no server to manage CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pip install hindsight-all -U # hindsight-all-slim on Intel Macs Embedded mode in Python CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import os from hindsight import HindsightServer, HindsightClient with HindsightServer( llm_provider="openai", llm_model="gpt-5-mini", llm_api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"], ) as server: client = HindsightClient(base_url=server.url) client.retain(bank_id="my-bank", content="Alice works at Google") print(client.recall(bank_id="my-bank", query="Where does Alice work?"))

Three paths, in increasing order of control. The LLM wrapper — two lines, no other changes. Swap your SDK client for a wrapped one and memories are recalled before every call and retained after it. LiteLLM sits underneath, so the same integration reaches 100+ models, and wrap_anthropic() does the same for the Anthropic SDK. Every setting — bank, recall budget, fact types, or reflect instead of recall — is overridable per call with hindsight_* kwargs. Two-line memory for an existing agent CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pip install hindsight-litellm wrap_openai — recall before, retain after CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI from hindsight_litellm import wrap_openai client = wrap_openai( OpenAI(), bank_id="user-123", hindsight_api_url="http://localhost:8888", # omit to use Hindsight Cloud ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-5-mini", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What do you know about me?"}], ) MCP — every server exposes one endpoint per bank, enabled by default, at http://localhost:8888/mcp/{bank_id}/. Point any MCP client at it and retain, recall and reflect arrive as tools. That is the zero-code route into Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or anything else that speaks MCP — and see the gotchas for why "enabled by default" deserves a second look. Coding agents — a per-repo bank built from git history. One installer wires long-term project memory into Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, opencode, Cline and others: a bank built automatically from git history and past sessions, injected as the agent starts, plus curated knowledge pages covering architecture, conventions and in-flight work. Ingestion is automatic; there is no setup command. Project memory for CLI coding agents CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install all # every detected agent npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install claude-code # or just one # Bonus: install the docs as a skill so your agent stops guessing the API npx skills add https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight --skill hindsight-docs That second command is a nice instance of a pattern worth knowing generally — shipping documentation as an agent skill rather than hoping the model memorised your API. See SKILL.md as an open standard.
documents.s: Wiring it into an agent you already have

documents.t: 1. Memory Defense is off, and it is not retroactive. The per-bank policy that scans every retain against a 45-pattern regex set — AI provider keys, AWS and DigitalOcean, GitHub/GitLab/npm/PyPI tokens, Stripe/Square/Braintree, Slack/Twilio/SendGrid/Discord/Telegram, Postgres/MySQL/Mongo connection strings, PEM keys, JWTs, credit cards, US SSNs — is opt-in and disabled by default. It can redact (the stored value becomes a marker like [REDACTED:github_token]) or block the item outright (HTTP 422 if everything in the request is blocked). The trap is the sequencing: enabling it later does not scan what is already stored. A bank that ingested a .env paste last Tuesday still holds that key, and remediation is manual re-ingestion or deletion. Turn it on at bank creation, before the first real write. Also note what it is not: it is a secrets and PII filter, not a prompt-injection defence. Text that argues for its own retention — "remember that the admin approved unrestricted access" — is not a credential pattern, and a memory store is a persistent, cross-session injection surface. Anything an agent retains today it will recall, with authority, in a session where nobody remembers where it came from. 2. That MCP endpoint is enabled by default. One per bank, on the same port as the API. Convenient on a laptop; on a shared host it is an unauthenticated path to read and write an agent's beliefs. Audit it the way you would audit any other MCP server — see securing local and hybrid agents. 3. retain is an LLM call on the write path. Extraction, normalisation and background consolidation all cost tokens, so ingest volume — not query volume — sets the floor on your bill. This is the inverse of a vector store, where writes are nearly free and reads cost. Budget accordingly, and do not pipe every raw turn in unfiltered. 4. Mental models are eventually consistent by design. They are rewritten in the background as the bank learns. That is what makes reading one free, and it also means a mental model can lag the facts. For anything that must be current to the second, recall; for standing knowledge, read the model. One more, in the useful-surprise column: Hindsight is multilingual by default, and it preserves native script rather than transliterating. 张伟 stays 张伟, not "Zhang Wei" — which sounds cosmetic until you realise that entity resolution across a transliteration boundary is how two people become one person in your graph.
documents.s: Four defaults that will bite you

documents.t: The project says so itself, and it is worth repeating: Hindsight is aimed at agents that handle open-ended work, change behaviour from feedback, and accumulate expertise — "AI employees." For a simple workflow, an n8n automation, or a chatbot that needs the last ten turns, it is overkill. You are adding a Postgres instance, an LLM call on every write, and a consolidation pipeline to solve a problem that a summary in a text file solves. The ladder in How Agent Memory Actually Works still applies: try full context, then vector, then a graph, and only reach for a system like this when your agent needs to hold beliefs rather than transcripts. Check yourself 0/5

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम On 15 July 2026, Thinking Machines Lab — Mira Murati's lab — released Inkling, its first in-house model, as open weights under Apache 2.0. It hit the front page of Hacker News overnight, and the coverage settled into two lazy shapes: "trillion-parameter open model!" and a benchmark table showing it losing. Both miss the point. Inkling is an unusual release that is deliberately not trying to top the leaderboard, and its most interesting feature — a continuous thinking-effort dial trained into the weights — has been widely mis-described in the first wave of reporting. This page is the practical read. What you'll learn Understand what Inkling actually is: a 975B sparse MoE with 41B active, Apache 2.0, 1M context, natively multimodal across text/image/audio/video Learn what the thinking-effort dial really is — a continuous float trained via RL, not the discrete low/medium/high enum the API wrappers show you See why 'open weights' does not mean 'runs on your machine' — the real VRAM floor is ~600 GB even quantized Know why Inkling loses benchmarks on purpose, and the one metric where it wins that nobody put in a headline

Inkling is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 975B total parameters and 41B active per token, pretrained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video, supporting a 1M-token context window, released under Apache 2.0 — positioned not as the best model available, but as the best base to customize. That last clause is the whole strategy. Thinking Machines says so plainly: Inkling "is not the strongest overall model available today, open or closed." Shipping a model alongside that sentence is not modesty, it's positioning — and it explains every design decision below.

This is the headline feature and it's the most mis-reported detail of the launch. Several outlets described the effort parameter as ranging "0.2 to 0.99," or as a named enum — none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh. The official Tinker documentation says something different. Effort is continuous reasoning-effort conditioning: any float from 0.0 inclusive up to, but not including, 1.0. The default is 0.9. The named levels are just recommended sweep values, not the actual interface: Preset Value none 0.0 minimal 0.1 low 0.2 medium 0.7 high 0.9 xhigh 0.99 The 0.2 floor that got reported is simply the low preset — not a limit. Nothing stops you passing 0.45. Note also how non-linear the presets are: the gap from low to medium is 0.5, while high to xhigh is 0.09. The useful resolution is bunched up at the top of the range. This matters because most people will meet Inkling through an OpenAI-compatible wrapper exposing reasoning_effort="high". That enum is a lossy adapter over a continuous knob. If you're tuning cost against quality, the enum hides most of the dial. Set effort directly via the Tinker renderer CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ renderer = TmlV0Renderer(get_tokenizer("thinkingmachines/Inkling")) messages = [Message(role="user", content="Solve this problem step by step.")] prompt = renderer.build_generation_prompt(messages, effort=0.9) The same effort argument carries into fine-tuning, which is the part worth pausing on — you can train at a chosen effort level: Fine-tune at a fixed effort level CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ model_input, weights = renderer.build_supervised_example( messages_with_assistant_response, effort=0.9, ) आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-07-16। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: 1. The effort dial is a float, and the news got its range wrong

documents.t: The reason the dial is continuous is that it wasn't bolted on at inference time. During reinforcement learning, the team set effort by changing the system message and adjusting the per-token cost — literally taxing the model for thinking. The model learned to spend different token budgets on different rollouts, and the dial is the residue of that training. That's a genuinely different mechanism from "please think step by step, but briefly," and it's why the payoff is real: Thinking Machines reports Inkling matches Nemotron 3 Ultra on Terminal Bench 2.1 while using roughly one-third as many reasoning tokens. It also explains the caveat the docs are careful to state, which you should take seriously: "Larger values generally encourage more reasoning, but do not guarantee longer responses or higher accuracy on every sample." Effort is a learned tendency, not a guarantee. Turning it to 0.99 and expecting monotonic improvement is a misread of what it is. And higher effort "may require a larger generation budget to avoid truncation" — crank effort without raising max tokens and you'll cut the model off mid-thought.
documents.s: 2. Effort isn't a prompt trick — it was trained in with a token tax

documents.t: "975B parameters, Apache 2.0, weights on Hugging Face" invites an assumption the hardware table demolishes: Numeric Aggregated VRAM floor Example configuration BF16 at least 2 TB 8× NVIDIA B300, or 16× NVIDIA H200 NVFP4 (W4A4) at least 600 GB 4× NVIDIA B300 NVFP4 (W4A16) at least 600 GB 8× NVIDIA H200 Even fully quantized to 4-bit, the floor is roughly 600 GB of aggregated VRAM. This is a multi-GPU-cluster model, not a workstation model, and not remotely a laptop model. The 41B active parameters make it cheap to run a token through; they do nothing to reduce what you must hold in memory. All 975B parameters have to be resident, because the router may reach for any of them on any token. If your interest in open weights is "run it locally," Inkling is the wrong model and running models locally with Ollama is the right page. If your interest is legal freedom to modify and commercialize — Apache 2.0, genuinely permissive — then Inkling qualifies, and you'll rent the GPUs from TogetherAI, Fireworks, Modal, Databricks or Baseten. Those are different reasons to want open weights, and this release serves only the second one.
documents.s: 3. Open weights, but you almost certainly can't run it

documents.t: The benchmark table is unflattering, and Thinking Machines published it anyway: Benchmark Inkling A stronger competitor Terminal Bench 2.1 63.8% GLM 5.2: 82.7% SWEBench Verified 77.6% Kimi K2.6: 80.2% SimpleQA Verified 43.9% DeepSeek V4 Pro: 57.0% FORTRESS Adversarial 78.0% Nemotron 3 Ultra: 77.6% Three losses, one narrow win. But the interesting result isn't in that table at all — it's calibration. The team trained with reinforcement learning based on proper scoring rules, which reward a model for saying "I'm 70% sure" and being right 70% of the time, rather than for sounding confident. The model was rewarded for estimating its own uncertainty well instead of confidently producing wrong answers, and it shows up on forecasting evaluations like ForecastBench and Prophet Arena. For anything where a wrong-but-confident answer costs more than a hedged one — triage, research, routing, extraction with a human reviewer downstream — a well-calibrated 44% is worth more than an overconfident 57%. That property doesn't fit in a leaderboard column, which is roughly why nobody led with it.
documents.s: 4. It loses benchmarks on purpose — and wins the one nobody reported

documents.t: The pieces worth knowing, beyond the parameter count: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Sparse MoE routing⌄ A 66-layer decoder-only transformer. Each layer holds 256 routed experts plus 2 shared experts, with 6 routed experts active per token. The shared experts always fire — they carry general capability — while the router picks specialists per token. ←PreviousNext→ 2Relative positional embeddings, not RoPE⌄ A deliberate departure from the near-universal default. The stated reason is better extrapolation to longer sequences, which is how a 1M-token context window is meant to hold up rather than degrade at the tail. ←PreviousNext→ 3Attention shape⌄ Sliding-window and global layers mixed at a 5:1 ratio with 8 KV heads, plus short convolutions applied at the attention inputs. Five cheap local layers per one expensive global layer is what makes 1M context affordable. ←PreviousNext→ 4Native multimodality⌄ Images enter as 40×40 pixel patches through a four-layer hMLP; audio as dMel spectrograms. Both pass through a lightweight embedding layer and are processed jointly with text tokens — one stream, not a bolted-on vision encoder. Output is UTF-8 text only. ←PreviousNext→ 5Hybrid optimizer⌄ Muon for large matrix weights, Adam for everything else — an unusual choice at this scale, and consistent with the lab's public research interest in optimizer behavior. ←PreviousNext→

Reach for Inkling when: You need to own and modify a capable multimodal model. Apache 2.0 plus real multimodality plus first-class fine-tuning support on Tinker is a rare combination. This is the intended use. Cost per task matters more than peak score. The effort dial at one-third the reasoning tokens is a real lever, and you can tune it continuously rather than in three steps. Calibration matters. If your pipeline can act on "the model isn't sure," this is unusually well-suited. Don't reach for it when you want the strongest coding agent (the table says GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 beat it), when you want to self-host on your own hardware (see the VRAM floor), or when you want maximum factual recall (SimpleQA 43.9% is not competitive). One safety note that the model card states directly: Inkling has a residual "occasional tendency to comply with role-play and indirectly framed prompts concerning harmful topics," and the card explicitly recommends layering external moderation — it names Llama Guard — rather than relying on built-in refusals. VentureBeat framed the model's posture as "resistance to censorship"; read the model card's own language as the operative guidance instead, and budget for a moderation layer if you deploy this. The card also lists the usual residual limits: hallucination, imperfect instruction-following, and degraded performance in long multi-turn conversations. Check yourself 0/4

If you already read Kimi K2 for Claude users, the shape is familiar — a trillion-ish-parameter sparse MoE with permissive licensing — but the intent differs. Kimi K2 optimizes for long agentic tool chains. Inkling optimizes for being reshaped: multimodal input, a tunable effort budget, and fine-tuning as a first-class path. For the broader picture, see choosing a model, DeepSeek and Qwen open models for the rest of the open-weights field, and what AI costs across providers for the economics the effort dial is aimed at. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-07-16। Inkling was released on 15 July 2026. Benchmark comparisons and competitor scores move quickly, and hosted pricing was not published at launch. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत On 14–16 July 2026, xAI published Grok Build — the coding agent behind its CLI — as a public Apache 2.0 repository at xai-org/grok-build. Not the weights. The harness: the agent loop, the tool implementations, the terminal UI, the extension system. It went to the front page of Hacker News within hours. This is a rare artifact. Almost every serious coding agent — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex — ships as a binary or a bundle. Here, roughly 800,000 lines of production Rust are sitting in a repo you can read. That's worth more as a textbook than as a product. This page is the practical read: what's actually in there, what the structure teaches you about building agents, and two things about this release that most of the coverage got backwards. What you'll learn Understand what was published and what wasn't — harness yes, weights no, development history no Read the crate map as a checklist of what a production coding agent actually needs Learn why Apache 2.0 here means source-available, not open-development — and why that distinction is load-bearing See the data-collector code still present in the published tree, and what its constants confirm about the July exfil incident Know what's genuinely reusable from this repo and what is a dead end
documents.s: Inside Grok Build: Reading an Open Agent Harness

documents.t: The repository is 99%+ Rust, licensed Apache 2.0, and describes itself as a coding agent harness and TUI — fullscreen, mouse-interactive, extensible. It builds on macOS and Linux with a pinned Rust toolchain. Three things it is not: Not the model. Grok 4.5's weights are not here and are not open. The harness talks to a hosted endpoint. You can read every line of how the agent thinks about your codebase and still not run it without xAI's API. Not a development history. The repo has two commits: Publish harness and TUI open-source, then Synced from monorepo. There's a SOURCE_REV file at the root containing a single internal revision hash. This is an export of a private monorepo, re-synced periodically — not a repository that was developed in public and not one you can archaeologize for design decisions. Not open to you. CONTRIBUTING.md states plainly that the repository does not accept external pull requests or unsolicited patches, that xAI develops the software internally, and that the tree is published "for source transparency and local builds." GitHub issues are disabled at the repo level. ★ The distinction that matters: Apache 2.0 is a license, and it grants you real rights — read, fork, modify, ship derivatives. It says nothing about governance. Grok Build is source-available under an open-source license with a closed development model. You may fork it; you may not influence it. Read "open source" in the headlines as "you can read the source," because that is exactly and only what is on offer.

Ignore the marketing. The directory listing under crates/codegen/ is the most useful thing in the repo, because it is an honest inventory of what a shipping coding agent needs. A selection: Crate What it tells you xai-grok-agent, xai-grok-shell The agent runtime and its entry points — interactive, stdio, headless xai-grok-tools, xai-grok-tools-api Tool implementations, split from the tool interface — a real boundary xai-grok-workspace, xai-fast-worktree Filesystem, version control, execution, checkpoints — and fast git worktrees xai-codebase-graph Structural understanding of a repo, not just grep xai-grok-memory Memory is a subsystem, not a prompt trick xai-grok-mcp MCP is a first-class integration surface xai-grok-hooks, xai-hooks-plugins-types Hooks and plugins have their own type layer xai-grok-subagent-resolution Resolving which subagent handles what is hard enough to need its own crate xai-token-estimation Counting tokens before you spend them xai-hunk-tracker Tracking diff hunks across an editing session xai-grok-pager, xai-ratatui-inline The TUI — scrollback, prompts, modals, inline rendering xai-acp-lib Agent Client Protocol — editors embed the agent xai-grok-telemetry, xai-mixpanel Telemetry and product analytics, as first-class crates ptyctl, xai-tty-utils, xai-grok-crash-handler Terminals are hostile and processes crash Read that list again as a build plan. The naive mental model of a coding agent is "a loop that calls a model and runs tools." The actual decomposition includes a codebase graph, a memory subsystem, checkpointing, worktree management, hunk tracking, subagent resolution, token estimation, crash handling and a PTY control layer — before you write a single prompt. ★ The scale check. Simon Willison counted 844,530 lines of Rust in the tree, only ~3% of it vendored dependencies, and noted that OpenAI's Codex sits at roughly 950,933 lines. Two independent teams, converging near a million lines, for "a loop around an LLM." If your agent project feels like it's ballooning, this is the calibration: it is not you, and the hard part was never the loop. There's also a xai-grok-mermaid crate — a terminal renderer that draws Mermaid diagrams with Unicode box-drawing characters. It is not important. It is a nice reminder that shipping polish is a large fraction of any real agent. आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-07-16। Verified directly against the repository (license, commit count, CONTRIBUTING.md, crate listing). The star count, the enabled/disabled state of the upload path, and the crate list all move; the repo is re-synced from an internal monorepo. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.
documents.s: The crate map is the real lesson

documents.t: This is where the repo stops being a textbook and starts being evidence. In July 2026 a researcher's wire capture showed Grok Build uploading entire repositories — full git history, never-read files, .env contents — to a Google Cloud Storage bucket, through a channel unrelated to what the model read. AILmanac covers that incident and the general failure mode in What your agent uploads. xAI disabled the behavior server-side and said the retained data would be deleted. The published source contains that machinery. Verifiable from the repo directly: crates/codegen/xai-grok-shell/src/upload/gcs.rs exists. crates/codegen/xai-file-utils/src/upload_config.rs defines DEDUP_GCS_PREFIX = "repo_changes_dedup". That constant is the interesting one. The researcher's intercepted upload went to object paths of the form gs://grok-code-session-traces/repo_changes_dedup/v2/…. The path prefix captured on the wire is a named constant in xAI's own published source. The same file defines both ARCHIVE_SCHEMA_VERSION (v2) and ARCHIVE_SCHEMA_VERSION_V3 — meaning the archive format had been iterated to a third version. This was maintained infrastructure, not a stray debug path. The module documentation in gcs.rs is blunter than any press statement. It refers to the upload helpers as "the data-collector helpers," and the file's entire reason for existing is an engineering fix: threading refresh-aware credentials through so that stale tokens stop causing POST /v1/storage 401s. Someone was debugging the reliability of the repository upload path as production work. Simon Willison reports that the upload path is now disabled in the published tree, returning a hard-coded error. That is consistent with xAI's stated position, and we were not able to independently confirm the specific mechanism by code search — treat it as reported rather than verified here. ★ What to take from this. Not "xAI is uniquely bad" — the wider lesson from the security page stands: this class of channel exists in some form in many agents, and reading the source is the only way to know. Take instead the meta-point: this is what source transparency is actually for. You cannot audit a binary's data flows in an afternoon. You can grep a published tree for bucket_url in about ten seconds. The release is genuinely valuable precisely because it makes the uncomfortable parts greppable. Check yourself 0/4
documents.s: The data-collector code is still in the tree

documents.t: Be honest about the constraints before you fork: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Read it for architecture, not for code⌄ The crate boundaries are the product of a well-funded team shipping to real users. That decomposition — tools split from tools-api, workspace from agent, subagent resolution as its own concern — is the transferable asset. Copying Rust out of it buys you far less than copying the shape. ←PreviousNext→ 2Treat the tool implementations as a survey⌄ Willison notes the tool implementations show signs of being adapted from competing products including Codex, Claude and Cursor. That makes the tool layer a convergent-design reference: where three or four agents independently landed on the same tool contract, that contract is probably right. ←PreviousNext→ 3Audit before you trust any agent, including this one⌄ The value of a published tree is that you can check claims instead of believing them. Grep for HTTP clients, bucket URLs, telemetry crates and upload call sites. xai-grok-telemetry and xai-mixpanel are first-class crates here — that is not a scandal, but it is a fact you can only learn by looking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Don't plan on upstreaming anything⌄ No PRs, no issues. If you fork, you own your fork forever, and you rebase against monorepo exports on xAI's schedule. Budget accordingly. ←PreviousNext→ If you want to explore the tree without building it: Clone and map the crate structure CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build cd grok-build # The inventory of what a production coding agent needs ls crates/codegen/ # Where does data leave the machine? Start here, not with the README. grep -rn "bucket_url\|/v1/storage\|upload_bytes" crates/ --include=*.rs | head -30 # Which internal revision was this cut from? cat SOURCE_REV

If you drive Claude Code, Grok Build is the same category of tool with its guts exposed — read it as a second opinion on problems you already have. Coding agent CLIs compared places it against the field, and Grok for Claude users covers the xAI ecosystem around it. For the architecture ideas the crate map gestures at, see long-running agent harnesses and agent memory architectures — xai-grok-memory and xai-grok-subagent-resolution are one team's answers to exactly those problems. And read What your agent uploads alongside this page. That one shows you how to catch a channel like this on the wire with mitmproxy and a canary repo. This one shows you what it looks like in the source. The two techniques together are the whole audit.
