Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम On 28 September 2026 Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) — the second model in the 5.5 family, after Opus 5.5 six days earlier. The rate card is the interesting part precisely because it did not move: $2 in / $10 out per MTok, byte-for-byte Sonnet 5's prices, same tokenizer, same cache and batch rates. Anthropic's claim is nonetheless output more than 30% faster and up to 30% less per task. Both can be true at once, and understanding why is the whole point of this page: on Sonnet 5.5 the saving lives in the token count and the turn count, never in the price per token. That changes what you measure, and it changes which knob you reach for first. The second thing worth knowing on day one: the cheap model is not uniformly behind the expensive one. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 Sonnet 5.5 scores 70.6% against Opus 5.5's 66.4% — the one published row where the half-price model is ahead. And on knowledge-work Elo the two are a statistical tie. The gap that remains is concentrated somewhere specific, and this page says where. What you'll learn Know the real numbers: $2/$10 per MTok unchanged from Sonnet 5, 1M context, 128K max output (300K on Batches), June 2026 cutoff, default effort high Fix the five breaking changes that 400-error a Sonnet 5 codebase, and the sixth that returns 200 and makes your progress UI go silent Use between_tools correctly — the replacement for thinking disabled, which is rejected at xhigh and max effort and rejects every companion field Read the launch table honestly: where Sonnet 5.5 beats Opus 5.5, where it is 8 points behind, and why one row reads 10.3% Calibrate effort from scratch instead of carrying a setting over, and recover the ~1/3 of session cost that max effort spends on self-started review Handle the quieter failure modes: structured-output requests that think until max_tokens, tool names off by letter case, and real user messages mistaken for prompt injection आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-28। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

Sonnet 5 Sonnet 5.5 Opus 5.5 Claude API ID claude-sonnet-5 claude-sonnet-5-5 claude-opus-5-5 Input / output per MTok $2 / $10 $2 / $10 $4 / $20 Cache read / 5m write $0.20 / $2.50 $0.20 / $2.50 $0.20 / $5 Min cacheable prompt 1,024 tokens 512 tokens — Context 1M 1M 1M Max output (sync) 128K 128K 128K Thinking settings accepted adaptive, disabled adaptive, between_tools adaptive only Default effort high high medium Reliable knowledge cutoff — Jun 2026 Jun 2026 Retirement no sooner than — 28 Sep 2027 22 Sep 2027 Four things in that table are genuinely new, and only one of them is a headline anywhere: The minimum cacheable prompt halved, 1,024 → 512 tokens. If your system prompt sits in the 600–1,000 token range it was silently uncacheable on Sonnet 5 and is cacheable now, at 10% of input price on reads. No code change, no beta header. This is the cheapest win on the whole page. thinking: {"type": "disabled"} is gone, replaced by between_tools. Sonnet 5.5 sits between Sonnet 5 (which accepted disabled) and Opus 5.5 (which accepts neither) — it can still skip up-front thinking, just under a new name and with new limits. Default effort stayed high — note that this is higher than Opus 5.5's medium default. The cheaper model thinks more per turn out of the box than the expensive one. temperature, top_p and top_k return 400 at any non-default value, as on the rest of the 5.x line. Sampling-parameter sweeps are not a tuning surface here; effort is. The tokenizer is unchanged from Sonnet 5, so the same text produces the same token counts. Any change you measure in your bill is a change in how many tokens the model chose to emit.
documents.s: Specs, and the four numbers that changed

documents.t: This is the part most launch coverage compresses into "30% cheaper" and gets subtly wrong. The rate card is identical. Anthropic's claim decomposes into three separate effects, and they are not equally easy to capture: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Fewer output tokens for the same work⌄ Output is the expensive side at $10/MTok against $2 input. Sonnet 5.5 reaches the same result in fewer output tokens than Sonnet 5, which includes thinking tokens — thinking is billed as output even when its text is never returned to you. This effect you get for free, on the same code. ←PreviousNext→ 2Fewer tool calls, so fewer round trips⌄ Each avoided tool call removes a whole request: the resent conversation prefix on input, the latency, and a turn of overhead. In an agent loop that is usually a bigger line item than the output tokens themselves. Anthropic's own framing of Terminal-Bench 4.0 is that this is where token efficiency pays. ←PreviousNext→ 3More than 30% faster output generation⌄ Latency is not cost, but it is a cost in every interactive product, and it is the effect most likely to survive your own measurement unchanged. Note the ceiling: at medium effort and above the model thinks briefly before nearly every reply, greeting included, which adds to time-to-first-token no matter how fast generation is. ←PreviousNext→ Effects 1 and 2 are exactly what a carried-over effort setting can cancel out. Which is why the next section is the one to read before you change your model ID.
documents.s: Why the bill drops when the price does not

documents.t: Anthropic is explicit that effort levels are recalibrated — a level does not buy the same amount of thinking it bought on Sonnet 5. There is no conversion table, by design. Re-run your sweep. The published starting points are not the default: Workload Start at Why General / unsure high The API default. Agentic coding, multistep tool use, well-specified medium Then move to high for harder or longer tasks. Chat, latency-sensitive medium or low Higher effort means a longer wait before the reply starts. Anything xhigh / max Only where you have measured a quality gain. Three consequences that bite in production: Changing the top-level effort between requests invalidates the prompt cache. If you want a cheap interactive session that escalates on hard turns, use the per-message effort beta (output_config.effort on one message), which keeps the cache. This beta is new on 5.5 and was not available on Sonnet 5. max_tokens has to cover thinking plus the reply. Thinking counts against it even when the thinking text is omitted from the response. A limit sized for a no-thinking request will truncate. For agentic coding Anthropic's guidance is blunt: set max_tokens to 128,000 and stream. Asking the model to think less does not reliably work. Lowering the effort level does. From medium up it thinks before almost every reply; at low it skips thinking on most simple requests.
documents.s: Effort: recalibrate, do not carry over

documents.t: At xhigh and max, Sonnet 5.5 does not stop when the task is done. It starts its own rounds of review and verification, and if your harness offers subagents it will launch reviewer subagents — unasked. Anthropic published the fix and, unusually, the size of it: in their testing on coding tasks at max effort, the paragraph below cut session cost by about a third with no change in quality. Stop self-started review rounds at xhigh and max effort CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ When the work the user asked for is done and its checks pass, stop and report. Don't start extra rounds of review or hardening on your own, and don't launch reviewer sub-agents unless the user asked for a review. If you think a deeper review is worth doing, say so at the end. It makes self-started reviews rarer rather than impossible. The mirror-image problem exists at the bottom of the range: at low and medium on long agentic tasks the model is more likely to stop and check in before finishing, and at low it sometimes reports a code change done without running a check that exercises it.
Each of these returns HTTP 400 invalid_request_error on code that worked on Sonnet 5.

thinking: {"type": "disabled"} returns 400 with a message that names its replacement: "thinking.type.disabled" is not supported for this model. Use "thinking.type.between_tools" for the lowest thinking setting, or "thinking.type.adaptive" and "output_config.effort" to control thinking behavior. between_tools is the lowest thinking setting on Sonnet 5.5. It needs no beta header and works on every platform that offers the model. But it is fussier than disabled ever was: Accepted at low, medium, high. At xhigh or max it returns 400 — those levels require adaptive thinking (omit thinking, or send thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}; they are equivalent). Effort cannot change mid-conversation. A per-message output_config.effort that differs from the level in effect returns 400. Per-turn effort needs adaptive thinking. It takes no companion field. display, budget_tokens or block_binding sent alongside it returns 400. Manual budgets (thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}) return 400 too. With server-side fallback, a between_tools request that falls back to Sonnet 5 runs there with thinking: {"type": "disabled"} — the settings map across the fallback for you. One more trap: with between_tools, remove any instruction telling the model not to think. Those lines make it more likely to write internal XML tags into its visible output. Migrating a thinking-off integration — Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Before — accepted on Sonnet 5 client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=16000, thinking={"type": "disabled"}, output_config={"effort": "xhigh"}, # fine with disabled on Sonnet 5 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}], ) # After — on Sonnet 5.5: rename the type AND drop effort to high or below client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=16000, thinking={"type": "between_tools"}, # xhigh/max with this -> 400 output_config={"effort": "high"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}], ) # If you need xhigh or max, use adaptive thinking instead of between_tools: # thinking={"type": "adaptive"} (or omit the field entirely) # SDKs that predate between_tools fail type checking on the literal. # Update the SDK, or pass the value as raw JSON.

tool_choice set to {"type": "any"} or {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} returns 400: tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model. auto (the default) and none still work. The same check applies on the token-counting endpoint, which is easy to miss in a test suite that only exercises /v1/messages. Forced tool use was doing two jobs; split them: Schema validity comes from strict tool use (strict: true on the tool) or from structured outputs. Steering — making the model call the tool at all — comes from the prompt saying when the tool applies.

Every thinking block records which model produced it, and models only read some other models' blocks. The graph is asymmetric and not intuitive: Blocks produced by Can Sonnet 5.5 read them? Sonnet 5.5 itself Yes Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Haiku 4.5 and earlier Yes Opus 5, Opus 5.5 No Any Fable or Mythos model No And in the other direction: no other model reads Sonnet 5.5's thinking blocks. So a conversation that migrates up from Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5 keeps its reasoning; a conversation that moves off Sonnet 5.5 to anything else — including Opus 5.5, a tempting escalation path — runs every subsequent turn without it. Unreadable blocks are dropped before the model sees them, the request succeeds, and dropped blocks are not billed. With the thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 beta header the drops are itemised in a top-level input_transformations array. Two further bindings sit on top: Conversation prefix. The API checks whether the system prompt, the tools list, or any earlier message changed since a Sonnet 5.5 thinking block was produced. It enforces this by default for accounts created on or after 31 August 2026, 00:00 UTC on the Claude API, Bedrock and Google Cloud — replaying a block after such an edit returns 400 there. To drop the affected blocks instead of failing, send thinking-binding-controls-2026-08-01 and set thinking.block_binding.prefix_mismatch_behavior to "drop_block". Note block_binding only works with adaptive thinking; under between_tools your only options are append-only history or stripping thinking blocks from the edited turn onward. Account. Sonnet 5.5's thinking blocks work only in the account that produced them, or a linked one. Another account sending them gets them dropped, with reason: "organization_binding_mismatch" under the binding-controls beta. Blocks from earlier models are unaffected. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Keep history append-only and none of this can fire⌄ Claude Code, claude.ai, Claude Managed Agents and the Claude Agent SDK already do this. Append-only integrations need no change. ←PreviousNext→ 2Change instructions with mid-conversation system messages, not by editing the system prompt⌄ Appending a line to system mid-session edits the prefix and invalidates every earlier thinking block. A mid-conversation system message appends instead — and it is newly supported on Sonnet 5.5, not on Sonnet 5. ←PreviousNext→ 3Declare every tool in the first request of the session⌄ Adding an entry to tools later edits the prefix too. If you must add one mid-session, the inline-tools-2026-09-15 beta lets a tool_addition block carry a full tool definition inside a mid-conversation system message, without touching tools and without losing the cache. ←PreviousNext→ 4Compact with the API rather than rewriting history yourself⌄ The compact-2026-09-04 beta returns a signed compaction block summarising the conversation, which you send first in place of the messages it replaces. Thinking blocks in the turns you keep can stay valid across the swap — which matters far more here than on Sonnet 5, precisely because these blocks are conversation-bound. ←PreviousNext→ 5Do not plan to escalate mid-conversation to Opus 5.5 and keep the reasoning⌄ It cannot read Sonnet 5.5 blocks. If a hard turn needs more depth, raising effort with the per-message beta keeps the reasoning; switching models does not. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: 3. Thinking blocks are bound to the model, the conversation, and the account

documents.t: On the Claude API and Google Cloud, Sonnet 5.5 supports computer use only through the computer_toolset_20260801 toolset. Declaring the older computer_20251124 tool returns 400: 'claude-sonnet-5-5' does not support tool types: computer_20251124. On Amazon Bedrock, Sonnet 5.5 still accepts computer_20251124. That asymmetry is the kind of thing that makes a multi-platform deployment pass CI on one cloud and fail on another. Migrating means: drop the old beta header, replace the tools entry with {"type": "computer_toolset_20260801"}, and update the agent loop for member tool_use blocks, batch actions, and toolset_name on results. Integrations already on the toolset, and anything using the browser use tool, need no change.
documents.s: 4. computer_20251124 is rejected — on two platforms out of three

documents.t: With the advisor tool (beta), a Sonnet 5.5 executor accepts Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, Mythos 5, Fable 5, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, or Sonnet 5.5 itself as advisor. Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 5 are rejected with 400 — all three of which worked as advisors for a Sonnet 5 executor. Every advisor Sonnet 5.5 accepts returns its advice encrypted, as an advisor_redacted_result block, so your client cannot read the advice text.

This one fails nothing and is the most likely to reach your users before it reaches your logs. Between tool calls, Sonnet 5.5 writes user-facing notes about what it just found and what it is doing next. Notes longer than a sentence or two now come back as progress-update thinking blocks; shorter remarks stay text. At the default display: "omitted" a progress-update block's text field is empty. A client that renders only text blocks therefore shows nothing at all during a long agentic turn — no error, no warning, just silence where narration used to be. Three ways out, in order of how little work they are: Use between_tools. The notes come back with their summary text, no display field needed (and none accepted). Set display: "updates" with the thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18 beta header. You get a short summary of each progress update while the reasoning itself stays hidden. Give the model a tool for sending the user a message, for the cases where it needs to show exact text mid-turn — a code snippet, a question it needs answered. Tell it to use that tool only for such content, and declare the tool in the first request so tools never changes later. Then clean up around it: delete instructions like "hold all findings for the final response", and if you want updates at predictable points, ask for them explicitly — a line before the first tool call, a recap at the end. The model follows that. If long turns still go quiet, your harness can nudge — carefully. Count consecutive tool-calling steps that sent the user no text, and after several (say five) append a one-turn reminder after the latest tool results, as a turn-scoped system message: Harness nudge for a silent agentic turn CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ The user hasn't heard from you in a while — say in a few words what you're doing, then continue. Stop after the second or third if it does not take. Frequent harness text after tool results makes the model suspect a prompt injection — which is the next section. Because the reminder is appended rather than inserted and later removed, the prompt cache and the preserved thinking both survive. Anthropic's measurement: at high effort with a message-the-user tool available, this shortens the longest silent stretches with no measurable change in task quality.
documents.s: The sixth change: HTTP 200, and your UI goes quiet

documents.t: आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-28। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत. Benchmark Sonnet 5 Sonnet 5.5 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 as % of Opus 5.5 Terminal-Bench 4.0 10.3% 70.6% 66.4% 106% GDPval-AA v2.1 (Elo) 1449 1844 1846 99.9% AA-Briefcase v1.1 (Elo) 1359 1811 1822 99.4% OSWorld 2.1 (partial credit) — 80.1% 81.8% 98% CursorBench 4.0 34.1% 55.5% 57.8% 96% Chartography (no tools) — 61.6% 64.4% 96% Humanity's Last Exam (tools) 54.9% 64.5% 67.7% 95% FrontierCode 1.1 (max effort) 42.4% 46.2% 54.4% 85% Four honest readings of that table: The gap is not uniform, and averaging it away hides the useful signal. On knowledge-work Elo the two models are inside noise of each other. On the hardest coding benchmark, FrontierCode 1.1, Sonnet 5.5 is 8.2 points behind — 85% of Opus 5.5. That single row is the honest basis for Anthropic's own framing that Opus 5.5 remains clearly stronger on complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment. Terminal-Bench 4.0 is the one row where the half-price model wins, 70.6% against 66.4%. That benchmark is the closest published proxy for "run an agent in a shell until the job is done," which is exactly where fewer tool calls and fewer tokens compound. Treat Sonnet 5's 10.3% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with suspicion, not awe. A 60-point generational jump on one benchmark version tells you at least as much about the harness and the scoring version as about the model. Use it to conclude "this version of this benchmark punishes Sonnet 5's agent behaviour," not "Sonnet 5.5 is seven times better at agentic coding." Sources disagree on FrontierCode at the top of the effort range. Anthropic's table reports 46.2% at max effort; at least one aggregator reports a higher 52.1% at xhigh. We have not been able to confirm the second figure against the primary table, so read it as unverified — but note that "more effort scored lower" is consistent with the docs' own advice to reserve xhigh and max for cases where you have measured a gain, rather than assuming monotonic improvement. Independent measurement, as always, lands lower than vendor measurement on agentic benchmarks. Run your own evals before you commit a number to a slide.
None of these throw. All of them cost you accuracy or trust.

Ask for a JSON answer to a task that needs a few steps of working out — totalling figures from a document, applying a rule, ranking items — and Sonnet 5.5 often answers without thinking first, especially at low and medium effort. With structured outputs the response text holds only the JSON, so the working has nowhere to go except the thinking; skip the thinking and accuracy drops. With adaptive thinking, appending Think the problem through before you answer. to the system prompt brings high-effort accuracy close to xhigh for a modest increase in output tokens. between_tools is the wrong setting for these requests: with no tools in play, it means no thinking at all, and that line has no effect. At low and medium with structured outputs, the model occasionally keeps thinking until it hits max_tokens. Treat any response with stop_reason: "max_tokens" as failed and retry, even when its text happens to contain valid JSON. This is the single most likely way to ship a confidently wrong number. If you cannot use structured outputs and ask for JSON in the prompt, the model tends to work the problem out in the response text and put the JSON at the end. Do not slice from the first { to the last } — it occasionally writes a draft before the final answer and you would capture both. Extracting the final JSON value from a mixed response CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Read only text blocks. Treat stop_reason == "max_tokens" as a failure and retry. # Starting at each { or [, try to parse a JSON value; continue from the END of a value # that parses, so values nested inside it are not counted on their own. Keep the LAST one. import json def last_json_value(text): dec, best, i = json.JSONDecoder(), None, 0 while i < len(text): if text[i] in "{[": try: value, end = dec.raw_decode(text, i) except ValueError: i += 1 continue best, i = value, end # jump past it: skip nested values else: i += 1 return best # Then check the fields you expect are present, and retry once if they are not.
documents.s: Structured outputs that think until they run out

documents.t: Sonnet 5.5 is trained to resist indirect prompt injection — instructions arriving through tool results and other content it reads mid-task. Sometimes it misclassifies a genuine user message that way, tells the user the tool result contained text posing as a message from them, and either ignores it or asks for confirmation. The trigger is placement: text arriving immediately after tool results, especially on every step. Never put user text inside a tool_result block. This is the placement it misreads most often. Deliver mid-turn user input as a user turn: append their words as a text block in the user message that carries the tool_result blocks, after the last tool_result. Keep harness notices in a separate mid-conversation system message, after the user's words. Never put a notice and the user's words in the same block. Drop your own token/budget countdown after tool results in interactive sessions where users can type mid-turn. A per-step countdown is the classic cause. The Task budgets beta adds a similar countdown but has not been seen to cause this misread.
documents.s: Real user messages read as prompt injection

documents.t: Sonnet 5.5 occasionally calls a declared tool by a name differing only in case — bash for Bash — or passes a known parameter under a slightly different name. Do not treat that as fatal. Either accept the call when the match is unambiguous, or return a tool_result with is_error: true that states the exact expected name; the model usually corrects itself on the next turn.
documents.s: Tool names off by letter case

documents.t: For dense charts and technical drawings, give the model a way to crop, zoom, or run code on the image. The measured result is worth internalising: with tools at high effort it read charts more accurately than without tools at max effort, at a fraction of the cost. On technical drawings the tools only help from high up, and most at xhigh and max. Reach for the tool, not the dial.
documents.s: Charts: give it tools before you give it effort

documents.t: A declined request is HTTP 200 with stop_reason: "refusal" and a stop_details object naming the category. Sonnet 5.5 is the first Sonnet to ship with cyber safeguards comparable to Anthropic's most capable models, and the first with classifiers that block reasoning extraction. stop_details category What it covers Server-side fallback retries it on Sonnet 5? cyber Could enable cyber harm — malware, exploit development. Finding vulnerabilities in source code is allowed; high-risk dual-use work is not. Yes frontier_llm Could assist development of competing AI models. Yes bio Could enable biological harm. Everyday health and educational questions unaffected. No reasoning_extraction Asks the model to reproduce its internal reasoning in the response text. No general_harms Another usage-policy area. Benign work can also trigger this. No Two practical notes. First, if your prompts ask the model to include its reasoning in the answer, remove those lines — they invite reasoning_extraction declines. Read reasoning from summarized thinking blocks (display: "summarized") instead. Second, whether a refusal that arrives before any output is billed depends on its category, and it counts against your rate limits either way. Legitimate life-sciences work blocked by the bio classifier can apply to Anthropic's Life Sciences Verification Program.
documents.s: Refusals: five categories, and only two get retried

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Sonnet 5.5 is the new default for well-scoped work⌄ Everyday tasks, bug fixes, multistep tool use, polished documents and spreadsheets. Start at medium effort for agentic coding, high for general work, and measure. At $2/$10 with 1M context it is the cheapest model in the lineup that is still frontier-adjacent on knowledge work. ←PreviousNext→ 2Opus 5.5 for complex, open-ended, sustained-judgment work⌄ The FrontierCode row is where the 2x price buys something real — 54.4% against 46.2%. Also note it cannot read Sonnet 5.5's thinking blocks, so treat the choice as per-conversation, not per-turn. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fable 5.1 only when Opus 5.5 at higher effort still fails your evals⌄ That is Anthropic's own stated criterion, and at $10/$50 it is 5x Sonnet 5.5's list price. ←PreviousNext→ 4Stay on Sonnet 5 only for a specific reason⌄ Two exist: code that depends on forced tool_choice, and code that depends on thinking: disabled with xhigh or max effort — a combination between_tools does not allow. Both are migrations, not blockers. ←PreviousNext→ 5Haiku 4.5 remains the floor⌄ 200K context, $1/$5, no effort parameter. For classification, extraction and routing the 5.5 family is overkill. ←PreviousNext→ The migration itself is a model-ID swap plus six checks, and Anthropic ships an automation for it: in Claude Code, /claude-api migrate this project to claude-sonnet-5-5 applies the ID swap and the breaking parameter changes across a codebase and hands you a checklist of what to verify by hand. It asks you to confirm scope before editing anything. If you use Claude Managed Agents rather than the Messages API directly, the model name is the only change required. Check yourself 0/6
documents.s: So which model do you actually run?

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम On 30 June 2026 Anthropic shipped Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5) and, quietly, made it the default model in Claude Code (today Claude Code defaults to Sonnet 5 on Pro and Team Standard, and to Opus 5 on Max, Team Premium, Enterprise and the API). On paper it's a drop-in for Sonnet 4.6 at a lower list price. In practice, three API constraints will make naive migrations return 400 Bad Request, a new tokenizer produces roughly 30% more tokens for the same text (which changes both your context budget and your per-request bill), and the effort scale has shifted enough that "keep everything the same" isn't the same. If you were on Sonnet 4.6 at high, running Sonnet 5 at high is closer to Sonnet 4.6 at max. This page is the practical field guide: what changed, what breaks, the exact migration checklist, the pricing math on the tokenizer shift, and the prompting patterns most teams re-tune first. What you'll learn Understand what Sonnet 5 actually is — 1M context by default, adaptive thinking on by default, first Sonnet with real-time cybersecurity safeguards Know the three API constraints that will 400 your existing code and the one-line fix for each Model the new-tokenizer pricing math: same $/token but ~30% more tokens = a different per-request bill Re-calibrate effort levels: Sonnet 5 medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 high, and Sonnet 5 high ≈ Sonnet 4.6 max Adjust the prompting patterns that shift the most: verbosity, tool-use triggering, code-review recall, and design defaults आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-07-23। Model ID, context window, output cap, pricing, tokenizer behavior, and API constraints verified against Anthropic's official "What's new in Claude Sonnet 5" page and the platform release notes on 23 July 2026. claude-sonnet-5 shipped 30 June 2026. Launched at $2 in / $10 out per MTok as introductory pricing; Anthropic has since made $2 / $10 the standard price and cancelled the scheduled 1 September 2026 increase to $3 / $15 (re-verified on the pricing page on 15 September 2026). 1M-token context by default (no smaller variant), 128k max output, adaptive thinking always on unless explicitly disabled. Priority Tier is not available. Cross-check the Current Models & Pricing table before pinning a model. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

Sonnet 5 is the balanced "start here" Sonnet tier, positioned above Sonnet 4.6 at a lower list price, and Claude Code's default on Pro and Team Standard. It supports the 1M-token context window by default (there is no smaller-context variant), a 128k max output, and adaptive thinking on by default. Three API contracts break on migration: manual extended thinking (thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}) is removed and returns a 400, non-default sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, top_k) return a 400, and the tokenizer changed — the same input text produces roughly 30% more tokens than on Sonnet 4.6. Priority Tier is not available on Sonnet 5. That's the whole shape of the release.

Anthropic's own docs describe Sonnet 5 as a "drop-in replacement for Claude Sonnet 4.6" — and for prompt content, that's true. But the API surface changed enough that "swap the model string and ship" will produce errors on requests that ran fine yesterday. There are four things that will bite you, in order of how often we see them break integrations: temperature, top_p, or top_k set to non-default values now return 400. Not silently ignored. Not clipped. A hard error. This is new for Sonnet-class models; Opus 4.7 introduced the same constraint. If your SDK wrapper always sends temperature: 0.7, it will now always fail. Manual extended thinking is removed. thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N} was deprecated on 4.6 and returns 400 on Sonnet 5. Use adaptive thinking with the effort parameter instead. Adaptive thinking is on by default. Requests without a thinking field on Sonnet 4.6 ran without thinking; on Sonnet 5, they run with adaptive thinking. max_tokens is a hard cap on total output — thinking plus response text — so a limit sized for "just the answer" on Sonnet 4.6 can truncate the answer on Sonnet 5. The new tokenizer produces roughly 30% more tokens for the same text. Not an API change — request and response shapes are identical — but everything you measure or budget in tokens now measures higher.

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Non-default sampling parameters return 400⌄ Remove any temperature, top_p, or top_k that isn't the API default. If your app needs stylistic variety, use system-prompt instructions instead of temperature (that's now the only lever). If you need diverse design outputs, ask the model to propose N distinct directions and pick one — that gives you variety across runs even with fixed sampling. ←PreviousNext→ 2Manual extended thinking returns 400⌄ Delete any thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N} in your request builder. Set effort instead (low / medium / high / xhigh / max) and let adaptive thinking decide when to think. If you were dynamically computing a thinking budget per request, replace that logic with an effort selector — Anthropic explicitly recommends against trying to reproduce the old behavior. ←PreviousNext→ 3Adaptive thinking on by default eats your max_tokens budget⌄ On Sonnet 4.6, an omitted thinking field meant no thinking. On Sonnet 5, it means adaptive thinking. Since max_tokens is a hard cap on total output (thinking blocks + response text), you can end up with a mostly-thinking response and a truncated answer with stop_reason: "max_tokens". Either raise max_tokens, drop effort to medium, or pass thinking: {type: "disabled"} if you truly want no thinking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Assistant message prefilling is still unsupported⌄ This is inherited from Sonnet 4.6, not new — but many teams migrating from Sonnet 4.5 or earlier hit it for the first time when they touch this surface. Use structured outputs, system-prompt instructions, or output_config.format instead. Prefilling returns a 400 error. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal safe migration — one diff CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Before (Sonnet 4.6) — worked response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=4096, temperature=0.7, # 400 on Sonnet 5 thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8000}, # 400 on Sonnet 5 messages=[...], ) # After (Sonnet 5) — one-liner replacements response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=8192, # raise: thinking now shares the budget # temperature removed — use system prompt instead # thinking removed — adaptive is on by default extra_body={"effort": "high"}, # was implicit in budget_tokens messages=[...], )
documents.s: The API constraints that will 400 you

documents.t: The new tokenizer is the change most likely to surprise your finance team. Requests and responses look identical over the wire, but the same input text produces roughly 30% more tokens than on Sonnet 4.6. The exact multiplier depends on the content — code, English prose, non-English text, and structured data all shift differently — but 30% is the number Anthropic quotes. Three things this changes at the same time: Per-request cost. Sonnet 5's standard price is $2 / $10 per MTok versus Sonnet 4.6's $3 / $15 (the scheduled 1 September 2026 increase to $3 / $15 was cancelled). Even with ~30% more tokens for the same text, the same text costs roughly 13% less than on Sonnet 4.6. Context capacity in text terms. The context window is still 1M tokens, but each token now covers less text on average. The same document takes up ~30% more of your window. max_tokens truncation risk. An output cap tuned for "roughly this much text" on Sonnet 4.6 can silently truncate equivalent output on Sonnet 5. Revisit any limit sized close to your expected output length. The pricing math, laid out honestly: Period List price Same text → cost vs Sonnet 4.6 Standard (introductory price made permanent) $2 in / $10 out Roughly 13% cheaper (30% more tokens × $2 vs. Sonnet 4.6 at $3) If you modeled a 1 September 2026 flip to $3 / $15, re-run the numbers: Anthropic cancelled that increase. Recount your prompts under the new tokenizer CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Recount before you migrate — don't trust old numbers count = client.messages.count_tokens( model="claude-sonnet-5", # count under the NEW tokenizer messages=[{"role": "user", "content": your_prompt}], system=your_system, ) print(count.input_tokens) # roughly 30% higher than on claude-sonnet-4-6
documents.s: The tokenizer shift is a pricing story, not an API story

documents.t: The effort parameter (low / medium / high / xhigh / max) still has the same five values, but Anthropic gives an explicit cross-model mapping when migrating that most teams miss on first read: Sonnet 5 at medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 at high. Sonnet 5 at high ≈ Sonnet 4.6 at max. xhigh is recommended for the hardest coding and agentic tasks. max removes token-spending constraints entirely. Two implications: If you were running Sonnet 4.6 at high and swap the model without changing effort, you're now running with more thinking, more tokens, and probably better outputs — but a bigger bill. Consider dropping to medium. If you were running Sonnet 4.6 at max and swap to Sonnet 5 at max, you may be paying for headroom you don't need. Try xhigh first. Anthropic also warns Sonnet 5 respects effort strictly, especially at the low end. low and medium scope work to what was asked; they don't "go above and beyond." That's good for latency and cost, but on moderately complex tasks at low there's a real risk of under-thinking. The recommended fix is to raise effort rather than prompt around it.
documents.s: The effort scale shifted — recalibrate before you compare

documents.t: Claude Code v2.1.197 (30 June 2026) made claude-sonnet-5 the default model. Today the default model setting resolves to Sonnet 5 on Pro and Team Standard, and to Opus 5 on Max, Team Premium, Enterprise and the Anthropic API (model configuration). On a plan where Sonnet 5 is the default, if you don't set anything, your sessions run on Sonnet 5. Practical consequences: You get 1M context, but your max_tokens and effort settings are inherited. Claude Code's defaults are tuned for the new model; custom CLAUDE.md configs that pinned max_tokens or set an effort override should be re-verified. Faster, more agentic default behavior. Sonnet 5 is more agentic than Sonnet 4.6 out of the box — it reaches for tools and runs self-verification loops more readily. If you were used to Claude Code being conservative about running commands, expect more initiative. Regular user-facing progress updates. Sonnet 5 already provides higher-quality interim updates on long traces. Prompt scaffolding like "after every 3 tool calls, summarize progress" can usually be removed. Sonnet 4.6 is now a legacy model. Still available (pin claude-sonnet-4-6 if you have a reason), but no longer the on-ramp.
documents.s: Sonnet 5 as the Claude Code default — what changes

documents.t: Sonnet 5 chooses response length based on the complexity of the task rather than defaulting to a fixed verbosity. Simple lookups get shorter answers; open-ended analysis gets longer ones. If your product wants a consistent style, tune the prompt — Anthropic's own snippet works: Tame verbosity when you need a fixed voice CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Provide concise, focused responses. Skip non-essential context, and keep examples minimal. Positive examples ("here's how to phrase this concisely") work better than negative ones ("don't over-explain").

Sonnet 5 reaches for tools more readily than 4.6. Two levers: Effort. high or xhigh show substantially more tool usage in agentic search and coding workloads. low and medium scope the work tightly. Thinking off. With thinking: {type: "disabled"}, the model is less likely to reach for tools. If you disable thinking but still rely on tool calls, add an explicit nudge in the system prompt.
documents.s: 2. Tool-use triggering is more agentic — and can be dialed

documents.t: If your review prompt says "only report high-severity issues" or "don't nitpick," Sonnet 5 may follow that faithfully — investigating just as thoroughly, finding the same bugs, then not reporting findings it judges below your stated bar. Precision typically rises, recall can appear to fall. Anthropic's recommended fix separates the finding stage from the ranking stage: Recall-oriented code-review prompt for Sonnet 5 CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Report every issue you find, including ones you are uncertain about or consider low-severity. Do not filter for importance or confidence at this stage - a separate verification step will do that. Your goal here is coverage: it is better to surface a finding that later gets filtered out than to silently drop a real bug. For each finding, include your confidence level and an estimated severity so a downstream filter can rank them. You don't need to actually build the second step for the prompt to help — moving confidence filtering out of the finding step is what changes behavior.
documents.s: 3. Code-review harnesses may see recall drop — that's the model being more literal

documents.t: On open-ended frontend and design briefs, Sonnet 5 tends toward a consistent default visual style. That reads well for some products, wrong for dashboards, dev tools, fintech, healthcare, or enterprise apps. Generic pushback ("make it less generic") tends to shift the model to a different fixed style rather than producing variety. Two patterns that work: Specify a concrete alternative — hex codes, typeface names, layout rules. Sonnet 5 follows explicit specs precisely. Ask the model to propose N options before building. Because non-default temperature returns 400, this is now the recommended way to produce meaningfully different design directions across runs. Force design variety without temperature CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Before building, propose 4 distinct visual directions tailored to this brief (each as: bg hex / accent hex / typeface, plus a one-line rationale). Ask the user to pick one, then implement only that direction.
documents.s: 4. Design defaults settle into a "house style" — override it explicitly

documents.t: Sonnet 5 is the first Sonnet-tier model with real-time cybersecurity safeguards. When a request is declined, it returns as a successful HTTP 200 with stop_reason: "refusal" — not an error. If you have not built out a refusal-handling branch, your app will treat the empty response as a successful empty answer and quietly ship it to the user. The fix is one branch on the response: Handle refusals cleanly CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5", messages=[...]) if resp.stop_reason == "refusal": # Show a graceful message. Optionally retry on a fallback model # (Opus 4.8 is a common choice). You are NOT billed for a refusal # returned before any output was generated. return handle_refusal(resp) # Otherwise process resp.content as normal This is the same shape as Fable 5's in-band refusals — if you already handle those, you're covered. If you're new to it, see the Fable 5 field guide for the fuller pattern including the fallbacks parameter.

Priority Tier is not supported on Sonnet 5 (nor on Opus 5, Fable 5.1 or the Mythos models), and new Priority Tier commitments are no longer sold — only organizations with an existing commitment can use it (service tiers). If you have an enterprise workload that depends on Priority Tier commitments today, your options are: Keep the workload on Sonnet 4.6 (still supported, still on Priority Tier). Migrate the workload to Opus 4.8, which is on Priority Tier and is the model Sonnet 5 gets compared against for hard tasks anyway. Move to standard tier on Sonnet 5 and accept unreserved capacity. There's no beta header workaround. If Priority Tier is load-bearing for you, this is the migration blocker to plan around first.
documents.s: Priority Tier is not available — plan around it

documents.t: Choice Pick it when Sonnet 5 The balanced pick for new work when speed and cost matter (Anthropic recommends starting with Opus 5 for most workloads). Coding, agentic tasks, 1M context, and price sensitivity all point here. Sonnet 4.6 You need Priority Tier, you have prompts that depend on non-default sampling params you can't rewrite yet, or you're mid-eval and want a stable baseline. Opus 4.8 Reasoning depth or long-run stability that Sonnet 5 doesn't reach, or you need Priority Tier at the top end. Pair with an effort override — xhigh on Opus 4.8 is a common sweet spot. Fable 5 / Mythos 5 You've validated that Opus 4.8 isn't enough and you're willing to pay 5× Sonnet 5 output pricing for multiday autonomous runs. See the Fable 5 field guide.
documents.s: Sonnet 5 vs Sonnet 4.6 vs Opus 4.8 — the pick

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Recount your prompts under the new tokenizer⌄ Use the token counting API with model="claude-sonnet-5" for every prompt whose length matters. Anywhere you compare against a fixed 1M-token budget, assume ~30% more usage. Anywhere max_tokens is tight, raise it. ←PreviousNext→ 2Delete non-default sampling parameters⌄ Grep your codebase for temperature, top_p, top_k. Any non-default value now returns 400 on Sonnet 5. Delete or set to the default. ←PreviousNext→ 3Delete manual extended thinking, set effort instead⌄ Grep for thinking={"type": "enabled" and delete. Add an effort selector (start at high). If you don't want thinking at all, pass thinking: {type: "disabled"} explicitly. ←PreviousNext→ 4Add a stop_reason: "refusal" branch⌄ Cybersecurity safeguards are new on Sonnet-tier. Refusals are HTTP 200, not errors — if you don't branch, you silently ship empty answers. ←PreviousNext→ 5Verify your Priority Tier commitments⌄ If any workload depends on Priority Tier, keep it on Sonnet 4.6 or migrate to Opus 4.8 — Sonnet 5 does not offer Priority Tier. ←PreviousNext→ 6Re-model pricing on the standard rate⌄ The introductory $2 / $10 per MTok price is now standard — the planned 1 September 2026 increase was cancelled. With ~30% more tokens for the same text, the same text still costs roughly 13% less than on Sonnet 4.6. Recount your prompts rather than reusing Sonnet 4.6 token numbers. ←PreviousNext→
Check yourself 0/5

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत What you'll learn Understand the three architecture facts that make a 125B model interactive on a 12 GB card — and why none of them is 'aggressive quantization' Read Strata's own benchmark table honestly: the headline 94 tok/s is the *lowest* quant on the ladder, and the top quant costs 43% of it Price the quality bill precisely: 91.3% of SWE-bench Verified next to 98.7% of LiveCodeBench, and what that gap tells you about where pruning actually hurts Know the four gotchas the README headline does not carry — including a default that passes needle-in-haystack while quietly losing long-document accuracy Decide between Strata, plain llama.cpp with --n-cpu-moe, and a hosted API for your specific job On 24 September 2026 a repository called Strata appeared with a one-click installer and a claim that reads like a typo: run a 125-billion-parameter multimodal model on a gaming PC, at speeds you can hold a conversation with. Ten days later it has 10,622 stars, 935 forks and 265 open issues, and its Hacker News thread is at 473 points with 245 comments. One commenter's summary of the moment: "LLM threads the world over are spammed with Strata links." The claim is true. The interesting part is what it costs, because almost nobody is writing that part down — the project's own headline numbers contain no accuracy column at all. This page supplies it.
documents.s: Strata: a 125B MoE at 94 tok/s on a 12 GB Card — and the Exact Bill

documents.t: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next activates only about 6B of its 125B parameters per token, so Strata keeps the per-token path (attention, routers, shared expert, output head) in VRAM, pins all 24,576 experts in system RAM, and streams a 28.8 GB lookup table from SSD — buying interactive speed instead of the batch speeds that expert-streaming engines settle for. If you have met Colibrì, this is the opposite end of the same hierarchy. Colibrì puts the experts on disk to reach 744B-parameter models at 0.05–6.8 tok/s. Strata puts the experts in RAM to reach 44–94 tok/s on a model a fifth the size. Different tier, different use case: one is for overnight batch, this one is for a coding agent you actually wait on.
People assume the trick is brutal compression. Compression is involved, but three properties of the model do most of the work, and knowing them lets you predict behaviour on your own machine.
documents.s: Three architecture facts, none of them "quantization"

documents.t: Quantity Value Total transformer parameters 125B Activated per token ~6B MoE experts per layer 512 (10 routed + 1 shared active) Layers 48 Total experts in the model 48 × 512 = 24,576 Hidden size 2,560 Ten routed experts out of 512 means roughly 2% of the expert bank is touched for any given token. Expert weights are therefore large but cold — exactly the profile you want to push down the memory hierarchy. The per-token path that stays hot is small enough to sit on a 12 GB card.
documents.s: 1. The sparsity ratio is roughly 20 to 1

documents.t: This is the fact that explains the surprisingly modest 32 GB RAM floor, and it is almost always reported wrong. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is 176.9B parameters in total: a 125B transformer, a 51B n-gram embedding table, and a 4B multi-token-prediction module. The n-gram table is a fixed lookup structure used for prompt lookup — it is not matrix-multiplied, so it does not need to be resident. Strata reads it unbuffered from SSD. Take ISTA-DASLab's Coder release as the worked example: Component File size Resident in RAM? Stored at Transformer weights (256/512 experts kept) 29.6 GB Yes 1.89 bpw effective over the original 125B N-gram table 28.8 GB No — read from SSD fixed 4.5 bpw Total on disk 58.4 GB 29.6 GB resident vs 354 GB at BF16 So a 58 GB download has a 29.6 GB memory budget. That is the whole reason a 32 GB machine is on the compatibility list, and it is why putting this model on a mechanical drive is a configuration error rather than a slow choice — the table is on the hot path for every prompt.
documents.s: 2. The model is bigger than "125B" and smaller in RAM than its file size

documents.t: Flash-Next is a hybrid-attention model. Three of every four layers use Gated DeltaNet (GDN), a linear-attention mechanism that compresses history into a fixed-size recurrent state. The remaining layer uses Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) for precise retrieval across the full context. The split is 36 GDN layers to 12 QSA layers. The consequence is the one local-inference guides keep missing: on a conventional 48-layer transformer, context cost scales with all 48 layers. Here it scales with 12. That — not quantization — is why a 262,144-token native window (extensible to 1M) is affordable on consumer hardware, and why Strata can offer a --kv-resident flag that keeps the context cache in RAM with only attention's working set in VRAM.
documents.s: 3. Only 12 of the 48 layers grow a KV cache

documents.t: Tier What lives there VRAM Attention and DeltaNet mixers, routers, shared experts, output head, MTP draft layer, part of the KV cache above 64K — then an expert cache that fills whatever VRAM remains with the most-used experts RAM All 24,576 experts, pinned. The CPU computes non-cached experts in place with AVX-512/AVX2 kernels, concurrently with GPU work SSD The 28.8 GB n-gram table, read unbuffered (--ple-io direct; use --ple-io ram on a rotational disk) Two mechanisms make the expert cache work better than a static split. The shipped expert profile ranks all 24,576 experts by how often they fired on training data, so the cache starts warm. And from 0.1.31 there is router lookahead: while the CPU works on one layer, a background thread runs the next layer's router to predict which experts are about to be needed and prewarms the OS file-cache pages for them, overlapping I/O with compute. An adaptive tier system (--adapt-every) then reshapes the cache around your actual conversation.

These are the project's own measurements. Note what the quantization column does to them. RTX 5070 (12 GB), Ryzen 5 7600, 64 GB RAM Quantization Decode (tok/s) Prefill (tok/s) Q2_0 94 2,650 IQ2_XS 79 2,090 IQ3_XXS 62 1,750 IQ3_S 53 1,620 Coder (pruned) 55 2,180 RX 9070 XT (16 GB), Ryzen 9 3900X, 47 GB RAM Quantization Decode (tok/s) Prefill (tok/s) Q2_0 60 1,160 IQ2_XS 52 1,110 Coder (pruned) 44 1,420 The headline "94 tok/s" is Q2_0 — the bottom rung. IQ3_S, which the project labels highest quality, runs at 53 tok/s: you surrender 43% of the advertised speed to climb the ladder. Community reports fill in the rest of the spread, and they are wide: 124 tok/s on a 4090 with 128 GB of DDR5 and a 7950X3D; about 30 tok/s on a 3080 (10 GB) with a 3600X; 33 tok/s on an RTX 2060 at Q2_0 but 21 at IQ3_XXS; around 25 tok/s on an M1 Max at 3-bit; and 7 tok/s decode with 60 tok/s prefill on a GPU-less 8845HS laptop with 96 GB. Read that list as a rule rather than a leaderboard: decode speed tracks RAM bandwidth and quantization level, not GPU class. The 2060 beating the 3080 at Q2_0 is not a measurement error. The card holds the hot path; the system memory streams the experts.
Here is what the headline numbers leave out. There are two separate compressions in play, and they fail in different ways.

Gumbel-Softmax Quantization is post-training scalar quantization that learns grid assignments and group scales jointly, which narrows the usual gap to vector quantization at low bit-widths while keeping files loadable as standard GGUF. Retained experts land at 3.5 bits per weight.

Riemannian Constraint Optimization chooses which experts to delete. It treats the feasible set as a smooth manifold so per-layer budgets are enforced exactly, with no penalty coefficient to tune, and supports a different budget per layer simultaneously. The Coder release keeps 256 of each layer's 512 experts — still 10 active per token — calibrated on code, agentic and vision data.

Benchmark BF16 base GSQ-RCO Coder Retention SWE-bench Verified 82.80 75.60 91.3% LiveCodeBench v6 87.43 86.28 98.7% Do not read those as "roughly the same." The gap between them is the single most useful number on this page. LiveCodeBench is short-horizon: read a problem, emit a solution. It barely notices that half the expert bank is gone — 1.3% off. SWE-bench Verified runs long agentic trajectories against real repositories, and there the same model drops 7.2 points. Same weights, same quantization, six times the relative damage. Expert pruning costs you horizon, not knowledge. The model still knows how to write the function. What degrades is holding a plan across forty tool calls — exactly the capability an agentic coding loop is made of. One commenter's word for it was "lobotomizes," and the benchmark pair is the receipt. The authors are explicit about the matching scope limit: calibration covered code, agentic and vision data, and "degradation outside this set is an accepted cost." If you point the Coder variant at prose, translation, or non-code reasoning, you are off-distribution by design, with no published number for how far.

Watch out The speed mode called ESP is documented by the project as removing refusal directions. That is a safety-behaviour change shipped inside a performance feature — treat it as a different model, not a faster one. 1. ESP trades alignment and output distribution for speed. The project's own documentation records that its speed-projection path degrades safety by removing refusal directions, raises perplexity on code by 15%, and drops top-1 token agreement with the stock model to about 93%. A 7% disagreement rate on next-token choice compounds hard across a long generation. If you enable it, you are no longer running the model you benchmarked. 2. 4-bit KV passes needle tests while losing long-document accuracy. The shipped default is 8-bit KV. --kv q4_0 applies a Hadamard rotation before quantizing, halves cache memory and is about 4% faster at 128K — at the cost of 8–12% higher perplexity on long documents. The documentation notes needle tests still pass. That is the trap: needle-in-haystack retrieval surviving is not evidence that long-context reasoning survived. The installer offers you 4-bit above 4K context, so this is a decision you will be asked to make before you have any reason to understand it. There is also a --kv k8v4 hybrid — 8-bit keys, rotated 4-bit values — for 23% less KV memory with measurably slower prompts. 3. Identical weights, different engine, different answers. One HN commenter ran a 50-image coordinate-localization benchmark through both engines using the same GGUF and the same vision adapter: Strata produced a median error of 154.8 pixels (mean 168.8); llama.cpp produced 46.5 (mean 81.4). Their assessment was that the gap "is as large as the jump from a 9B model to a 35B model." The project's documentation supplies a plausible mechanism in the same family of problems — its IQ-pack multi-token kernels round differently from the single-token CPU paths, with an opt-in reproducibility flag (STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1) added in 0.1.30. The lesson generalises past this project: when a new engine claims a large speedup on weights you already have, run your own eval on your own task before you trust the output, because "same file" does not mean "same answers." 4. Past 262K you are in untested territory. Beyond the native window, yarn RoPE scaling applies, and the documentation describes it as experimental with quality measured on a single machine. Community reports of tool-calling failures and spelling errors at 150K+ are consistent with that caveat.
documents.s: Four gotchas the headline does not carry

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Check the floor before you download 58 GB⌄ Minimum is 12 GB VRAM on an NVIDIA RTX 20/30/40/50 series or a supported AMD Radeon (RX 7700 XT and up, RX 9060 XT, RX 9070/9070 XT, Radeon AI PRO R9700, RX 6800/6900), 32 GB system RAM, and about 80 GB of free space. Make the storage an SSD: the 28.8 GB n-gram table is read on every prompt, so a rotational disk is not a slow configuration but a broken one. ←PreviousNext→ 2Run the installer and let it pick the variant⌄ Windows: START-HERE.bat. Linux: ./setup.sh. It detects your hardware and recommends a model size from your available RAM. Expect roughly an hour end to end on a first run — most of it download — and about 15 minutes for model load on subsequent starts. ←PreviousNext→ 3Decline 4-bit KV on the first run⌄ Above 4K context the installer offers 4-bit KV. Say no the first time. Establish what the model does for you on the 8-bit default, then decide whether 8-12% higher perplexity on long documents is a trade you want for ~4% speed. You cannot evaluate a degradation you never measured a baseline for. ←PreviousNext→ 4Point your existing tooling at localhost⌄ The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible surface at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1, the OpenAI Responses API at /v1/responses, and an Anthropic-shaped endpoint at /v1/messages. Anything already written against those shapes — including Claude Code via its base-URL override — connects without code changes. ←PreviousNext→ 5Run your own eval before you trust it⌄ Twenty to fifty tasks from your actual work, scored the same way twice: once through Strata, once through stock llama.cpp with the ggml-org GGUF. The vision regression above was found exactly this way by one person in an afternoon. This step is not optional diligence on a ten-day-old project with 265 open issues. ←PreviousNext→ Expose the server on your LAN with an API key CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ START-HERE.bat --setup --host 0.0.0.0 --api-key <your-secret> The flags worth knowing, and what each one trades CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ --ple-io direct # unbuffered n-gram table reads (use 'ram' on a rotational disk) --kv-resident 32768 # keep the context cache in RAM, only attention's working set in VRAM --prefill auto # chunk prompts up to 8,192 tokens for GPU streaming --pcie-frac N # share of missing experts fetched over PCIe vs computed on CPU --pool-workers N # CPU threads computing non-cached experts --adapt-every N # how often the expert cache re-ranks around your conversation --kv q4_0 # halve KV memory: ~4% faster at 128K, 8-12% worse perplexity on long docs --kv k8v4 # 8-bit keys, rotated 4-bit values: 23% less KV memory, slower prompts --spec-min-p # draft-acceptance confidence threshold for speculative decoding What you'll learn Settings are split between CLI arguments, the per-model strata-<model>.json args block, and STRATA_* environment variables, and the documentation does not consistently say which lives where. Useful env vars include STRATA_PF_FUSED (fused prompt kernels), STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1 (profile decode windows), STRATA_RESIDENT_PIN=0 (disable page-locking in low-RAM resident mode) and STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1 (single-token-path rounding for reproducibility).

Your job Pick Why Agentic coding, long tool-call trajectories Full model at IQ3_S or Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (~80 GB RAM) SWE-bench is where pruning costs 7.2 points. Do not pay that on your main workload One-shot code generation, snippets, review Coder (pruned, 32 GB RAM) 98.7% of LiveCodeBench for half the expert bank. This is the rung the pruning was designed for Vision and coordinate work Stock llama.cpp with ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF The one head-to-head measurement on identical weights favours llama.cpp by 3x on localization error Maximum tok/s for throwaway drafting Q2_0 94 tok/s, and roughly 80% of the model's "memories" at 2 bits by one commenter's information-theoretic estimate. Fine for drafts, not for facts Long documents, 128K+ context Full model, 8-bit KV, stay inside 262K 4-bit KV and yarn scaling are both documented as lossy or experimental Reliability over speed Stock llama.cpp with --n-cpu-moe Slower on the same hardware, but it is the reference implementation your eval should be measured against Anything where being wrong is expensive A hosted API The HN consensus from people who own this hardware: they still default to cloud for demanding work
documents.s: Which rung do you actually want

documents.t: Strata is not a from-scratch engine. It is built on llama.cpp / ggml (MIT), transcribes i-quant GPU kernels from upstream, uses llama.cpp's quantized MMQ dot-product kernels, and takes its vision encoder from llama.cpp's mtmd library. The packaging and the Flash-Next-specific scheduling are the contribution. That matters practically: the baseline is one flag away. --n-cpu-moe N moves the MoE feed-forward weights of the first N layers to CPU. The reasoning is the same sparsity argument this page opened with: expert stacks are large and rarely touched, so they buy the most VRAM for the least speed penalty, while attention, embeddings and the KV cache are small and touched every token and belong on the GPU. More VRAM means a lower N and a higher ceiling before the CPU side becomes the bottleneck. If the model already fits in VRAM, raising N degrades throughput steadily — the flag is a way to fit, not a way to go faster. Reported community numbers put llama.cpp around 21 tok/s where Strata reaches 100+ on comparable hardware. That is a real and large gap. It is also the gap you are buying with a ten-day-old codebase, 265 open issues, documented kernel-rounding divergence, and no accuracy column. Decide deliberately rather than by headline. What you'll learn The GGUF ecosystem for this model is unusually crowded: ISTA-DASLab's GSQ-RCO releases (1.89M and 351k downloads), unsloth (1.4M), the official ggml-org build, bartowski, and several abliterated and 'uncensored' community variants. Download count is popularity, not quality. The two with published benchmark tables are ISTA-DASLab's; the reference build for comparison is ggml-org's.

Strip out the specific project and three durable lessons remain, and they will apply to the next engine that trends too: Sparsity, not compression, is what makes big models local. A 125B MoE with 6B active can be more comfortable on consumer hardware than a 32B dense model, because the constraint it puts you under is RAM capacity and bandwidth rather than VRAM capacity. Check the active-parameter count before the total. Compression has a shape, not a magnitude. "91% retained" and "99% retained" came from the same artifact on the same day. Which number you get depends entirely on whether your task is short-horizon or long-horizon. Ask which benchmark the retention figure was measured on. An engine is part of the model. Identical weights produced a 3x difference in localization error between two engines. Kernels round, caches quantize, speed modes project. Your eval has to cover the engine, not just the checkpoint. Check yourself 0/6 आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-10-04। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। स्रोत: Niko1221/Strata README and docs/DETAILS.md; GitHub API (10,622 stars, 935 forks, 265 open issues, MIT, created 2026-09-24); ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF model card; Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model card; Hacker News thread 49953495 (473 points, 245 comments). Benchmark tables are the respective projects' own measurements. This repository is ten days old and moving daily — flags, defaults and variant names will drift; re-read DETAILS.md before relying on any flag here.

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम Coding-agent leaderboards mostly measure pull-request diffs against a test suite — SWE-Bench and its cousins. That's useful, but it's not what a Supabase user actually does: build a schema, fix a broken RLS policy, debug a failed Edge Function, wire up auth. On August 1, 2026, Supabase open-sourced a benchmark that grades coding agents on those real tasks, running them against actual containerized Supabase stacks with real MCP servers and real CLIs. It's Apache-2.0, runs locally on a laptop, and its early scores already say something surprising about how different agents use documentation. This page is the practical field guide to it. What you'll learn Understand what makes Supabase Evals different from SWE-Bench-style benchmarks Read the cross-agent findings honestly — where Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Kimi K3 and the GPT-5 line actually diverge See the effect of loading skills on the same model (before vs after) Run the benchmark yourself against your own agent and model in under an hour आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-08-03। The score table, eval count and skill effects on this page reflect the leaderboard and README as of the August 1, 2026 release. Live scores at supabase.com/evals update as new models and experiments land; the shape of the benchmark (real stacks, deterministic + LLM-judge scoring, one retry) is durable, the specific percentages are not. इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

Supabase Evals is a benchmark, an evaluation harness and a public leaderboard rolled into one Apache-2.0 repo at github.com/supabase/evals. It exists because SWE-Bench-style tests answer the wrong question for backend work — they measure "can this agent close a filed GitHub issue against a Python test suite" — while most real Supabase work is closer to ops on a running system: your RLS policy started rejecting valid requests, your Edge Function is 500ing in prod, your migration didn't take. Three things separate it from what came before: Real stacks, not mocks. Every scenario boots a fresh Docker sandbox that mounts the host Docker socket, so supabase start spins up the local stack as sibling containers. The agent talks to a Management-API-compatible surface (@supabase/lite) and real MCP servers and the real Supabase CLI. Nothing is stubbed. Deterministic checks first, LLM-as-judge only where needed. A scorer can query the resulting database, hit the deployed Edge Function, or run repo-root vitest on the produced files. The LLM judge is a backstop for freeform answers ("did the agent's explanation match the actual root cause?"), not the primary grade. One retry, then it's final. No cherry-picked best-of-N. This alone makes the numbers less flattering than most agent PR benchmarks.

The August 2026 release ships 38 eval scenarios under evals/<id>/. They're organized on three axes so results can be sliced meaningfully: Nine products — database, auth, storage, edge functions, realtime, cron, queues, vectors, data-api Nine topics — RLS, security, migrations, SQL, SDK, observability, self-hosting, tests, declarative-schema Four stages — build (make something new), deploy (ship it), investigate (figure out what's wrong), resolve (fix it) Each eval is a directory with a PROMPT.md (the task the agent sees, plus frontmatter metadata), an EVAL.ts scorer, and optional remote/ (seeded hosted-project state — SQL, logs, already-deployed functions) and local/ (starting files copied into the agent's sandbox workspace). The scenarios come from real support tickets and GitHub issues, not synthetic prompts.

Every eval runs in one of two modes, decided automatically by its shape: Tools mode. No sandbox. The agent gets an MCP/tool surface (Management API, SQL, storage, etc.) and its answer is scored by inspecting resulting project state. Used for evals that live entirely inside the platform (no local/ directory, no interface: cli). Local-stack mode. A fresh Docker sandbox with the real Supabase CLI installed. The agent gets a bash tool plus file tools, and can run supabase init/start/db/test against a real local stack that spawns as sibling containers. After the agent stops, the harness docker cps the workspace out and runs vite/vitest from the host to score it. Used when a local/ workspace exists or interface: cli is declared. The clever bit: the host's toolchain scores what the sandbox produced. Scorers don't need to live inside the sandbox image.

The initial leaderboard runs pit first-party agents (Claude Code, Codex, Claude API executor experiments) against model-agnostic OpenCode across the Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, Kimi K3 and GPT-5.4/5.6 lineups. Numbers below are for the build stage, which is where the initial post reports the sharpest results. Agent + model Build (no skills) Build (with skills) Claude Code + Opus 5 100% 100% OpenCode + Kimi K3 100% 100% Claude Code + Sonnet 5 78% 100% Codex + GPT-5.6 (Sol) 89% 100% Codex + GPT-5.4 mini 78% 89% Two things stand out: Opus 5 and Kimi K3 max out build with no help. Kimi K3 running through OpenCode matching Opus 5 running through Claude Code is a real signal about open-weight models catching up on backend-shaped work — not a general SOTA claim, but a specific, reproducible one. Skills are a large multiplier on smaller/mid models. Loading the Supabase skill takes Sonnet 5 from 78% to 100% on build, and takes the Postgres-best-practices skill's hit rate from ~10% to 60% across the wider suite. If you're running Sonnet 5 (or any mid model), not loading the relevant skill is leaving 20+ points on the floor.

The single most interesting number in the release isn't a score, it's a behavior: Codex / GPT-5.6 reads roughly 8 docs pages per scenario. Claude Code reads about 2 — and consults docs in under 40% of scenarios even with skills loaded. The two agents were staring at the same tasks, the same MCP tools and the same skills. Codex reflexively pulls documentation before acting; Claude Code more often tries from memory and only reads docs when it hits a wall. Neither is "right" — Opus 5 through Claude Code still scored 100% on build. But it's a very different mode of operation, and it explains a lot of anecdotal reports about the two agents feeling different. ★ Insight ───────────────────────────────────── Benchmark reports usually collapse an agent to one number. Supabase Evals is unusually valuable because it instruments the agent's behavior — how often it reads docs, which skills it loaded, how many tools it called — and that behavior is often the story, not the score. The gap here isn't a model gap, it's a harness policy gap. The same base model in a different harness would likely behave differently. See Coding Agent CLIs Compared for why the harness matters at least as much as the model. Deterministic scorers plus one retry (no best-of-N) is what makes the numbers here comparable across agents. Most public agent leaderboards silently allow retries or self-consistency, which flatters slower/weaker models. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
documents.s: The finding nobody expected: models use docs very differently

documents.t: Regardless of model, every tested agent tripped on the same three patterns: Hand-writing migrations instead of using declarative schemas. The declarative-schema workflow is newer; the training data is heavy with old-style create table migrations, so agents default to those even when the project is set up for declarative. Verifying auth manually instead of using @supabase/server. Agents wire up cookie-parsing and session-checking by hand rather than using the newer server-side helpers that exist for exactly this. Inconsistent docs consultation. As above — the same agent will look up docs in one scenario and try from memory in the next, with no obvious rule for which. These are the sort of failures that don't show up in pass@1 on a synthetic benchmark, because there's no "wrong but working" answer to grade — the code compiles, it just uses the outdated pattern. Real-container evals catch them because a scorer can inspect the produced project and check "did they use declarative schema, yes/no."
documents.s: Three consistent stumbles across every agent

documents.t: You need Docker, pnpm, and an API key for whichever provider you want to grade. Ports 54321–54329 must be free (stop any local supabase start stacks first). The whole thing runs on a laptop; a small run finishes in minutes. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Clone with submodules⌄ The skills live in a submodule — a plain clone will leave you missing the Supabase agent skills. Use --recurse-submodules the first time. ←PreviousNext→ 2Install and configure⌄ `pnpm install`, then copy `.env.example` to `.env` and paste the provider key you need (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, etc.). ←PreviousNext→ 3Run one eval against one experiment⌄ Start narrow. Pick a single scenario and a single agent/model config, so you can watch the agent's turns and confirm your setup works before spending time or tokens on a full sweep. ←PreviousNext→ 4Compare experiments head-to-head⌄ Once one run works, extend the `--experiment` flag to compare, e.g., Sonnet 5 with vs. without skills, or Claude Code vs. Codex on the same scenario. ←PreviousNext→ 5Export results and inspect them⌄ `pnpm export-results` writes `eval-results.json`; `pnpm web` opens a local viewer with per-turn traces so you can *read what the agent actually did* — this is where the real learning is. ←PreviousNext→ Clone the repo with submodules CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/supabase/evals.git cd evals pnpm install cp .env.example .env Run a single eval against a single experiment CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pnpm eval -- \ --eval resolve-dataapi-001-empty-results \ --experiment claude-code-sonnet-5 Head-to-head: same model, skills on vs off CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pnpm eval -- \ --experiment claude-code-sonnet-5 \ --experiment claude-code-sonnet-5-no-skills \ --suite benchmark Full benchmark sweep across all shipped experiments CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pnpm eval -- \ --suite benchmark \ --experiment-suite benchmark,no-skills pnpm export-results pnpm web

An experiment file under experiments/<name>.ts is where you wire up an agent, a runtime and a model into one comparable configuration. That separation is deliberate: it means "Claude Code with Sonnet 5 and no skills" is a different experiment from "Claude Code with Sonnet 5 and skills loaded", and both are different from "OpenCode with Kimi K3". You can hold two of the three axes constant and vary the third. The -no-skills variants shipped in the repo (e.g. claude-code-sonnet-5-no-skills.ts vs. claude-code-sonnet-5.ts) are what makes the "skills lifted us from 78% to 100%" claim measurable rather than a vibe. If you're running a custom agent — a homegrown loop, an internal fork, an experimental harness — the pattern is: write an experiment file that declares your agent, opt into localStack: localStackRuntime() if you want the sandbox evals too, and run it against the benchmark suite. Your numbers land in the same table as everyone else's.
documents.s: Anatomy of an experiment (so you can add your own)

documents.t: Both runtimes use progressive disclosure for skills: only each skill's name and description sits in the system prompt at all times; the agent pulls the full instructions on demand. That's why "skills on" costs only a few extra tokens per turn but can lift a score by 20+ points — the agent only pays for a skill's body when it decides the skill is relevant. The two runtimes differ only in how the body is fetched: Local-stack (sandbox) mode. Skills are installed into the sandbox with Vercel's skills CLI (baked into the sandbox image, sourced from the local skills/ directory — never the network) under .claude/skills/. When a task matches, the agent reads .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md and any files it references with its file tools. Tools mode. No filesystem, so a load_skill tool returns a skill's full instructions when the agent calls it by name. For context on the emerging cross-agent skills standard this uses, see SKILL.md as an Open Standard.

Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for Coding — the model half. ★ Insight ───────────────────────────────────── Benchmarks like this are most useful directionally, not absolutely. "Sonnet 5 gained 22 points with the Supabase skill loaded" transfers to your own project; "Sonnet 5 scores 100% on build" doesn't necessarily. The right question after reading a leaderboard isn't "which agent won", it's "what does this benchmark test that resembles my work" — and then only the sub-scores on those slices matter. ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
