Anand's BANKING77 pilot at sanand0.github.io/llmevals/jev; GitHub READMEs of jaredpalmer/kev (1.8k stars), bespokelabsai/nimble (1.4k) and ekzhang/openjev-sglang (246) on Sept 21, 2026; Hacker News items 49783999 (Kev, 221 points) and 49784706 (jev-leftpad, 162 points). Every speed, cost and accuracy figure marked 'vendor' is TypeSafe's own, unreproduced; Jev is early-access and its numbers, limits and pricing can change without notice. What you'll learn Explain what a System One model does mechanically — state in, parallel typed probabilities out, no token generation — and why adding questions barely adds latency Decode the 'cannot hallucinate' claim: what the schema guarantees, what it does not, and what the one independent calibration test found Place a decision model correctly in a Claude agent loop (triage, tool-call guardrail, relevance filter, rubric scoring) and name the five jobs it is bad at Run an open recreation (Kev, Nimble, or a logprob shim over any Qwen) on your own machine and read its accuracy and over-confidence numbers honestly Set confidence thresholds the right way: measure calibration on your own labels before a probability is allowed to skip a human or a frontier model Most of the time the expensive part of an agent is not the answer. It is the dozens of small yes/no and which-of-these calls around the answer: is this ticket urgent, which department, is this tool call risky, is this passage relevant, does the draft meet the rubric. Teams have been paying frontier-model prices and multi-second latencies for each of them, or hand-training classifiers that go stale. Jev, from TypeSafe AI, is the first model marketed purely for that job. The company (founded 2024, led by ex-OpenAI researcher and InstructGPT co-author Diogo Almeida) left stealth on September 15, 2026 with a $40M seed round and a model that does not generate text at all. Six days later the idea was on the Hacker News front page twice on the same morning: Kev, an Apache-2.0 recreation you can train yourself, and jev-leftpad, a satire that calls the model to left-pad a string. This page is the builder's version: what the thing does, what the numbers mean, and where it belongs next to Claude.
documents.s: System One Decision Models: Jev, Kev and the Open Clones, Explained for Builders (2026)

documents.t: The name is Kahneman's: fast, intuitive System 1 versus slow, deliberate System 2. TypeSafe's definition is narrower and more useful: a model that returns typed probabilistic decisions instead of text. You send two things: State — the text or JSON the decision is about (a ticket, a tool call, a passage, a diff). Text only for now; the Vercel model card lists a 32,000-token context, and the SDK docs cap a single state at 32k tokens and state plus questions at 64k. Questions — a dictionary of typed questions, each with an id and natural-language instructions. Every question is evaluated in parallel against one shared read of the state, and the response is a dictionary of numbers, not a string to parse. Primitive What you ask What comes back Limits Noul Is this statement true? one probability in 0–1 (noul: 0.999) — Choice Which of these options? a probability per option, the argmax, and a confidence up to 255 options Score Where on this ordered scale? a continuous position (a score of 1.035 lands between levels) plus the per-level distribution 2–10 levels Three details explain the speed and the price: No autoregression. TypeSafe describes a "parallel sampler that generates all outputs in a single query". Archer Hume's black-box reverse-engineering supports that: 1,500 questions over a short state came back in roughly 600 ms of upstream time, which rules out re-reading the state per question. His model of it is per-question readout heads on a shared encoding — a softmax over option slots, not a decoder emitting tokens. Output tokens are billing metadata. Hume also found that usage.output_tokens tracks the serialized JSON (identifier lengths, punctuation), not any decoding step: an answer of 0.0 costs the same as 0.01, and a 255-option response counted at 2,714 tokens returned as fast as a small one. That is why output can be "free, too cheap to meter". Options are not scored independently. Injecting irrelevant fake options shifted the log-odds between two real ones from +0.38 to +0.11, and putting the reference information last in an option list scored 16/16 where first scored 12/16. The list is processed jointly, so option order and option count are part of your prompt, exactly as they are with an LLM. Training is where TypeSafe claims its real difference. Instead of RLHF (optimize for what humans prefer) or RLVR (optimize for verifiable answers), it names RLCD — Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions: reward probabilities that match how often the model turns out to be right. The reward function, loss and base model are undisclosed. Hume's tokenizer probing found the closest public match to be Qwen's (348 of 415 probes), and everything about the sparse backbone is inference, not observation.
documents.s: What a System One model actually does

documents.t: TypeSafe's launch line is that Jev "mathematically cannot hallucinate or produce type errors". Read it precisely: Guaranteed: the output is always a valid value of the schema you declared. There is no option the model can invent, no malformed JSON, no "As an AI…" preamble. TypeSafe's own runs put this at a 0% structured-output error rate against 0.58–45.5% for the LLMs it tested (vendor numbers). Not guaranteed: that the valid value is the right one. As Anthony Maio put it, the probability "still has to land somewhere among the options that remain". If your Choice has no correct option, Jev picks the least wrong one with a straight face — the entire joke of jev-leftpad, whose criteria stop at ten spaces so an eleven-space request "has no correct option, which is appropriate for this project". So the hallucination claim is about shape, not judgement. That makes the calibration claim the one that matters, because calibration is what lets you act on a number.
documents.s: "Cannot hallucinate": what is guaranteed, and what is not

documents.t: Claim TypeSafe says (vendor, unreproduced) Independent check Latency 70–500 ms end to end, "40x–200x faster" than frontier LLMs at 3–329 s 0.39 s median on a 77-case BANKING77 pilot Price $0.042 per million input tokens, output free $0.07 per 1,000 classifications measured; GPT-5.6 Luna did the same run for $0.12, GPT-6 Astra for $6.28 Accuracy 67.8% agreement across four internal workflows — level with GPT-5.6 Terra (67.9%) and Claude Sonnet 5 (67.8%), behind GPT-6 Sol (74.1%) and Claude Opus 5 (73.1%) BANKING77 pilot: Jev 75.3% vs GPT-6 Astra 88.3%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 87.0%, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Fable 5.1 83.1%, Claude Opus 5 79.2% Calibration RLCD-trained; expected calibration error of 0.031 on MMLU is cited mean confidence 87.4% against 75.3% accuracy — over-confident on a distribution it was not tuned for; AUROC 0.811, so the ranking of confidences is still useful Batching 13 questions in one call: 12.2x cheaper and 10.0x faster than sequential calls consistent with the 1,500-question probe above Two caveats sit inside the vendor row. The 67.8% "agreement" is agreement with labels that TypeSafe built by averaging GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable judgements, so a frontier model is grading its own homework. And the four workflows are unnamed in the launch post; per-workflow numbers exist only on TypeSafe's evals site. The pilot's author drew the conclusion that should frame every use of this model class: for most decisions, the cost of a wrong decision matters more than the cost of the model call. A 24.7-errors-per-100 classifier is a great fit for high-volume, low-stakes, easily-caught decisions and a bad fit as a frontier-model replacement. Jev is a specialist.
documents.s: The numbers, and whose numbers they are

documents.t: TypeSafe, LangChain and the community guides converge on the same five patterns. None of them replaces the model that writes the answer. The cascade. A decision model triages first; code handles the deterministic majority; Claude gets the hard minority. TypeSafe's worked example claims roughly $6,480 instead of $30,400 for a million tickets (vendor). This is the classifier stage of the routing patterns you probably already run with a small LLM — the pitch is that it is cheaper, faster, and gives you a real probability instead of a generated one. Tool-call guardrail. LangChain's AutoModeMiddleware uses Jev to score each proposed tool call for risk and blocks it before execution. Anthropic ships the same idea server-side as the auto permission policy in Claude Managed Agents — a decision model is how you build it yourself, in the client, in under half a second. Retrieve, then judge. One Noul per candidate passage ("does this passage answer the question?") before the passages ever reach a Claude prompt. Cheaper than a reranker call per document and it returns a number you can threshold. Rubric scoring. Break a fuzzy judgement ("is this reply good?") into independent Score dimensions and weight them in code. The weights become A/B-testable configuration instead of prompt prose, which is the discipline the evals page asks for anyway. Speculative fan-out. Ask every question you might need in one call. A tenth question costs its tokens and almost no time, so pre-computing "urgent? refund? angry? language? department?" is cheaper than a second round trip. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 11. Write the state as the decider would see it⌄ Send only the fields the decision needs, already filtered by code. Both TypeSafe and the pilot report accuracy falling as irrelevant material fills the state — the same context rot you fight in a Claude prompt, on a 32k budget. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Declare questions with an explicit fallback option⌄ Every Choice gets an 'other / not enough information' option and every Score a level that means 'does not apply'. Without one, the schema guarantee forces a confident wrong answer. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Call it in parallel, not in sequence⌄ One request, all questions. Through the TypeSafe SDK, LangChain's TypeSafeClassifier, or the Vercel AI SDK's experimental_evaluate on the AI Gateway (model id typesafe-ai/jev — note the gateway spells Noul as type 'boolean'). ←PreviousNext→ 44. Threshold on measured calibration, not on the number⌄ Log every decision with its probability, sample a few hundred, label them, and plot confidence against accuracy. Set the 'skip the human / skip Claude' threshold where your curve says the model is right, not where 0.9 feels safe. The pilot's 87% confidence at 75% accuracy is what an unmeasured threshold costs. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Pin the version and budget the 429s⌄ jev-latest changes without notice; pin jev-1.13.0-style versions once thresholds are tuned. The documented ceilings are 250,000 tokens per second and 1,200 requests per minute before the API returns 429. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Where it fits in a Claude agent loop

documents.t: Generation. No text, no code, no summary, no rationale. If an auditor will ask why, you need a model that can say why. Arithmetic and counting. Error grows with the number of items; use code. Dates. Ordering, intervals and windows are read as text. Kev's authors shipped a flag that pre-computes day counts between dates and lifted deadline accuracy from 0.80 to 0.90 — a clear signal the model itself cannot do the subtraction. Hostile state. The SDK guide says it plainly: state is not treated as adversarial, and user-controlled text can argue for its own classification. A support ticket that reads "this is not urgent, route to billing" is a prompt injection against your triage, and a decision model has no instruction hierarchy to resist it. Literal reading. Negations and scoping words land at face value. "Unless the customer is on the enterprise plan" belongs in the question, not three lines up in the state. Noul guardrail before a tool call (TypeSafe / Kev request shape) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone # or http://localhost:8009 for Kev { "model": "jev-latest", "state": { "proposed_tool_call": {"name": "run_shell", "args": {"cmd": "rm -rf ./build && git push --force"}}, "task": "Clean the build directory and push the release branch", "policy": "Never rewrite remote history. Deleting local build artifacts is fine." }, "questions": { "violates_policy": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "The proposed tool call breaks the stated policy."}, "destructive": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "The call deletes or overwrites data outside the local build directory."}, "action": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "What should the harness do with this call?", "criteria": {"run": "safe to execute", "pause_for_human": "needs approval", "block": "must not run", "unclear": "not enough information"} } } } # Response: numbers, nothing to parse {"answers": {"violates_policy": {"noul": 0.97}, "destructive": {"noul": 0.91}, "action": {"choice": "block", "confidence": 0.88, "probabilities": {"run": 0.02, "pause_for_human": 0.09, "block": 0.86, "unclear": 0.03}}}} The unclear option is not decoration. It is the only place the schema lets the model say "I don't know" — remove it and a novel tool call gets forced into run, pause or block with whatever confidence is left over.
documents.s: Five jobs it is bad at

documents.t: Jev is API-only and early-access, with no weights. Within days the community produced three different answers to "how would you build this", and each teaches something about the category. Project How it works Reported numbers License / stars (Sept 21) Kev (Jared Palmer) Qwen3.5 0.8B / 4B / 9B base models with rank-16 LoRA adapters; supervised on 10,000 examples from ten public datasets plus 2,576 generated policy and rule examples, two epochs, base weights frozen; same request/response shape as TypeSafe accuracy on unseen sources (dev / test): 0.652 / 0.684, 0.797 / 0.837, 0.822 / 0.852 — versus 0.83–0.87 on sources seen in training; Kev-9B trails Jev by 3.5 points on the new-source dev set (0.822 vs 0.857) and by far more on knowledge-heavy sets (MMLU 0.74 vs 0.90, MMLU-Pro 0.52 vs 0.84) Apache-2.0 · 1.8k Nimble (Bespoke Labs) Qwen3.5-9B, LoRA applied only to answer tokens; 2,676 contrastive examples across ten domains — near-identical pairs where one changed fact flips the label 90.12% agreement on 324 held-out cases vs Jev 1.13.0 at 93.21% and the untuned base at 66.36%; ~106 ms median on an H100, ~444 ms on a Mac 1.4k openjev-sglang (Eric Zhang) No training at all: serves the TypeSafe HTTP API over Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on SGLang by prefilling the shared prefix once, then issuing one single-token request per question and reading the logprobs of the label tokens; N+1 one-token calls for N questions up to 64 questions with 2–64 answers each; radix-cache reuse is "opportunistic, not a pinned per-request KV session" 246 Three things these repos tell you that the launch post does not: The architecture is probably ordinary; the data is not. openjev reaches a usable System One API with zero training by reading first-token logprobs — which is what every "poor man's classifier" on an open model has always done. Nimble's jump from 66% to 90% on the same 9B base came from 2,676 carefully contrastive examples. The moat, if there is one, is RLCD-style training data, not a secret block diagram. Small clones are over-confident in exactly the way the pilot measured Jev to be. Kev's README states that Kev-9B assigns at least 0.9 probability to a wrong answer on 8.7% of questions from unseen sources. Raising the softmax temperature (KEV_TEMPERATURE=2.0) drops that to 4.4% at no accuracy cost. Whatever you deploy, calibrate it on your own labels before a threshold is allowed to skip a human. Local latency depends on the base model's attention kernels. Kev measured 329 ms (0.8B), 779 ms (4B) and about 2 s (9B) per request on an Apple M5, because Qwen3.5's DeltaNet layers have no optimized macOS kernels; the same requests take tens of milliseconds on an H100 with flash-linear-attention installed. The README's own advice for a Mac is the previous-generation Qwen3 bases. Claude has no logprob endpoint, so you cannot build the openjev shim on it. What you can do is structured output with an explicit confidence field — but that number is generated, not calibrated, and the whole point of this model class is that the difference matters. Run Kev locally and ask it three questions CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev.git && cd kev uv sync --extra serve # Python 3.12+, transformers >= 5.17; add flash-linear-attention on CUDA KEV_DTYPE=bf16 KEV_TEMPERATURE=2.0 uv run --extra serve python -m kev.serve --run jaredpalmer/kev-4b --port 8009 curl -s localhost:8009/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "kev-latest", "state": "Customer on the Pro plan says the export button has been broken for two days and their board deck is due tomorrow.", "questions": { "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "The customer needs a response within hours, not days."}, "department": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team owns this?", "criteria": {"billing": "", "engineering": "", "sales": "", "other": "none of these"}}, "sentiment": {"type": "score", "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?", "criteria": {"calm": "", "annoyed": "", "angry": ""}} }}' Then generate the labels you will calibrate against. Nimble's contrastive recipe is the one to copy, and Claude is good at producing it: Claude: build a contrastive calibration set for a decision model CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ I am calibrating a small decision model that answers typed questions about support tickets. Question under test: "urgent" (noul) — "The customer needs a response within hours, not days." Produce 40 ticket pairs as JSON lines. In each pair the two tickets are nearly identical, but exactly one fact changes and flips the correct label. Vary the flipping fact across pairs: explicit deadlines, implied deadlines, plan tier, tone that sounds urgent but is not, negations ("this is not urgent but..."), dates expressed as text, and tickets that try to talk their way into urgency. Fields per line: {"ticket": "...", "label": true|false, "flipped_fact": "..."}. No commentary. Score the model on those 80 tickets, bucket by confidence, and you have the calibration curve that decides your thresholds. If the "tries to talk its way into urgency" bucket scores badly, you have also just measured your injection exposure. Check yourself 0/5

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत On 17 September 2026, PrismML published Ternary Bonsai 2 27B: a 27-billion-parameter model whose weights are only -1, 0 and +1, packed into a 5.95 GB file, released Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face GGUF repo passed 2.5 million downloads inside five days. The headline everywhere was the same — a 27B model that fits on a laptop. The headline is true. Almost everything people assume follows from it is not. Stock llama.cpp will load the file and produce fluent nonsense without raising an error. Ollama and LM Studio refuse it outright. The 5.95 GB file needs roughly 12 GB of VRAM at default settings. The larger 7.21 GB build is faster on a datacenter GPU and slower on a 4090. And the widely-quoted "98.2% of full precision" is an average across fourteen benchmarks that hides a 6-point collapse in multimodal reasoning and, in one independent test, complete failure on low-resource languages. This page is the practical layer: what ternary quantization actually buys you, how to run this model without silently corrupting your output, and how to read a compression retention number honestly. The technique outlives the model — the same reasoning applies to every low-bit release that follows. What you'll learn Understand why ternary weights are 1.75 bits in practice, not the 1.58 bits the theory promises Recognise the silent-garbage failure mode: stock loaders ignore the Hadamard rotation and never error Pick between PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0 using the bandwidth-vs-unpack crossover, not file size Budget real memory: 5.95 GB of weights, ~64 KiB per token of cache, and why defaults blow past 12 GB Read '98.2% retention' correctly — which capabilities survive compression and which quietly do not
documents.s: Ternary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB

documents.t: A normal model stores each weight as a 16-bit float. A ternary model stores each weight as one of three values — -1, 0, +1 — with a single shared FP16 scale per group of weights. Reconstruction is w = scale_g * t, where t is the trit. Three states need log₂(3) ≈ 1.58 bits. That is the number the research literature uses, from Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 onward. It is not the number you get on disk. Bonsai 2 27B ships at 1.75 bits per weight for its densest build. The extra 0.17 bits per weight is the part nobody explains: Group scales. One FP16 scale per group of 128 weights is 16 bits amortised over 128 weights — 0.125 bits per weight before anything else. Packing waste. Trits do not divide neatly into bytes. Dense packing recovers most but not all of the theoretical density. Unquantized components. Embeddings, output projections and normalisation layers stay at higher precision. On a 27B model these are a small fraction of parameters but a noticeable fraction of bytes. So the real ratio is not 16/1.58 ≈ 10×. It is 53.8 GB → 5.95 GB, or about 9× — which is exactly what the model card reports. Why ternary is fast, and it is not the maths The intuition most people have is that ternary multiplication is cheap: multiplying by -1, 0 or +1 is a sign flip, a skip, or nothing. True, but that is not where the win comes from on real hardware. Token generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Every generated token requires streaming the entire weight matrix from memory. Cut the bytes by 9× and you cut the dominant cost by 9×. The arithmetic was never the bottleneck. This matters practically: a CPU or GPU without native ternary support must dequantize back to a normal format to use its existing multiply-accumulate units, which throws away the arithmetic saving while keeping the bandwidth one. Which is why the packing format you pick changes performance in a direction that looks backwards — see below.

This is the single most important thing on this page, and it appears in almost no coverage of the release. Bonsai 2's weights have a blockwise Hadamard rotation folded into storage. A matching inverse transform must be applied to the activations at runtime. The rotation is a standard trick for low-bit quantization — it spreads outlier magnitudes across a block so the ternary grid has less to lose — but it means the stored weights are not directly usable by a loader that does not know about it. A stock llama.cpp build does not know about it. Depending on version it will either reject the tensor types or, worse, load the file successfully and generate fluent, confident, completely wrong output. There is no error, no warning, no degraded-quality flag. The model card states this plainly: stock llama.cpp will not run these files, and standard builds produce garbage because the Hadamard activation transform is missing. Downstream tools inherit the problem in different ways: Runtime Behaviour with Bonsai 2 27B GGUF PrismML's llama.cpp fork (branch prism) Works — the only local GGUF path today Stock llama.cpp Rejects the tensor types, or loads and emits nonsense Ollama Import fails with a tensor size overflow error LM Studio Rejects ggml tensor types 142 and 143 MLX (Apple) Separate mlx-2bit build required; larger footprint The Ollama and LM Studio failures are the safe outcome. The stock-llama.cpp silent success is the dangerous one, because a benchmark script or an eval harness will happily record the nonsense as a result. If you are evaluating a low-bit model, verify the loader first Run one known-answer prompt before you run anything else. If a model that scores 95+ on HumanEval cannot answer "what is 2+2" coherently, you have a loader problem, not a model problem. This applies to every exotic quantization format, not just this one.
documents.s: The trap: stock llama.cpp loads it and lies

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Build PrismML's fork, not mainline⌄ git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp, then cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j for NVIDIA. On Apple Silicon drop the CUDA flag — Metal is on by default. On AMD use -DGGML_HIP=ON. The default branch is prism; the README explicitly warns against building from prism-v6 and against mixing this fork's libraries with a stock llama.cpp install on the same machine. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick the right GGUF before downloading 7 GB⌄ PTQ1_0 is 5.95 GB at 1.75 bits per weight — dense trits. PQ2_0 is 7.21 GB at 2.13 bits per weight — each trit gets its own 2-bit slot. Same weights, same quality, different packing. The choice is a throughput decision, not a quality one. See the crossover table below. ←PreviousNext→ 3Download, and check the byte count⌄ hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . — PTQ1_0 is 5,946,648,928 bytes and PQ2_0 is 7,206,168,928 bytes. A truncated download is another way to get plausible-looking garbage. Add the mmproj file (629 MB at Q8_0, 931 MB at BF16) only if you need vision. ←PreviousNext→ 4Serve it with an explicit context size⌄ ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080. The -c flag is not optional in practice: -c 0 defaults to the full 262K window and will try to allocate roughly 16 GB of attention cache before it has generated a single token. ←PreviousNext→ 5Verify with a known-answer call, then wire up your tooling⌄ The server exposes an OpenAI-shaped /v1/chat/completions endpoint, so anything that speaks chat-completions can point at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1. Send one trivial prompt and read the answer with your own eyes before you point an eval harness or an agent loop at it. ←PreviousNext→ 6If PQ2_0 crashes on CPU, disable repacking⌄ PQ2_0 can crash during llama.cpp's CPU repack step. Pass --no-repack, or set LLAMA_ARG_REPACK=0 in the environment. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal end-to-end: build, fetch, serve, verify CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Fork only — stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j # 2. Fetch (PQ2_0 = 7.21 GB, faster on big GPUs; PTQ1_0 = 5.95 GB, fits 8 GB cards) hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \ Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . # 3. Serve — always set -c explicitly, never leave it at 0 ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \ --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 # 4. Verify the loader BEFORE trusting any output curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"bonsai-2-27b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2? Answer with one number."}]}' # Coherent "4" => loader is correct. Fluent nonsense => wrong build, stop here.

Two builds of the same weights. PTQ1_0 packs trits densely at 1.75 bits. PQ2_0 gives each trit its own 2-bit slot at 2.13 bits — 21% more disk, but the unpacking is far cheaper because slots are byte-aligned. Measured generation throughput, tokens per second: GPU PQ2_0 (7.21 GB) PTQ1_0 (5.95 GB) Winner RTX 5090 129.9 120.5 PQ2_0 RTX 4090 81.2 91.1 PTQ1_0 L4 (24 GB) 29.8 32.1 PTQ1_0 M5 Pro (Metal) 28.1 — — The pattern generalises: PTQ1_0 wins on Ada-generation and lower-end GPUs, PQ2_0 wins on H100, A100 and Blackwell. That is the opposite of the usual quantization rule of thumb, where smaller is always faster. The reason is the bandwidth-versus-unpack tradeoff from earlier. On a bandwidth-starved card, moving 21% fewer bytes dominates and the dense packing wins. On a card with enormous memory bandwidth, bandwidth stops being the constraint and the bit-shuffling cost of dense unpacking becomes the bottleneck instead — so the fatter, byte-aligned format runs faster. Prompt processing tells the same story more loudly: on an RTX 5090, PQ2_0 processes prompts at 3,893 tok/s against PTQ1_0's 1,805 — more than double, because prefill is compute-bound, where unpacking cost hits hardest. Rule of thumb: below 12 GB of VRAM you have no choice, take PTQ1_0. Above it, take PQ2_0 unless you are on a 4090 or an L4, where PTQ1_0 measurably wins.
documents.s: PTQ1_0 vs PQ2_0: the crossover that looks backwards

documents.t: Three different "size" numbers are circulating for this model — 5.9 GB, 7.2 GB and 8.6 GB — and all three are defensible, because they measure different things. Here is the actual budget: Weights: 5.95 GB (PTQ1_0) or 7.21 GB (PQ2_0). Vision projector: +629 MB (Q8_0) or +931 MB (BF16), if you need images. Attention cache: roughly 64 KiB per token. That is ~0.5 GB at 8K context, ~2 GB at 32K, and ~16 GB at the full 262K window. Parallel slots: llama.cpp allocates cache per slot. Defaults allocate several. One independent test measured just over 12 GB of VRAM at default settings, dropping to about 8 GB when the server was restricted to a single parallel slot. The disk footprint they measured — around 7 GB — corresponds to the PQ2_0 build, which is where part of the number confusion comes from. Practical context headroom by card, using PQ2_0 unless noted: VRAM Build Usable context 8 GB PTQ1_0 ~16K tokens (~6K with vision) 12 GB PQ2_0 ~56K tokens 16 GB PQ2_0 ~118K tokens 24 GB PQ2_0 ~240K tokens 32 GB+ PQ2_0 Full 262K window The "runs on a laptop" claim survives all of this — but "runs on a laptop with an 8 GB GPU and a 16K context" is the honest version, and that is a materially different product.
documents.s: File size is not memory requirement

documents.t: PrismML reports an aggregate of 84.78 against the full-precision base model's 86.32 across fourteen benchmarks — the 98.2% figure. Averages are where compression damage goes to hide. The per-benchmark spread: Benchmark Bonsai 2 27B FP16 base Delta AIME26 95.83 94.58 +1.25 MATH-500 98.80 99.80 −1.00 LiveCodeBench 90.07 90.05 +0.02 HumanEval+ 95.12 93.29 +1.83 MMLU-Redux 89.09 91.46 −2.37 MMMU-Pro 75.49 81.73 −6.24 Three things to take from this table. First, the damage is not uniform — it is structural. Maths and code are essentially untouched. Knowledge recall drops (composite knowledge-and-reasoning lands near 79.9 versus 85.6 for full precision). Multimodal reasoning takes the real hit: MMMU-Pro falls 6.24 points, and OCR Bench v2 drops from 60.99 to 56.88. Compression costs you breadth of stored fact, not procedural skill — which is exactly what you would expect when you crush the precision available to store long-tail associations. Second, be suspicious of the positives. The compressed model "beating" its own full-precision base by 1.83 points on HumanEval+ and 1.25 on AIME26 is not evidence that compression helps. It is evidence that these benchmarks have run-to-run variance of a couple of points. Which should also make you discount the small negatives. Third, the vendor's own numbers do not fully agree. The model card's benchmark table aggregates to 84.78, while PrismML's launch post reports an aggregate of 83.9. Both are described as the same 98.2% retention. The discrepancy is small and unexplained; we report it rather than pick one. The failure mode benchmarks did not catch One independent hands-on test found behaviour no benchmark row predicts: asked to translate into low-resource languages including Tamil, the model entered a repetitive loop and never completed the task — worse than the previous Bonsai generation. The same test found it identified a real timezone bug and then talked itself out of the correct conclusion, and failed to produce a working reset button in a small HTML task across three correction rounds. This is the characteristic signature of aggressive quantization: aggregate scores hold, while the long tail — rare languages, long-horizon self-correction — degrades in ways that only show up in use. Community reports also describe recall and coherence degradation past roughly 200K tokens of the advertised 262K window.

There is a parallel effort to get ternary Bonsai into upstream llama.cpp, and its current state is a useful lesson in how low-bit formats fragment. PrismML proposed group-128 ternary packing for the smaller Bonsai models. The llama.cpp maintainer pushed back in favour of group size 64, on the grounds that it costs under 6% extra memory while supporting more tensor shapes and giving better quality. Q2_0 with group-64 became the official format and has been merged into multiple backends including CUDA and Vulkan. PrismML kept their group-128 variants in the fork. So "does llama.cpp support ternary models" has two correct and opposite answers: Yes — Q2_0_g64 builds run on mainline across backends, and the fork's own README points at them as the portable path. No, not for this model — as of verification, the published Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf repo contains F16, PQ2_0, PTQ1_0 and the two mmproj files. There is no Q2_0_g64 build of the 27B. The fork is the only path. Two older ternary formats, TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, already exist in ggml but use group size 256, which is incompatible with how these models are natively packed. TQ2_0 is also the tightest faithful ternary layout in ggml at roughly 2.06 bits per weight — and in current mainline it implements a CPU-only dot product with no CUDA, Metal or Vulkan path. Seeing "ternary supported" in a changelog tells you very little about whether your GPU will use it. For the next low-bit model you evaluate, the question to ask is not is it quantized but which group size, which packing, which backends have kernels, and is there a portable build — because that determines whether you are running on mainline or maintaining someone else's fork.
documents.s: The mainline story, and why it matters for the next release

documents.t: Worth it when: You need a capable maths or coding model on hardware that cannot hold a 27B at higher precision. That is where retention is near-perfect and the value is highest. You are bandwidth-constrained — a laptop GPU, an edge box, a shared L4 — and 9× fewer bytes per token is the difference between usable and not. Energy matters. PrismML reports 0.714 mWh per token on an RTX 4090, which they put at 40% more efficient than a full-precision 8B model. The Apache 2.0 licence and fully local execution are requirements, not preferences. Not worth it when: The work is knowledge-heavy or multimodal. That is precisely where the compression bill lands. You need non-English long-tail language coverage. The independent evidence here is bad and benchmarks did not predict it. You cannot maintain a forked inference runtime. Ollama and LM Studio do not load it today, and a stock build fails silently rather than loudly. You were going to run it past ~200K tokens of context on the strength of the 262K spec.
documents.s: When this is the right tool

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-22। इस पेज में ऐसे तथ्य हैं जो समय के साथ बदलते हैं — ऊपर दी गई तारीख को इसकी ताज़गी मानें। स्रोत: PrismML launch post and the prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf model card and file listing on Hugging Face; PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp README (branch prism, 716 stars at check); ggml-org/llama.cpp discussion #22019; independent hands-on testing and benchmark tables published by MindStudio, DataCamp and Atomic Chat. Throughput, VRAM and retention figures are vendor or third-party measurements on specific hardware and will move as the fork, mainline kernels and published GGUF builds change — re-check the model card's file list before assuming a portable build does or does not exist.

PrismML — Bonsai 2 27B launch post (ternary scheme, bits per weight, aggregate benchmark, hardware throughput and energy figures): https://prismml.com/news/bonsai-2-27b Hugging Face — prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf model card and file listing (PTQ1_0 / PQ2_0 / F16 / mmproj sizes, Hadamard rotation note, run commands, 262K context, Apache 2.0): https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf Hugging Face — the full Bonsai 2 collection, including the MLX 2-bit build and the WebGPU demo space: https://huggingface.co/prism-ml PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp — the required fork, branch prism, with the PQ2_0 / Q2_0_g64 guidance and the warning against mixing builds: https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp ggml-org/llama.cpp discussion #22019 — group-128 versus the group-64 Q2_0 standard, TQ1_0/TQ2_0 group-256 incompatibility, backend merge status: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/22019 Microsoft — BitNet b1.58 2B4T technical report, the reference point for ternary LLM training: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.12285 Microsoft — bitnet.cpp: efficient edge inference for ternary LLMs (why the win is bandwidth, and why hardware without native ternary support must dequantize): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.11880 MindStudio — independent hands-on testing of the 98.2% claim, including the multilingual failure and measured VRAM: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/bonsai-2-27b-real-world-test Atomic Chat — local install guide with the per-GPU throughput table, context headroom table and the --no-repack workaround: https://atomic.chat/blog/guides/how-to-run-bonsai-2-locally DataCamp — per-benchmark comparison against the full-precision base and the long-context degradation reports: https://www.datacamp.com/blog/bonsai-2-27b SiliconANGLE — launch coverage and positioning: https://siliconangle.com/2026/09/18/prismml-launches-bonsai-2-27b-a-high-intelligence-ai-model-so-small-it-fits-on-consumer-hardware/

Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें उन्नत आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-09-29। Every accuracy, latency and training-time figure on this page is self-reported by the project that published it, on benchmarks that project chose. Nothing here has been independently replicated. Both repositories are days old and moving fast — star counts, model names, checkpoint ids and CLI flags are the most perishable facts here; read the current README before you copy a command. Neither project is affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe, the makers of Jev. स्रोत: README of firelex/jeff (created 2026-09-28, 895 stars at time of writing) and PostHog/jeeves (created 2026-09-29, 107 stars); denis-pplx/autojev README; Hacker News items 49883844 (Jeff, 536 points / 204 comments) and 49891290 (Jeeves, 105 points / 44 comments). What you'll learn Explain the actual training recipe behind an open decision model — cross-entropy over option letters, one epoch, and a temperature fitted afterwards — and why calibration is a separate step from accuracy Read the published benchmark tables honestly: the three rows where a 0.8B model beats the commercial API, and the two rows where it loses by 20–26 points Decide between four options — hosted API, zero-shot open weights, your own fine-tune, or a plain embeddings classifier — using the one baseline number that kills most of these projects Train and serve a Jev-compatible model yourself in an afternoon on a single GPU, including the checkpoint-selection rule that keeps the result honest Know when adding reasoning back to a decision model is worth 11x the latency, and how a confidence threshold buys most of the accuracy for a third of the wait System One decision models explained the category: you send program state plus typed questions, and you get calibrated probabilities back instead of text. That page ended where the open recreations were in mid-September — Kev, Nimble, a logprob shim. In the last week of September the story changed shape. The question stopped being "can we clone the API" and became "should you train your own?" On September 28 a project called Jeff shipped 0.8B and 2B fine-tunes that land within four points of Jev's overall benchmark score and run in ~22–28 ms on a laptop-class GPU, trained in about two hours on one workstation card. It was the top AI story on Hacker News that day. Twelve hours later PostHog published Jeeves, which does the opposite thing — bolts reasoning onto a decision model — and reports beating Jev on Jev's own hard tier. Both are MIT code with Apache-2.0 weights. Both are honest enough in their READMEs to publish the rows where they lose. This page is about what those rows mean for you.
documents.s: Train Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Date (2026) What shipped Why it matters Sep 15 Jev (TypeSafe AI), API-only Defined the category and the /v1/systemone request shape Sep 21 Kev, Nimble, openjev-sglang Proved the interface was reproducible on open weights — AutoJev (denis-pplx) The recipe: full-weight SFT of Qwen3.8-27B, 73,000 examples, one H200, 84.60% vs a 69.83% base Sep 28 Jeff (firelex) Shrank it — 0.8B/2B students, ~2 h on one workstation GPU, MLX serving, game evals Sep 29 Jeeves (PostHog) Reversed the premise — a thinking decision model, LoRA + RL on Qwen3.5-9B The through-line: in two weeks a category went from a closed API with undisclosed training to a recipe you can run overnight. AutoJev is the hinge — it published the loss function, and everything after it is a variation on that one idea.
Strip the marketing and a decision model is a startlingly small change to a normal LLM.

The model is not taught to "make decisions". It is taught to put probability mass on a single letter token — A, B, C — at one specific position. You lay the options out as a lettered panel, you train with plain cross-entropy on the correct letter, and at inference you read the logits for the letter tokens and renormalise them over just the options you offered. That one implementation detail explains the headline limitation. Jeff caps you at 26 options, and the README is blunt that positions past that are "effectively never selected" — because the alphabet ran out, not because of anything architectural. (Jev itself advertises up to 255 options, which tells you it encodes options differently.) Jeeves takes the other road: a pointer head that scores a projected hidden state against each option's embedding with a scaled dot product. No letters, no alphabet ceiling. It marks the structure with rare tokens borrowed from Qwen's tokenizer that real text essentially never uses — <|fim_prefix|> for state, <|fim_middle|> for questions, <|box_start|>/<|box_end|> around options, <|fim_suffix|> at the decision point. Reusing dead tokens as delimiters is the cheap trick that avoids growing the vocabulary or colliding with content.
documents.s: 1. The loss is cross-entropy over option letters

documents.t: This is the part people skip, and it is the part that makes the output trustworthy. Accuracy and calibration are different properties. A model can rank the right answer first almost every time and still say "91%" when it is right 75% of the time — the independent BANKING77 pilot on Jev found exactly that shape of over-confidence. So all three projects fit a single scalar temperature on a held-out development set after training, and ship it alongside the checkpoint. Divide the logits by it, softmax, done. AutoJev publishes what that buys, and it is the cleanest before/after in the whole stack: Metric Base Qwen3.8-27B AutoJev-27B Accuracy 69.83% 84.60% ECE (expected calibration error — lower is better) 0.06483 0.04282 Brier score (lower is better) 0.40834 0.22027 Note that all three moved, but by different amounts. Accuracy climbed ~15 points while ECE fell ~34% — training made the model both righter and more honest, and the honesty is measurable separately. If you train your own and only report accuracy, you have not finished.
documents.s: 2. The calibration is a separate, one-parameter stage

documents.t: One epoch. Batch 256. Full-weight (Jeff, AutoJev) or LoRA r=16 (Jeeves). Checkpoint selection on a development set, never on the benchmark panel — Jeff states this explicitly, and it is the single line that separates a credible small-model result from a leaked one. Jeff also keeps at least half of each training family in the same panel layout it will see at inference, which matters more than it should; see the wording section below. Train a 0.8B decision model (Jeff's own recipe) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # 1. Build the training mix from public datasets uv run autojev-mix ... # 2. One epoch, full-weight, lr 5e-6 scripts/train.sh RUN data/mix/public.jsonl data/mix 5e-6 40 Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B <revision> --epochs 1 # 3. Evaluate the SELECTED checkpoint against a held-out panel uv run autojev-evaluate --data data/panel.jsonl --local \ --checkpoint checkpoints/RUN/selected --output runs/eval/RUN.json Reported cost of step 2: ~2 hours for 0.8B, ~3.5 hours for 2B, on one RTX PRO 6000. That is the number that made this a front-page story.

Here is Jeff's published panel — 4,599 questions across five public datasets plus JevBench's hard tier — with the commercial API in the last column. Read it by row, not by the overall line. Benchmark Jeff-0.8B Jeff-2B Jeff-Gemma4-E2B Jev (API) Overall 79.1% 83.1% 81.6% 83.0% Financial PhraseBank 96.4% 96.3% 96.1% 77.0% RAGTruth 86.1% 88.9% 87.4% 77.3% WinoGrande 68.6% 79.0% 77.4% 90.7% JudgeBench 62.6% 64.6% 60.6% 78.6% BBH 64.0% 68.0% 66.4% 94.3% JevBench Hard 47.6% 53.3% 48.6% 73.3% The overall scores are nearly tied. The rows are not close at all: Where the tiny model wins, it wins big. Financial PhraseBank: 96.4% against 77.0% — a 0.8B model beating a commercial API by 19 points. RAGTruth (does this answer stay faithful to the retrieved passage?): 86.1% against 77.3%. Both are narrow, high-volume, pattern-shaped jobs — sentiment on a fixed vocabulary, groundedness on a supplied passage. If your agent's hot path is that shape, a local 0.8B is not a compromise, it is the better tool. Where it loses, it is not close. BBH is 30 points down. JevBench Hard is 26 points down. Those are the rows that need multi-step reasoning, and the README says so plainly: small decision models give you "fast, calibrated choices between the options you describe" and no reasoning chain. The overall number is the average of those two facts and therefore describes nothing. This is the most transferable lesson on this page, and it is not specific to decision models: any single headline score is a weighted average over a benchmark mix that is not your mix.

Jeff also evaluated zero-shot game play — 20 episodes each of Doom, Frogger and Pac-Man — and the result is uncomfortable enough that publishing it earns trust: Model Doom (kills) Frogger (crossings) Pac-Man (pellets / 98) Random −0.05 0 11.2 Hand-coded rule bot 6.55 10.25 94.1 Jeff-0.8B 6.55 10.3 57.0 Jeff-2B −0.9 6.0 41.2 The 2B is worse at all three games than the 0.8B it outscores on every benchmark row. The README's read is that the bigger model came out more risk-averse. Whatever the cause, the pairing of those two tables is the point: benchmark rank did not predict behaviour in a loop. And the hand-coded rule bot still wins Pac-Man by 37 points — the reminder that "can a model do it" and "should a model do it" are different questions.
documents.s: The games table is the honest one

documents.t: Median latency per decision, ~200-token questions: Model RTX PRO 6000 Apple M4 Max (MLX) CPU (32 threads) Jeff-0.8B 22 ms 28 ms 463 ms Jeff-2B 24 ms 60 ms 708 ms Jeff-Gemma4-E2B 29 ms — 1.0 s Two things to take from this: "Tiny model" does not mean "runs anywhere fast." The same 0.8B checkpoint is 22 ms on a GPU and 463 ms on 32 CPU threads — a 21x gap. A decision model is only a decision model at GPU latency; on CPU it is a slow API call you happen to host. If your plan was "sprinkle these calls everywhere in the request path", the CPU column is the plan's budget. 2.5x the parameters cost 2 ms on the big GPU. 22 → 24 ms. At this size a single forward pass over ~200 tokens is dominated by overhead and memory bandwidth, not by arithmetic, so on a fast card the 2B is nearly free relative to the 0.8B — while on the M4 Max the same step costs you 2.1x (28 → 60 ms). Pick your model per deployment target, not from the parameter count. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Serve one locally before you train anything⌄ Install with uv, pull a checkpoint from Hugging Face, start the server. You want the zero-shot number on YOUR data before you decide training is necessary — the most common outcome reported by practitioners is that zero-shot is not good enough, and that is much cheaper to discover in twenty minutes than after a training run. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a labelled dev set of a few hundred real examples⌄ Real traffic, real label distribution, including the ambiguous ones you would normally throw out. This set does double duty: it selects your checkpoint and it fits your temperature. It must never overlap the panel you report numbers on. ←PreviousNext→ 3Measure the boring baseline first⌄ Embeddings plus a logistic-regression head, on the same dev set. On BANKING77 this approach was reported in the Jeff discussion at 93.0% with a model roughly 15x smaller. If it wins on your data, stop here — you have saved yourself a fine-tune and a GPU. ←PreviousNext→ 4Fine-tune only the gap you measured⌄ One epoch, batch 256, cross-entropy over the option letters, lr around 5e-6. Keep at least half your training examples in the exact panel layout you will use at inference. Select the checkpoint on the dev set. ←PreviousNext→ 5Fit the temperature, then report both numbers⌄ One scalar on the dev set, stored with the checkpoint. Then publish accuracy AND calibration error to yourself. An uncalibrated decision model is a classifier with a confidence field you are not allowed to trust — which defeats the entire purpose of the category. ←PreviousNext→ 6Set the threshold from the reliability curve, not from a round number⌄ Find the confidence at which observed accuracy is actually good enough to skip a human or a frontier model. Everything below it escalates. That number is a property of your data and will not be 0.9 just because 0.9 looks tidy. ←PreviousNext→ Serve a Jev-compatible model locally and send it a real request CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Apple silicon (MLX backend) uv sync --no-default-groups --extra mac uv run --no-default-groups hf download mstrasser/Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B --local-dir checkpoints/jeff-0.8b JEFF_BACKEND=mlx JEFF_CHECKPOINT=checkpoints/jeff-0.8b PORT=8765 \ uv run --no-default-groups --extra mac jeff-serve # Two independent questions, one request, one parallel pass curl -s localhost:8765/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "jeff-latest", "state": "Refund request: the customer says the parcel arrived crushed and wants their money back.", "questions": { "route": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": {"1": "Refunds and payments", "2": "Damaged or lost parcels", "3": "Account and login problems"}}, "angry": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer angry?"} } }'

The sharpest criticism in the Hacker News thread was not that Jeff performs badly. It was structural: if you have to fine-tune it on your own labelled data anyway, you have not bought a zero-shot classifier — you have bought a somewhat awkward way to train a classifier, and the field already has cheaper ones. The numbers in that thread support taking it seriously. A commenter reported testing the 0.8B zero-shot on job-ad classification and finding it unusable, with the 2B still missing categories. Another reported that plain embeddings plus a logistic-regression head reached 93.0% on BANKING77 using a model about 15x smaller than the decision models being compared — against the 87.4%-confidence/75.3%-accuracy shape the independent Jev pilot found on the same dataset. So the honest decision table: Situation Use Handful of fixed labels, plenty of examples, latency matters Embeddings + logistic regression. Smallest, fastest, trains in seconds. Beat this before considering anything else. Labels change often, or questions are written in prose per request Zero-shot decision model — the schema is the interface, which is the actual product One high-volume domain, you have labels, you have a GPU for an afternoon Fine-tune. Jeff's chess run went 15.5% → 55.8%; a voice-navigation fine-tune on ~11,000 examples went 31.7% → 95.8% in under 30 minutes Genuinely hard, multi-step judgements Reasoning — Jeeves, or a frontier model behind a cascade You need it working this afternoon and the volume is low Hosted API. Your own GPU is not free either The general rule underneath: a decision model earns its place when the schema is the valuable part — arbitrary typed questions, in prose, resolved in one pass. When your label set is fixed and known, you are paying model-shaped costs for classifier-shaped work.
documents.s: The uncomfortable question: do you need a model at all?

documents.t: Jev's founding pitch was that this class of model does not generate text. PostHog's Jeeves tests that premise directly by letting a decision model think first, then decide, on Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA r=16 and a pointer head. Training runs in three stages: SFT (19,126 questions from 12 public datasets plus synthetic policy data, half carrying reasoning chains, 2 epochs / 596 steps on 8 GPUs), then CISPO reinforcement learning (9,992 questions, 8 rollouts each at temperature 1, thinking capped at 2,560 tokens — a 624-step schedule deliberately stopped at step 402 because calibration was degrading past it), then the same scalar temperature fit. Reported results: Benchmark Jeeves Jev Kev-9B Test overall 0.889 0.857 0.822 JevBench overall (231 items) 0.935 0.866 0.715 JevBench hard (111 items) 0.865 0.730 0.451 And the ablation that matters more than any of those rows: 0.804 without reasoning, 0.840 with it. Thinking is worth about 3.6 points on this model. Now price it. On one H100, Jeeves answers in ~0.3 s with reasoning off and 3.3 s median with it on — 17.1 s at p90. That is roughly 11x the median latency and a tail an order of magnitude worse, for 3.6 points. The README's own mitigation is the interesting engineering: cap thinking at 2,560 tokens and add a 0.9 confidence threshold that stops early when the model is already sure, which brings the median to 2.0 s. Reasoning becomes something you spend only on the items that need it. Two caveats Jeeves publishes about itself: it is worse than Jev on knowledge-heavy tasks (MMLU 0.793 vs 0.900) — reasoning does not add facts — and its reasoning chains were never rewarded for language consistency, so they are not reliably readable. If you wanted the chain as an audit trail, check that it is legible before you promise anyone it is.

Wording consistency beats wording quality. Jeff reports Frogger crossings going from 15 to 23 purely by phrasing every option the same way as its siblings. Options are compared against each other in one pass — asymmetric phrasing is a thumb on the scale. Keep keys short and put the description in the text. Prompt formats do not port between decision models. Jev's bearing-number style did not transfer to Jeff; consequence-focused wording was needed instead. Treat a switch of decision model as a re-tuning job, exactly like porting prompts across models. The 26-option ceiling is silent. Nothing errors. Options 27+ simply never win. Chunk large label sets into a two-stage decision instead. English, text-only for Jeff. AutoJev accepts base64 images; Jeff does not. Zero-shot quality is workload-shaped and often disappointing. Multiple practitioners reported the small models being unusable on their own real classification tasks. Measure on your data on day one. Training-data leak filtering is your job. Jeff generates synthetic data locally with leak filtering precisely because a decision model trained near its eval panel produces a number that means nothing. Both repos are days old. Flags, checkpoint names and defaults are moving. Nothing here substitutes for the current README. Check yourself 0/5

PostHog/jeeves — three-stage training (SFT → CISPO → temperature), pointer head, rare-token markers, the reasoning ablation and the latency/threshold numbers. denis-pplx/autojev — the origin recipe: full-weight SFT of Qwen3.8-27B on 73,000 examples, one H200, with the accuracy/ECE/Brier before-and-after. Hacker News — Jeff discussion (item 49883844) — 536 points, 204 comments: the zero-shot failure reports, the ModernBERT critique and the embeddings + logistic-regression BANKING77 number. Hacker News — Jeeves discussion (item 49891290) — the reasoning-vs-latency argument. AILmanac — System One decision models: Jev, Kev and the open clones — the category itself, the independent BANKING77 calibration pilot, and the hosted API's limits and pricing.

System One decision models: Jev, Kev and the open clones — read this first if the category is new to you; it covers the API, the "cannot hallucinate" claim and the independent test. Model routing patterns — where a calibrated probability actually earns its keep: cascades, confidence gates and escalation. Markdown के रूप में कॉपी करें मध्यम "AI की लागत कितनी है?" का कोई एक जवाब नहीं है — यह इस पर निर्भर करता है कि आप कौन-सा प्राइसिंग आर्किटाइप खरीद रहे हैं और आप उसे असल में कितना इस्तेमाल करते हैं। डॉलर के आँकड़े हर कुछ महीनों में बदलते हैं; लागत की संरचना शायद ही बदलती है। यह पृष्ठ टिकाऊ आकार सिखाता है: AI की कीमत तय करने के तीन तरीके, बनाने से पहले किसी वर्कलोड का अनुमान कैसे लगाएँ, बिल घटाने वाले लीवर, और API किराए पर लेने बनाम सेल्फ-होस्टिंग के बीच का असली मोड़। What you'll learn तीन लागत आर्किटाइप में फ़र्क करें: per-token API, फ्लैट सब्सक्रिप्शन, और ओपन/सेल्फ-होस्टेड किसी भी वर्कलोड की लागत का अनुमान tokens × rate × volume से लगाएँ — शिप करने से पहले गुणवत्ता को चोट पहुँचाए बिना खर्च घटाने वाले बड़े लीवर खींचें जानें कब ओपन/सेल्फ-होस्टेड लागत में API को हराता है, और कब API जीतता है जानें कौन-से आँकड़े तेज़ी से पुराने पड़ते हैं — और आज का सच कहाँ जाँचें आखिरी बार सत्यापित: 2026-06-28। प्रति-टोकन दरें, सब्सक्रिप्शन टियर, कैश और बैच डिस्काउंट, और कौन-सा मॉडल सबसे सस्ता है — यह लगभग हर महीने बदलता है — हर विशिष्ट डॉलर आँकड़े को नाशवान मानें। यह पृष्ठ टिकाऊ मॉडल (आर्किटाइप + अनुमान कैसे लगाएँ + लीवर) सिखाता है; आज के आँकड़ों के लिए हर प्रोवाइडर का अपना प्राइसिंग पेज (Sources में लिंक), Artificial Analysis जैसा एक स्वतंत्र ट्रैकर देखें, और हमारे Cost Calculator में गणित चलाएँ। इसके विरुद्ध पुष्टि करें आधिकारिक स्रोत.

documents.t: AI के लिए भुगतान का लगभग हर तरीका तीन आकारों में से एक में सिमट जाता है। आकार सीखें, कीमतें नहीं। Per-token API (उपयोग-आधारित)। आप एक होस्टेड मॉडल को API पर कॉल करते हैं और प्रति टोकन भुगतान करते हैं — और इनपुट और आउटपुट की कीमत अलग-अलग तय होती है, जिसमें आउटपुट लगभग हमेशा दोनों में महँगा होता है। बड़े/स्मार्ट मॉडल प्रति टोकन अधिक लागत लेते हैं; छोटे मॉडल कहीं कम। ज़्यादातर प्रोवाइडर डिस्काउंट भी देते हैं: आपके द्वारा फिर से भेजे गए कैश्ड इनपुट के लिए एक घटी हुई दर, और गैर-अत्यावश्यक async जॉब्स के लिए एक फ्लैट बैच डिस्काउंट। जब आप Claude, GPT, या Gemini पर कोई प्रोडक्ट बनाते हैं तो आप इसी तरह भुगतान करते हैं। लागत सीधे उपयोग के साथ बढ़ती है — छोटे पैमाने पर पैसे-कौड़ी, बड़े पैमाने पर सबसे बड़ी लाइन आइटम। फ्लैट कंज़्यूमर/सीट सब्सक्रिप्शन। किसी चैट ऐप या IDE असिस्टेंट के लिए एक निश्चित मासिक शुल्क (Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini कंज़्यूमर प्लान, Copilot-शैली सीटें)। आप टोकन नहीं देखते; आपको एक उपयोग भत्ता और रेट लिमिट मिलती हैं। कीबोर्ड पर बैठे इंसान के लिए पूर्वानुमेय और सस्ता — लेकिन यह प्रोग्रामेटिक/उच्च-आयतन काम के लिए स्केल नहीं करता, और प्रति-सीट लागत एक टीम में जुड़ती जाती है। ओपन / लोकल (सेल्फ-होस्टेड)। आप एक ओपन-वेट मॉडल (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) अपने हार्डवेयर या किराए के GPU पर चलाते हैं। कोई प्रति-कॉल कीमत नहीं है — आप हार्डवेयर (या प्रति-घंटा GPU किराया) + बिजली + ops के लिए भुगतान करते हैं, चाहे मॉडल व्यस्त हो या निष्क्रिय। एक और कॉल की सीमांत लागत बड़े पैमाने पर लगभग-शून्य होती है, पर आप निश्चित लागत और परिचालन बोझ उठाते हैं। देखें Run Models Locally with Ollama। Pro tip मुख्य विभाजन: API और सब्सक्रिप्शन सीमांत (MARGINAL) लागत हैं (आप प्रति-उपयोग भुगतान करते हैं); सेल्फ-होस्टिंग ज़्यादातर निश्चित (FIXED) लागत है (आप क्षमता बनाए रखने के लिए भुगतान करते हैं, चाहे इस्तेमाल हो या न हो)। API पर, सबसे बड़ा आश्चर्य यह है कि OUTPUT टोकन आमतौर पर इनपुट से कई गुना अधिक लागत लेते हैं — बातूनी जवाब असली पैसा खर्च कराते हैं। फ्लैट सब्सक्रिप्शन एक इंसान के चैट करने का सही औज़ार है; per-token API एक ऐप द्वारा लूप में मॉडल कॉल करने का सही औज़ार है।

आप प्रोडक्शन कोड की एक लाइन लिखने से पहले एक API बिल का आकार आँक सकते हैं। पूरा मॉडल एक फ़ॉर्मूला है: cost ≈ (input tokens × input rate) + (output tokens × output rate), per call × number of calls दरें प्रति मिलियन टोकन पर उद्धृत होती हैं, और इनपुट व आउटपुट की अलग-अलग दरें होती हैं — इसलिए दोनों हिस्सों का अलग-अलग अनुमान लगाएँ और जोड़ें। टोकन का एक मोटा नियम: ~1 token ≈ अंग्रेज़ी के 4 अक्षर, या ~0.75 शब्द। सटीक गिनती के लिए Token Estimator क्षेत्र का उपयोग करें और Tokens & Pricing पढ़ें। टोकन कहाँ छिपते हैं इसका पूरा तंत्र The Token Economy में रहता है। Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1एक कॉल के टोकन का आकार आँकें⌄ इनपुट जोड़ें: system prompt + tools + retrieved context + history + यूज़र टर्न। फिर उस आउटपुट का अनुमान लगाएँ जो आप माँगते हैं। इनपुट और आउटपुट अलग-अलग गिनें — इनकी कीमत अलग है। ←PreviousNext→ 2हर पक्ष को उसकी अपनी दर से गुणा करें⌄ input tokens × input rate, साथ में output tokens × output rate। प्रोवाइडर के प्राइसिंग पेज से आज के प्रति-मिलियन आँकड़े इस्तेमाल करें (कोई याद किया हुआ आँकड़ा भरोसे में न लें — VerifyNote देखें)। ←PreviousNext→ 3असली आयतन से स्केल करें⌄ प्रति-कॉल लागत को calls per day × days से गुणा करें। एक लागत जो प्रति कॉल तुच्छ है (सेंट के अंश), लाखों कॉल पर आपकी शीर्ष लाइन आइटम बन जाती है — अपने ACTUAL ट्रैफ़िक का मॉडल बनाएँ, एक अनुरोध का नहीं। ←PreviousNext→ 4जो डिस्काउंट आप असल में इस्तेमाल करेंगे उन्हें लागू करें⌄ अगर इनपुट का एक बड़ा हिस्सा हर कॉल में दोहराता है, तो उसे पूरे इनपुट पर नहीं बल्कि CACHED दर पर आँकें। अगर जॉब ऑफ़लाइन है, BATCH डिस्काउंट लागू करें। ये बड़े पैमाने पर जवाब को नाटकीय रूप से बदलते हैं। ←PreviousNext→ 5किसी ट्रैकर के विरुद्ध सैनिटी-चेक करें, फिर काटें⌄ अपनी प्रति-टोकन धारणाओं की तुलना किसी स्वतंत्र ट्रैकर और हमारे Cost Calculator से करें, फिर नीचे दिए लीवर से बिल पर हमला करें। ←PreviousNext→ Back-of-envelope estimate (fill in today's rates) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Per call: input_tokens = system + tools + context + history + user_turn output_tokens = the answer you ask for call_cost = (input_tokens * input_rate_per_million / 1e6) + (output_tokens * output_rate_per_million / 1e6) Per month: monthly_cost = call_cost * calls_per_day * 30 Then adjust: - cached repeated input -> use the (lower) cache-read rate for that slice - offline / non-urgent -> apply the batch discount to the whole job Rates change monthly — pull today's numbers from the provider's pricing page.
documents.s: किसी वर्कलोड की लागत का अनुमान कैसे लगाएँ

documents.t: ज़्यादातर असली वर्कलोड में बेकार बोझ होता है। ये लीवर, मोटे तौर पर लीवरेज के क्रम में, गुणवत्ता को छुए बिना खर्च काटते हैं — पहले सस्ते संरचनात्मक लीवर खींचें। मॉडल को सही आकार दें। एक ऐसे काम के लिए फ्लैगशिप दर न चुकाएँ जिसे एक छोटा/सस्ता मॉडल ठीक-ठाक कर देता है। क्लासिफ़िकेशन, एक्सट्रैक्शन, राउटिंग, और सरल फ़ॉर्मैटिंग आमतौर पर सबसे छोटे टियर पर प्रति-टोकन कीमत के एक अंश पर बढ़िया चलते हैं। बड़े मॉडल को सचमुच कठिन तर्क के लिए आरक्षित रखें, और routing पर विचार करें: सस्ता मॉडल आसान बहुमत संभालता है, केवल कठिन मामलों को एस्केलेट करें। देखें Choosing a Model। जो कॉन्टेक्स्ट आप भेजते हैं उसे छाँटें। सबसे सस्ता टोकन वह है जो आप कभी भेजते ही नहीं। फूले हुए system prompts छाँटें, लंबे इतिहास को एक चलती हुई सारांश में संघनित करें, और केवल वही tools दिखाएँ जो काम को चाहिए — हर एक इनपुट है जिसका आप हर कॉल में फिर से भुगतान करते हैं। विशाल कॉन्टेक्स्ट ठूँसने के बजाय RAG। एक सवाल का जवाब देने के लिए 50-पन्नों का दस्तावेज़ चिपकाना हर कॉल में 50 पन्नों का भुगतान करता है। Retrieval केवल कुछ प्रासंगिक अंश लाता है — उसी (अक्सर बेहतर) जवाब के लिए बहुत कम इनपुट टोकन। किसी विशाल कॉन्टेक्स्ट विंडो की ओर तभी हाथ बढ़ाएँ जब आपको सचमुच पूरे कॉर्पस को एक साथ नज़र में चाहिए। प्रॉम्प्ट कैशिंग। अगर कई कॉल एक बड़ा अपरिवर्तित उपसर्ग साझा करते हैं (system prompt, tool catalog, reference doc), तो कैशिंग उसे एक बार प्रोसेस करती है और हर बाद की कॉल पर उसे तीव्र छूट पर फिर से परोसती है। चैट और एजेंट वर्कलोड के लिए सबसे अधिक-लीवरेज वाला संरचनात्मक बदलाव, क्योंकि यह हर टर्न में भुगतान लौटाता है। गैर-अत्यावश्यक को बैच करें। Evals, बल्क लेबलिंग, किसी आर्काइव का सारांश — कुछ भी जहाँ आपको जवाब सेकंडों में नहीं चाहिए — ज़्यादातर प्रोवाइडरों पर एक फ्लैट छूट पर एक async बैच पथ से चलता है। तात्कालिकता का सौदा एक भौतिक रूप से कम बिल के लिए करें। आउटपुट छोटा करें। आउटपुट महँगा पक्ष है। बातूनी पैराग्राफ़ के बजाय JSON या एक तंग स्कीमा माँगें: कम आउटपुट टोकन और कोई डाउनस्ट्रीम पार्सिंग अनुमान नहीं। आसान हिस्से के लिए छोटे / ओपन मॉडल। कॉल के उच्च-आयतन, कम-कठिनाई वाले बहुमत के लिए, एक ओपन या छोटा मॉडल प्रति-कॉल नाटकीय रूप से सस्ता हो सकता है — कभी-कभी लगभग-मुफ़्त अगर आप पहले से सेल्फ-होस्ट करते हैं। फ्लैगशिप मॉडल उन मामलों के लिए रखें जिन्हें सचमुच उसकी ज़रूरत है। Pro tip ये गुणात्मक रूप से जुड़ते हैं: कैश्ड इनपुट × सही-आकार मॉडल × कसा हुआ आउटपुट × बैच डिस्काउंट एक आसान काम पर एक बड़ी कुल कटौती में जुड़ जाते हैं — गुणवत्ता अपरिवर्तित रहते हुए। शब्दावली को सूक्ष्म-अनुकूलित करने से पहले संरचनात्मक लीवर (सही-आकार, कैश, RAG, बैच) खींचें — वे बिल को कहीं अधिक हिलाते हैं। बदलाव को हमेशा असली बिल के विरुद्ध MEASURE करें, अनुमान के नहीं। गहरा प्लेबुक The Token Economy है।

यह वह फ़ैसला है जो असल में आपके AI बजट को हिलाता है। यह एक fixed-vs-marginal-cost क्रॉसओवर है, और आयतन वह चर है जो इसे तय करता है। ओपन / सेल्फ-होस्टेड HIGH, स्थिर आयतन पर जीतता है। एक बार जब आप एक GPU को अधिकांश समय व्यस्त रखने भर की कॉल चला रहे होते हैं, तो प्रति-कॉल लगभग-शून्य सीमांत लागत हमेशा प्रति टोकन भुगतान करने से बेहतर होती है। आप निश्चित हार्डवेयर/किराया लागत को कॉल की एक विशाल संख्या में परिशोधित करते हैं, डेटा गोपनीयता और पूर्ण अनुकूलन पाते हैं — और परिचालन बोझ (प्रोविज़निंग, स्केलिंग, अपटाइम, MLOps) को प्रवेश की कीमत के रूप में स्वीकार करते हैं। API LOW या SPIKY आयतन पर, या बिना infra के जीतता है। अगर ट्रैफ़िक छोटा, फटकीला, या अप्रत्याशित है, तो प्रति टोकन भुगतान का मतलब है कि आप केवल जो इस्तेमाल करते हैं उसी का भुगतान करते हैं और निष्क्रिय होने पर कुछ नहीं — कोई GPU रात 3 बजे गरम बैठा नहीं। आप सारे ops भी छोड़ देते हैं। किसी प्रोडक्ट को शिप करने, प्रोटोटाइप करने, या फटकीले ट्रैफ़िक वाली अधिकांश टीमों के लिए, API दोनों सस्ता और कहीं कम काम है। Watch out सेल्फ-होस्टिंग शायद ही 'मुफ़्त' होती है। मॉडल वेट मुफ़्त हो सकते हैं, पर GPU, बिजली, और इसे चलाते रखने के इंजीनियर-घंटे नहीं — बचत का दावा करने से पहले इन्हें ईमानदारी से गिनें। निष्क्रिय GPU शुद्ध नुकसान हैं: निश्चित-लागत infra प्रति-टोकन प्राइसिंग को तभी हराता है जब उपयोग HIGH हो। कम या फटकीला ट्रैफ़िक हर बार API के पक्ष में है। क्रॉसओवर बिंदु तब हिलता है जब भी API कीमतें गिरती हैं या हार्डवेयर सस्ता होता है — गणित को समय-समय पर फिर से चलाएँ, एक बार तय करके भूल न जाएँ। Check yourself 0/3 Key takeaways तीन आर्किटाइप: per-token API (उपयोग-आधारित, इनपुट बनाम आउटपुट अलग-अलग तय), फ्लैट सब्सक्रिप्शन (पूर्वानुमेय, उच्च आयतन के लिए स्केल नहीं करता), और ओपन/सेल्फ-होस्टेड (निश्चित लागत, प्रति कॉल लगभग-शून्य)। बनाने से पहले अनुमान लगाएँ: (input × input rate) + (output × output rate), per call × volume — फिर कैश और बैच डिस्काउंट लागू करें। सबसे बड़े लीवर: मॉडल को सही-आकार दें, कॉन्टेक्स्ट छाँटें, विशाल कॉन्टेक्स्ट पर RAG, प्रॉम्प्ट कैशिंग, गैर-अत्यावश्यक को बैच करें, आउटपुट छोटा करें। सेल्फ-होस्टिंग HIGH स्थिर आयतन पर जीतती है (निश्चित लागत परिशोधित करें); API LOW/फटकीले आयतन पर या बिना infra के जीतता है (केवल उपयोग का भुगतान)। हर डॉलर आँकड़ा तेज़ी से पुराना पड़ता है — प्रोवाइडर के प्राइसिंग पेज और एक ट्रैकर पर सत्यापित करें, और अपने खुद के आँकड़े Cost Calculator में चलाएँ।
